articles.title: Cultural Representations of Memory in Contemporary Greek Audiovisual Culture: The Synthetic Revival of the Kaisariani Photographs as a Case Study
articles.authors: Nikolaos Aletras
articles.abstract: This article examines how the memory of the past is represented today within Greek audiovisual culture, taking as its case study the algorithmic colouring and animation of a set of rare photographs documenting the execution of two hundred Greek resistance fighters at the Kaisariani rifle range on 1 May 1944. The photographs, taken from the perspective of the perpetrators, were acquired by the Greek state, designated as a cultural monument, and shortly afterwards processed by users through generative artificial intelligence tools and disseminated across YouTube, TikTok, and the online press. Drawing on cultural memory theory, on recent scholarship concerning synthetic pasts, and on empirical evidence regarding the mnemonic effects of AI generated video, the study argues that the AI revival of archival photographs constitutes a new representational practice rather than a technical enhancement. Through a threefold methodology of structural image analysis, platform based performance analysis, and digital reception ethnography, the article demonstrates that the same source archive gives rise to divergent representations conditioned by the affordances of each platform, and that these synthetic representations exert measurable mnemonic and ideological effects on their audiences. The Kaisariani case thereby provides both an empirical demonstration and a methodological template for a wider research programme situated at the intersection of cinema, documentary, digital archives, and generative artificial intelligence.

articles.title: How does the level of media propaganda literacy differ among individuals under 18, between 18 and 30, and over 30 in Uzbekistan, and how does this difference impact their vulnerability to misinformation and critical thinking skills?
articles.authors: Jamshidbek Rasulov
articles.abstract:
This research investigates how varying levels of media propaganda literacy across
different age groups in Uzbekistan impact susceptibility to misinformation and critical
thinking. By categorizing participants into three distinct age groups—those under 18,
between 18 and 30, and over 30—the study identifies generational differences shaped by
historical and technological contexts. Data collected through surveys and interviews reveal
that while younger generations rely more on social media and demonstrate greater
adaptability to digital information, older individuals remain dependent on traditional media
like television, often lacking critical fact-checking skills. Despite a high level of self-reported
understanding of concepts like "propaganda," significant knowledge gaps persist, particularly
among older participants, highlighting the enduring impact of Soviet-era media practices. The
findings underscore the need for targeted media literacy initiatives tailored to age-specific
vulnerabilities to bridge generational divides and empower all citizens to evaluate
information critically

articles.title: An evaluation of the quality of published papers from researchers affiliated with the Australian Institute of Sport
articles.authors: Adrian Barnett; Alexander Gibson; Ran Tian; David N Borg; Paolo Menaspà
articles.abstract: The Australian Institute of Sport (AIS) has a central role in high-performance sport in Australia. An important part of this role is to support research in a range of sports disciplines. Sports science research has had many reproducibility issues; therefore, it is important to consider whether the research supported by the AIS is of high quality. To examine this, we conducted a retrospective audit of published papers to estimate the prevalences of good research practice and identify areas for improvement. We extracted information from papers using automated text extraction and research assistants. We identified 280 papers published between 2020 and 2024 with at least one author who was affiliated with the Australian Institute of Sport. The results showed a low engagement with robust study planning, including pre-registration, analysis plans, and sample size calculations. More encouraging results were that almost all papers had research questions that were well justified and answered. Overall, we found many areas where research quality could be improved by better adherence to established good research practices.

articles_hidden.title: Assessment of facilitators and barriers to open science implementation in the Brain-Heart Interconnectome Research Program: a qualitative study
articles_hidden.authors: Edward Xu; Marc Antonino Albert; Gustavo de Paula Dídimo; Anna Catharina Vieira Armond; David Moher; Emilio I. Alarcón; Ian D Graham; Krystina B. Lewis; Alexandra King; Malcolm King
articles_hidden.abstract: Open science improves research transparency, reproducibility, and equity. This qualitative study assessed facilitators and barriers to implementing open science practices within the Brain-Heart Interconnectome (BHI), an interdisciplinary research program funded by the Canada First Research Excellence Fund (CFREF) to advance prevention and treatment of brain-heart conditions (e.g., stroke and cardiac disease). The study aimed to explore perceptions and behaviours of BHI-funded investigators and teams regarding open science mandate implementation. Data were collected through virtual focus groups with 36 participants from 17 funded projects. Participants include principal investigators, research staff, trainees, and Indigenous Elders and Knowledge Holders. Focus groups were designed and analyzed using the Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF). Barriers included limited financial and logistical resources, intellectual property and ethical concerns, and a lack of guidance and training. Facilitators included mandates from journals and funders, along with perceived improvements in research accountability and quality. Findings were mapped onto the Behaviour Change Wheel (BCW) using the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation – Behaviour (COM-B) model, providing a comprehensive framework for understanding behaviour change and informed implementation strategy development. These insights will be critical to effective and efficient open science uptake within BHI and are likely transferable to other biomedical and interdisciplinary research programs.

articles_hidden.title: Structured-data reporting shapes the apparent causes of phase-3 trial failure: an automated decomposition of ClinicalTrials.gov records
articles_hidden.authors: Tommy Carstensen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective. To decompose the causes of phase-3 failure from ClinicalTrials.gov automatically, to identify where the registry misleads, and to compare the result with the manual study of Hwang et al. (2016).

Methods. Cross-sectional study of registry records: every phase-3 registration with posted results or with status terminated, withdrawn or suspended (18,466 in all). A failure is a trial that stopped early for a reason other than benefit, or that completed and missed its primary endpoint. The primary analysis covers trials that enrolled and started in 2017-2026; registrations withdrawn before enrollment enter a sensitivity analysis only. Primary-endpoint success was read from the structured statistical-analysis records. Termination reasons were classified by large-language-model agents, and a sample of first-pass labels was adjudicated blind by a stronger model. A stratum of 17 large pharmaceutical companies ("big pharma") is compared with Hwang et al., who classified failed drug programs of 1998-2008.

Results. Among trials that enrolled, efficacy (37.1%, 95% CI 34.9 to 39.5) and operational causes (36.5%, 34.3 to 38.8) were the two largest causes of failure. Counting withdrawn registrations as failures put operational causes first (operational 40.2%, efficacy 27.2%). Only 47.3% of completed trials with posted results carried a usable primary p-value; imputing misses for the others that had a comparator arm raised the efficacy share to 46.8% and lowered the operational share to 30.9%. In big pharma, efficacy accounted for 53.7% of failures (program-clustered 95% CI 47.6 to 59.6), not distinguishable from the 56.7% of Hwang et al. (clustered p = 0.46; 95% CI of the difference -11.0 to 5.0 points). The share was 48.3% among trials of drugs with no earlier phase-3 win (difference -17.1 to 0.2 points, unclustered p = 0.057), and 45.8%, lower than theirs, with withdrawn registrations counted (clustered p = 0.0052). Safety accounted for 3.1% of big-pharma failures (2.5% for all sponsors) against 17.2% in Hwang et al. First-pass labels agreed with the adjudication for 83.3% of a balanced sample (95% CI 77.0 to 88.2).

Conclusions. A registry-only decomposition of phase-3 failure depends on whether registrations that never enrolled count as failures and on how completed trials without a usable primary p-value are treated. With the former set aside, efficacy is the leading cause of failure in big pharma; its observed share is not distinguishable from the 2016 manual estimate, a comparison by proxy that does not establish agreement. For all sponsors efficacy is only slightly ahead of operational causes as observed, and further ahead under an imputation or a stricter win rule, each resting on assumptions. Safety is recorded far less often than in the manual estimate; the registry fields cannot show how many safety-driven stops are registered as sponsor or business decisions. The validation was model-based and covered the first classification pass only.

articles_hidden.title: Can grant evaluation still distinguish scientific excellence?
articles_hidden.authors: Martin Bulla; James Wilsdon; Peter Mikula
articles_hidden.abstract: Grant peer review increasingly depends on fine-grained numerical scores to rank many formally excellent proposals. In the era of generative and agentic AI, this architecture may be losing resolution. We analyse score-distribution data from EU Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) Postdoctoral Fellowships and show sharp compression of evaluation scores in the 2025 call. Compared to 2024, there was a 64.6% increase in the volume of applications received, low-scoring proposals became rare, and ~20% of proposals received evaluation scores of ≥95%. The timing is consistent with AI-assisted optimization, but alternative structural explanations remain possible. Nonetheless, the score compression exposes a structural vulnerability of highly standardized evaluation systems: evaluation precision near the top of the scale may be more apparent than real. We thus propose three testable predictions for cross-funder comparison: compression should be strongest in schemes with explicit scoring rubrics, become more visible after broad diffusion of advanced AI drafting and reasoning tools, and intensify as these tools gain capabilities. Data from Human Frontier Science Program (HFSP) Postdoctoral Fellowships and Research Grants, which first screen short Letters of Intent before inviting selected applicants to submit Full Proposals, show broadly similar score distributions across years, with no comparable compression. Systematic cross-funder score tracking is therefore needed to distinguish scheme-specific disruptions from broader temporal shifts and identify designs that preserve evaluative resolution. If compression is becoming more widespread, funders should reconsider whether fine-grained ranking remains an efficient and fair way to select among many excellent proposals.

articles.title: A clinician-informed framework for precision psychotherapy in psychosis
articles.authors: Shenaya Maria Lisboa; Maria Chiara Del Piccolo; Anna Georgiades; Sandra Vieira
articles.abstract: Background. Despite evidence supporting cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis (CBTp), engagement and treatment response remain highly variable, and robust predictors are lacking. Existing research may overlook clinically relevant factors. We aimed to identify candidate predictors of CBTp engagement and outcomes by integrating clinicians’ perspectives with the existing literature. Methods. Twenty clinical psychologists experienced in delivering CBTp participated in semi-structured interviews. Using a mixed-methods design, we first identified candidate predictors through inductive framework analysis of unprompted accounts. Clinicians subsequently rated the perceived importance of these and 32 literature-derived factors on a 10-point scale. Mean ratings and variability were examined to characterise clinician agreement. Findings were integrated into a candidate predictor framework linked to available measurement instruments. Results. Clinicians spontaneously identified 38 factors, of which 16 were absent from the literature-derived list. Frequently identified factors included readiness and motivation (90%), cognitive flexibility (85%), social support (80%), previous experiences of care and therapy (70%), and socioeconomic and environmental stability (70%). Clinicians emphasised therapy-related, contextual, and clinical management factors, including expectations of therapy, substance misuse, and medication, which remain underrepresented in prediction research. Literature-derived factors receiving relatively high importance ratings and agreement included insight, cognitive flexibility, hopelessness, and social functioning. Demographic characteristics were generally considered less important. Conclusion. Clinicians identified factors extending beyond those conventionally investigated as predictors of CBTp engagement and outcomes. The resulting clinician-informed measurement framework provides a broader, clinically grounded candidate predictor set to guide prospective studies and the development of personalised prediction models in psychosis. Keywords: Precision psychotherapy, psychological intervention, CBT, psychosis, schizophrenia

articles.title: Comparing Time- and Event-Contingent Ecological Momentary Assessments of Daily Stressors
articles.authors: Lara Oeltjen; Johannes Andreas Christoph Laferton
articles.abstract: Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) studies offer a unique access to within-person variability processes. Despite their widespread use in psychological research, we know very little about the factors that determine their successful application. This study combines time- and event-contingent assessments to examine the reliability of event-contingent reporting, person-level predictors of compliance, and qualitative differences between assessment methods in a 14-day EMA study of daily stressors. Our results indicate that stress beliefs, personality and mental health are associated with compliance and event-contingent reporting. There was no evidence that event-contingent reports might have been omitted in high-stress situations. On the contrary, event-contingent assessments were generally more extreme in terms of stress-intensity, affect and somatic symptoms. Event-contingent assessments may thus capture a more extreme subset of events and certain types of participants may be particularly likely to self-initiate these assessments. We discuss implications of these findings for the design of future EMA studies.

articles.title: Exploring Secondary School Staff’s Knowledge and Attitudes About Supporting Students Who Self-harm
articles.authors: Yasmin Safiani; Abigail Russell; Rowan Streckfuss Davis
articles.abstract: Background: Self-harm among adolescents is a major public health concern, with secondary school staff playing an important role in its prevention and intervention. However, limited research explores self-harm from a teacher’s perspective. Aim: This cross-sectional survey investigated the relationship between self-harm training status and staff knowledge, attitudes, available support, and perceived barriers/enablers. Methods: An online survey of UK secondary school staff (teaching ages 11–18) collected quantitative and free-text data on training, knowledge, and attitudes. Results: Forty-one participants responded. No statistically significant differences were found between trained and untrained staff, although trained staff showed slightly higher knowledge and more positive attitudes. Qualitative analysis generated three themes: school context and staff capabilities; barriers and enablers, particularly external collaboration; and experiences supporting students who self-harm. Conclusions: Findings highlight the need for universal staff training and improved integration between school and external support systems; however, small sample size limits generalisability. Further research should evaluate training effectiveness.

articles.title: White matter differences in adults with developmental language disorder
articles.authors: Noelle Abbott; Sophia Banel; Gabriel J Cler
articles.abstract: Developmental language disorder is a highly common yet underdiagnosed neurodevelopmental disorder which impacts receptive and/or expressive language abilities and cannot be attributed to another etiology such as hearing loss or a lack of early exposure to language. There is very little research into the brain differences that characterize developmental language disorder, especially in adult populations In this study, we used diffusion MRI to determine whether adults with DLD show differences in white matter microstructure of the brain when compared to adults with typical language. Participants included 23 adults identified as meeting criteria for developmental language disorder, as well as a group of 26 adults with typical language. White matter microstructure was examined with fractional anisotropy via diffusion tensor imaging and precise biophysical models of intra-axonal signal fraction and orientation coherence via the Standard Model of diffusion imaging, using tractometry to evaluate microstructure differences along white matter tracts. Analysis showed reduced myelin integrity in DLD in the corpus callosum, but increased myelin integrity in the left superior longitudinal fasciculus. It is yet unclear whether differences exist in childhood and are retained into adulthood, are a result of different language environments during childhood, or are a result of behavioral and neural compensation.

articles.title: Selective maintenance of aversive memories as a mechanism of spontaneous recovery of fear
articles.authors: Isabel Berwian; Yongjing Ren; Sashank Pisupti; Jialing Ding; Seohyun Moon; Jamie C. Chiu; Deepta Chandrasekhar; Yael Niv
articles.abstract:
Return of fear after exposure poses a significant challenge for treatment of anxiety dis-
orders. In this study, we used computational modeling to test competing mechanisms
underlying spontaneous recovery of fear over time. We fit computational models of a
novel theory of spontaneous recovery—selective maintenance of aversive memories—
to behavior from a fear conditioning and extinction task (N=316), and showed that they
uniquely captured spontaneous recovery and quantitatively outperformed alternative
models embodying theories from the literature. The results were supported across mul-
tiple datasets, including a preregistered replication (N=355) and a sample with mental
health symptoms (N=520). The selective maintenance modeling framework addition-
ally offers mechanistic insights into overgeneralization and the development of anxi-
ety. Indeed, in the symptomatic sample we found that symptoms of generalized anxiety
disorder correlated with estimates of overgeneralization in the model. Through simu-
lations, we further demonstrated that insights from our model can explain how targeted
interventions such as retrieval cues and cognitive interventions can prevent the return
of fear. These results highlight selective maintenance of aversive events in memory as
a critical and testable target for improving anxiety treatments and preventing relapse.

articles.title: Social Media Usage Profiles: A Multidimensional Approach Using Cluster Analysis
articles.authors: Myriam; Elena Bernabéu; Carlos Marchena Girárldez
articles.abstract: The heterogeneity of problematic social media use (PSMU) has led to the study of differentiated user profiles, although most research is based on correlational designs rather than multidimensional approaches. The integrated examination of compulsivity, emotional regulation, psychological distress, and usage patterns stays limited. The present study aimed to identify empirical clusters of young people based on psychological, emotional, and behavioural variables related to social media use, and to compare their characteristics to better understand the heterogeneity of the phenomenon. A total of 530 young people participated (67.5% women; M = 19.70 years), completing measures of problematic use, emotional distress, digital compulsivity, emotional regulation, and time spent using social media. Hierarchical and k-means cluster analyses (k=3) were conducted, complemented by ANOVA and post hoc tests. Validity and discriminative capacity indicators (R²) were calculated. Three profiles were identified: a profile characterised by compulsive use (PCU), defined by the highest levels of consumption and compulsivity; a profile characterised by the highest levels of emotional distress despite moderate levels of consumption, termed the pattern associated with psychological distress (PAD); and a functional profile (FP), distinguished by low consumption, fewer symptoms and better emotional regulation. The most discriminative variables were problematic use (R² = .66) and compulsivity (R² = .49), whereas emotional regulation appears to act as a possible protective factor. These profiles may help to guide more precise preventive interventions.

articles.title: “I’m Asking This Price Because…”: When Negotiation Rationales  Win Concessions but Cost the Relationship
articles.authors: Hannes M. Petrowsky; Yannik A. Escher; Alice Lee; Daniel Robert Ames; David D. Loschelder
articles.abstract: Negotiators often face a tension between claiming value and preserving the relationship with their counterpart. Rationales, the explanations negotiators attach to their offers (“I’m asking this price because…”), are assumed to ease this tension by making an assertive offer more persuasive and acceptable. The evidence is limited, however. Prior work examined a few rationales in isolation, with mixed results, and has not asked, across the rationales negotiators use, whether those that win concessions are the same ones that preserve relationships. We integrate various types of rationales in an overarching taxonomy and propose that a rationale conveys two kinds of information at once—about the negotiation (e.g., limits) and about the negotiator (e.g., motives). This information can move economic and relational outcomes in opposite directions. Across six studies (Ntotal=2,833), we identify six types of rationales negotiators commonly use (Studies 1a–c) and then test, in three preregistered experiments, how sellers’ rationales affect buyers’ counteroffers (Study 2), their impressions of the seller (Study 3), and why (Study 4). The most common rationale, sellers praising the product, neither helped nor hurt. Rationales citing financial constraints or appealing to sympathy won larger concessions but damaged the relationship with the counterpart. Only rationales citing market constraints appeared to avoid this trade-off. Mediation analyses indicated that economic benefits operated via limit perceptions and sympathy, whereas relational costs operated via perceived manipulativeness and disliking. Our results suggest that rationales work best when they inform counterparts about the negotiator’s situation without inviting negative inferences about the negotiator’s motives.

articles.title: Beyond the Big Five: Disintegration as a Predictor of Daily Depression, Anxiety, and Rumination
articles.authors: Ljiljana B. Lazarevic; Maja Ribar; Josip Razum; Goran Milas
articles.abstract: The Big Five personality traits, particularly Negative Emotionality, are well-established correlates of internalizing symptoms. However, less is known about whether Disintegration, a proposed basic personality trait reflecting proneness to psychotic-like experiences and beliefs, accounts for additional individual differences in internalizing experiences in everyday life. The present study examined the incremental contribution of Disintegration beyond the Big Five to daily depression, anxiety, and rumination. A sample of 156 psychology students completed measures of Disintegration and the Big Five, followed by seven days of daily diary assessments (916 observations). Multilevel models were used to examine associations between personality traits and daily internalizing experiences. When all six personality traits were considered simultaneously, Disintegration was uniquely associated with higher daily depression (β = .25), anxiety (β = .24), and rumination (β = .17), alongside Negative Emotionality. Adding Disintegration to the Big Five increased explained variance by 10.25% for depression, 7.79% for anxiety, and 2.69% for rumination. Sensitivity analyses excluding potentially overlapping symptom-related content supported the robustness of the associations with depression and anxiety. These findings suggest that Disintegration contributes to explaining between-person differences in everyday internalizing experiences beyond established personality dimensions, extending evidence for its incremental validity to repeated daily assessments.

articles.title: When Better Treatment Is Not Enough: Relearning Expectations of Harm at Work
articles.authors: Robin Umbra
articles.abstract: Better treatment can ease an employee’s anger without changing what they expect from the next encounter. When, then, does a new workplace encounter revise a learned expectation of harm? A theory of expectancy updating grounded in cue-appraisal learning explains why positive experiences can leave anticipated mistreatment intact, establish a narrow exception, or support broader change. Confirming encounters can strengthen expected harm and consolidate confidence even as immediate emotion subsides. Favorable encounters support revision when they provide credible evidence about the anticipated consequence and the conditions that made it likely. Safety attributed to exceptional monitoring can be learned as an exception; protection that extends across ordinary conditions offers grounds for broader revision. Harm expectancies can also spread to similar workplace cues and to actors judged responsible for producing or enabling harm. Credible differences in consequences, authority, or responsibility can limit that spread. Earlier and corrective expectations may nevertheless coexist, allowing anticipated harm to return with changes in context or the passage of time. Such return must be distinguished from responses to renewed mistreatment or withdrawn safeguards. Six propositions connect these processes with differentiated emotion and choices among protective distancing, accountability-oriented engagement, and punishment. The central prediction is that equally favorable encounters can produce unequal revision: the corrective value of better treatment depends on what it reveals about the harm employees expect to face again.

articles.title: Unresolved snack desire and subsequent snacking in daily life
articles.authors: Giuseppe Marrazzo; Trung Dung Tran; Leonardo Pimpini
articles.abstract: Snacking on calorie-dense foods is often assumed to follow from craving, yet in daily life craving and snacking are only loosely coupled. In an exploratory secondary analysis of a preregistered 21-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA) study of 136 young women with healthy-range BMI (3, 6, or 9 prompts/day), we examined whether snack desire reported without snacking was associated with consumption in the subsequent reporting interval. Because these EMA items referred to the period since the previous prompt, desire and snacking reported within the same window could not be temporally ordered. Across 8,492 eligible adjacent-window pairs, snack desire without snacking was associated with higher odds of snacking in the subsequent interval (within-person OR = 1.71, 95% CI [1.48, 1.97]). Participant-balanced model-standardized probabilities were 42.1% following desire-present intervals and 30.7% following desire-absent intervals, an adjusted difference of 11.4 percentage points (95% CI [8.2, 14.6]). The association remained positive in participant-day fixed-effects analyses (+12.66 percentage points, 95% CI [9.13, 16.20]) and exceeded expectations from a constrained surrogate distribution (observed unadjusted difference = 16.44 versus surrogate mean = 9.59 percentage points; empirical p = .0002). A complementary exploratory matched comparison showed that desire was modestly more frequent before snack than matched non-snack windows (+4.47 percentage points, uncorrected p = .019). Additional matched comparisons of the intervals surrounding snacking showed pronounced elevations in desire and low perceived control during snack-reporting windows, whereas stress showed a smaller difference. These findings identify snack desire reported without consumption as a prospective correlate of subsequent snacking, without establishing causality. More generally, they demonstrate why it is important to distinguish events reported in successive EMA intervals from events reported within the same interval.

articles.title: Developmental Language Disorder and Mental Health Related GP Visits: Evidence from Health Records in England
articles.authors: Megan Frith; Hannah Hobson; Melisa Parlak; Umar Toseeb
articles.abstract:
Introduction/Objectives. Developmental Language Disorder (DLD) is a childhood-onset neurodevelopmental condition. It is associated with elevated levels of psychopathology. There is no scholarship on the help-seeking behaviour amongst children and young people (CYP) with DLD from their General Practitioner (GP). We examined the relationship between psychopathology, mental health-related GP visits, and DLD. Methods. We analysed existing data from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC) with linked GP records up to the age of 25 years (maximum n=5,524; 51% female, 9% DLD). We fitted mixed-effects and logistic regression models to the data. Results. CYP with DLD had higher odds of visiting their GP for mental health needs than peers without DLD (OR 1.54, 95% CI 1.21-1.94) even after accounting for their levels of mental health need (adjusted OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.08-1.75). Among CYP with DLD, being identified as having special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) was associated with higher odds of mental health related GP contact (OR 2.10, 95% CI 1.29-3.40).
Conclusions. CYP with DLD are more likely to visit their GP for mental health needs. Those whose SEND is recognised in school are more likely to visit their GP for mental health needs. Increased awareness and recognition of DLD in educational settings may facilitate access to mental health care for CYP with DLD. GPs are likely to have a central role in supporting the mental health of CYP with DLD and thus need suitable support and resources to do so.

articles.title: A Network Perspective on Cyberbullying: Examining School Social Environment and Bullying Behaviors
articles.authors: Gabriel Baník; Mária Dědová; Kristína Dědová; Veronika Mihalikova
articles.abstract: This study examined the complexity of cyberbullying and its relationship with traditional bullying, school climate, and social support using network analysis. The sample consisted of 1,269 participants (359 boys), including 770 emerging adults and 499 teens, with a mean age of 18 (SD = 2.5). We measured 11 forms of cyberbullying across different roles (victim, aggressor, defender, bystander), five factors of school climate, social support (from parents, friends, teachers), and traditional bullying roles. Undirected weighted network models revealed strong interconnections between various types of aggressive behaviors and cyberbullying victimization. Unauthorized sharing of personal media showed negative relationships with online verbal attacks, while online group exclusion strongly associated with social isolation. The bystander role positively related to both verbal aggression and victimization. Defenders in cyberbullying were more likely to be victims of personal information exposure and verbal attacks, and strongly associated with defending in traditional bullying. School climate and social support demonstrated weak connections to cyberbullying, with student-student relationships, fairness in school, and parental support showing the most direct interconnections. Network comparisons revealed subtle structural differences between genders and between teens and emerging adults. Findings suggest prevention programs should focus on strengthening school relationships while supporting student defenders who may become targets themselves.

articles.title: Dissociating Accuracy and Metacognition in Nutritional Judgements
articles.authors: Kelly Hoogervorst; Francesco Bavato; Ashley Tyrer; Micah G. Allen
articles.abstract: The gap between nutritional knowledge and dietary behaviour remains poorly understood, yet may partly reflect systematic biases in how individuals evaluate food and assess their own nutritional judgements. Here, we introduce the MetaBites task, a novel two-alternative forced-choice paradigm in which 32 healthy volunteers compared foods on either caloric density or nutritional quality, quantified using the Nutrient-Rich Foods (NRF) 9.3 index, under adaptive difficulty control. Participants provided both trial-level and block-level confidence ratings, enabling assessment of metacognitive monitoring across multiple levels. Task validity was confirmed through staircase convergence, a clear speed-accuracy trade-off, and higher confidence in correct relative to incorrect trials. Results revealed a consistent dissociation across conditions: participants showed higher objective performance when judging nutritional quality, yet reported significantly higher confidence and greater metacognitive efficiency for calorie judgements. Global confidence decreased significantly in the NRF condition but remained stable for calorie judgements. Furthermore, familiarity with food items biased choice behaviour in opposing directions across conditions, consistent with a tendency to perceive familiar foods as more nutritious and less calorie-dense. These findings indicate that metacognitive monitoring in nutritional judgements is not a straightforward readout of objective performance, and that domain familiarity modulates choice behaviour. The MetaBites task offers a promising tool for investigating metacognitive contributions to nutritional decision-making in both healthy and clinical populations.

articles.title: Making AI-mediated decisions culturally repairable
articles.authors: Hadi Mohamadpour; Soomaahey Heysieattalab; Jean-Claude Dreher
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly influences high-stakes decisions, from employment and education to healthcare and public services. When such judgments are disputed, affected people may receive an explanation without being able to reach an authority empowered to change the outcome or remedy its consequences. We introduce cultural repairability: the institutional capacity to review an AI-mediated decision, correct the outcome and downstream records, provide meaningful restoration, and learn from failure through procedures people can understand and use. The framework addresses a visibility–accountability asymmetry: people are exposed to judgments about their standing but lack effective means of obtaining an answer or remedy. Culture matters because exposure, legitimate authority, and appropriate restoration may be understood differently across settings. Language accessibility also determines whether review mechanisms are usable in practice. We identify three measurable cultural mechanisms: the meaning of exposure, the credibility of review, and the meaning of restoration. We further distinguish affected people’s appraisals from institutional actors’ responsibility and capacity to respond. Four falsifiable propositions specify how reviewer authority and audience shape responses to repair, and how these effects vary with cultural orientation, institutional history, and the form of restoration. They predict whether people appeal or withdraw, how they recalibrate trust, and whether they remain willing to engage. The resulting Repairability Principle establishes a common floor of substantive review, correction, restoration, and prevention of recurrence, while allowing people to choose how restoration is delivered. Cultural repairability therefore shifts global AI accountability from whether procedures appear acceptable to whether institutions can correct harm in practice.

articles.title: People Don't Have to Be Native to Hear Size: Evidence From Voiced Obstruent Perception in L2 Learners of Japanese
articles.authors: Rean Du; Marco Aurelio Silva Fonseca
articles.abstract:
Voiced obstruents are sounds that are produced with complete closure of the vocal tract and vibration of vocal folds (e.g., /b/, /d/, /g/, /z/). They have been shown to be associated with largeness by native Japanese speakers using Pok\'emon-style nonce names, but whether this sensitivity extends to second-language (L2) learners remains unclear. Twenty-five L2 learners of Japanese rated 30 nonce names with fixed mora counts, containing zero, one, or two voiced obstruents, for perceived height and perceived weight on a sliding scale. Ratings increased with each additional voiced obstruent for both height and weight, and the same pattern was reported for native speakers. This sensitivity did not differ by Japanese proficiency or between English-Japanese bilingual and
multilingual learners.

articles.title: Disentangling Ethnicity from Nationality: Equivalence and Correlates of the CES-D Among Asian American, Asian National, and Euro American College Students
articles.authors: Takakuni Suzuki; Catelyn Kalm; Zachary Willett; P. Priscilla Lui
articles.abstract: The Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale (CES-D) is one of the most researched, freely available self-report measures of depression designed to be used in large-scale research. Although the four-factor structure originally identified by Radloff (1977) is well-replicated with Euro Americans, in whom it was developed, evidence suggests that the latent factor structure of the CES-D varies by demographic backgrounds. Thus, reliance on the original CES-D factor structure could mischaracterize depressive symptoms in non-Euro American individuals. Further, past studies have not clearly differentiated the roles of ethnic heritage and socializing culture in equivalence of the CES-D structure across groups. Specifically, both Asian American and Asian national (international) students would be categorized as “Asian” group in the United States but their socializing background and cultural experiences differ. This study investigated the CES-D factor structure and correlates in three ethnoculturally different samples to test for the effects of socializing culture and racial/ethnic differences using measurement invariance (MI) and nomological network analyses. Data were collected from 144 Asian American, 127 Euro American, and 168 Asian national college students. Asian American and Euro American students share a mainstream socializing culture while Asian American and Asian national students share racial/ethnic heritage. Euro American and Asian national students do not share either. MI analyses suggest that Radloff’s four-factor structure met strict invariance between Asian American and Euro American students. The four-factor structure was not identified in the Asian national group. Removing the Interpersonal Problems factor and Item 7 resulted in achieving up to scalar invariance across the three groups. Further, the external correlates of the modified CES-D factor scores indicated similar nomological network of cultural experiences of depressive symptoms in Asian American and Euro American students, as well as Asian American and Asian national students. However, Euro American and Asian national students did not share as much. These findings suggest socialization background to be a source variance underlying factor-structures of depression, and association of depressive symptoms and cultural experiences are affected by both. This study highlights the need to consider contextual information to fully understand how depression may manifest differently across individuals.

articles.title: Toward scalable identification of adults with developmental language disorder: Validation, participant profiles, and recruitment considerations for an online screener
articles.authors: Iris Mendoza Luna; Noelle Abbott; Gabriel J Cler
articles.abstract:
Purpose: This study evaluated the feasibility of an online adaptation of the Fidler diagnostic protocol for identifying developmental language disorder (DLD) in adults. Specifically, we examined (1) comparability of computerized versus face-to-face administration, (2) test-retest reliability, (3) agreement between two- and three-task scoring equations, (4) effects of demographic and cognitive factors on scores, and (5) the relationship between self-reported diagnoses and screener performance.
Method: Over 5,000 adults completed a language and medical history survey, and 526 subsequently completed an assessment over videoconference involving following auditory directions, spelling irregular words, and defining words (modified from Fidler et al, 2011). A subset (N = 53; 25 DLD, 28 with typical language development) then completed an in-person session comparing face-to-face and computerized administration of the following directions task, along with nonverbal IQ testing. Participants were recruited between 2022 and 2025 via online postings and flyers.
Results: No significant effect of administration modality on following directions task performance or Fidler scores was observed. Test-retest reliability was high (r = .91). Scores derived from the two- and three-task weighted equations from Fidler et al (2011) were highly correlated (r = .98), though the three-task equation produced lower (i.e., more typical) scores for participants with DLD-range profiles. Age, gender, and early bilingualism did not significantly influence scores. Although several self-reported diagnoses and concerns were higher among the group identified as DLD than the TD group, overall discriminative accuracy of self-report screening items was low (AUC range: 0.45–0.65).
Conclusions: Online administration of the Fidler protocol is comparable to the original face-to-face version and demonstrates adequate test-retest reliability, supporting its use as a scalable tool for identifying adults with DLD. Practical recommendations for recruiting and screening adults with DLD are discussed to facilitate future research with this population.

articles.title: A mode-coupling theory of phonological organization
articles.authors: Sam Tilsen
articles.abstract: Phonological theories provide macroscopic descriptions of order in speech, but have not given much attention to how those descriptions might be derived from the relatively microscopic dynamics of the nervous system. This paper proposes a microscopically inspired theory of phonological organization in which the systems that govern articulatory actions (gesturals) are composed of internal subsystems (gestural excitations). In the preparation of speech, gestural excitations can transiently couple (phase- and frequency-lock) to a generic set of oscillatory coordination modes. In the execution of speech, a feedback-regulated competitive selection process gives coordination modes heightened activation, causing coupled gestural excitations to exert strong influences on control of the vocal tract. Phonological organization in speech preparation is conceptualized as a stochastic process in which gestural excitations couple to coordination modes, governed by probabilities derived from hypothesized constraints. The framework is used to interpret segmental, moraic, syllabic, metrical, and prosodic word-related patterns.

articles.title: Lexical features reveal distinct developmental patterns in valence and arousal
articles.authors: Serena Maria Stagnitto; Serena Lecce; José Antonio Hinojosa; Daniele Gatti
articles.abstract: Affective word meanings are often treated as stable lexical properties, although their organization may change across development. Using representational content analysis, we examined how semantic and form-based lexical information predicts valence and arousal judgments from childhood to adulthood. Across two experiments, Spanish affective ratings from children aged 7, 9, 11, and 13 years were modeled within and across age groups and compared with adult judgments. Semantic representations were the strongest predictors of both dimensions, but valence and arousal showed distinct developmental patterns. Valence remained comparatively stable across childhood and showed strong correspondence with adult judgments already at age 7. Arousal, despite being systematically predictable within each child group, showed weaker cross-age generalization, with semantic transfer declining as developmental distance increased. Moreover, semantic information predicted word-specific age differences more accurately for arousal than for valence. Child-adult correspondence in arousal shifted from negative at age 7 to positive at ages 11 and 13, suggesting increasing similarity in lexical-affective mappings across development. These findings indicate that developmental variation in arousal does not reflect an absence of systematic organization in younger children but rather age-related differences in how lexical meaning relates to activation. Overall, affective lexical development combines a relatively stable evaluative structure with a more flexible organization of arousal.

articles.title: Quality of Life and the Case for Consent-Based Psilocybin Access – Questions on the Regulatory Framework and Cost
articles.authors: Janis Ancans
articles.abstract: Legal access to psilocybin almost always requires a medical diagnosis first, usually treatment-resistant depression (TRD) or severe PTSD, as though informed consent alone was not sufficient. This article makes two connected arguments. Extending the autonomy argument already accepted for terminally ill patients, competent adults who understand the potential benefits and risks of a psilocybin experience should be able to choose it for reasons of psychological wellness or existential anxiety relief, not only because a clinician has certified a qualifying illness, a right the legal literature calls “cognitive liberty”. Just as important, the cost of access is not fixed; it reflects the regulatory framework under which psilocybin is provided. No jurisdiction has yet completed medicines authorisation pathway; the furthest-advanced clinical programme, Compass Pathways' COMP360, met its Phase 3 primary endpoint and reported six-month durability data for TRD by July 2026, and its developer has since signalled an annual cost close to that of esketamine nasal spray, USD 50,000–65,000, or roughly USD 17,000–22,000 per dose. Meanwhile, Australia's narrower authorised-prescriber legal route for TRD, using GMP-manufactured but unregistered psilocybin, already costs AUD $20,000 per course. Three distinct non-medical routes cost far less. Truffles in the Netherlands, sold under food law with no diagnosis and no supervision required, and Colorado and Oregon's state-licensed psilocybin services, which require no diagnosis but do involve a supervising facilitator, cost up to $3,000 per session. Removing the diagnosis requirement while leaving this cost structure untouched risks replacing the regulatory barrier with the wealth-based one, unless expanded access is paired with public subsidy. Article also briefly reviews the safety evidence, the political origins of psilocybin's scheduling, and the double standard in how its risks are treated. A Canadian case illustrates the institutional and regulatory framework dysfunction, a dying man denied psilocybin for existential relief while approved for medical assistance in dying within weeks, before the article closes with policy recommendations addressing both access and funding.

articles.title: Biased Motive Inferences of Online Outrage Undermine Cross-Partisan Conversations
articles.authors: Chen-Wei Yu; William J. Brady
articles.abstract: Moral outrage spreads widely in online political discourse, but how do people understand others’ outrage expressions? Across three studies (N = 1,855), including behavioral experiments and a field study, we discovered that partisan-biased motive inferences underlie the divergent effects of online outrage expression: While people typically inferred that their in-partisans’ motives for expressing outrage were to raise awareness or inspire action, they tended to infer their political opponents’ motives were to shame or troll. These motive inferences were linked to greater political sectarianism and lower willingness to have a conversation about politics with the outrage expressor. In a fourth study (N = 720), we developed an intervention that changed people’s motive inferences, which improved willingness to have a conversation about politics. These findings highlight the role of motive inferences in shaping contemporary online political discourse filled with strong emotions, and suggest key levers to foster civil interactions among cross-partisans.

articles.title: Impacts of voice pleasantness and familiarity on enjoyment and engagement with spoken narratives
articles.authors: Carolyn McGettigan; Hannah Jones; Victor Rosi; Emma Soopramanien; Amrita Bains; Saloni Krishnan
articles.abstract: Recent experimental reading research has found that situational enjoyment of texts plays an important role in predicting both comprehension and motivation to continue reading. Here, we used narrative listening to test whether these findings generalise to spoken narratives, and to further investigate how different aspects of the narrator’s voice affect the experience and outcomes of listening. In Experiment 1, participants heard spoken book excerpts produced by a highly-naturalistic synthesised voice. After each excerpt, participants rated their enjoyment of the excerpt, answered a multiple-choice content comprehension question, and finally chose whether to wait to hear more of the narrative (or skip to the next one; a measure of motivation). Replicating the findings from reading research, we found that greater enjoyment was associated with increased probability of both correct comprehension and waiting. In Experiment 2, participants heard the same book excerpts, now narrated by 2 different synthesised voices that significantly differed in perceived pleasantness. Here, we found higher enjoyment for excerpts read by the more pleasant-sounding voice, but no effects of pleasantness on comprehension or waiting. In Experiment 3, we harnessed personalised voice cloning to show that both enjoyment and waiting were increased when listening to personally-familiar narrators (self, friend), compared with unfamiliar narrators. Our findings offer mechanistic evidence for the rewarding role of voice identity perception in spoken language processing, and present interesting implications for how personalised narrators could improve engagement with spoken book language.

articles.title: The effect of unconventional gender role advertisements (femvertising) on female purchase intentions and brand attitude: attitudes towards motherhood and culture: Korea vs. UK
articles.authors: Erin Lim; Adrian Furnham; Alastair McClelland
articles.abstract: This study examined the impact of culture and attitudes towards motherhood (ATM) on the effectiveness of traditional/non-traditional gendered advertisements. Korean and British participants viewed either traditional or non-traditional female portrayals in adverts and rated them for purchase intention and brand attitude. They also completed the Attitudes towards Fertility and Childbearing Scale (AFCS) containing three subscales: Fertility, Hindrance, and Social Identity. The results showed that there was a significant difference between cultures on ATM with more negative attitudes in Korean participants. However, there was no interaction effect between culture and advert type on advertising effectiveness, but main effects of culture and advert type were found. Favourable attitudes towards motherhood significantly positively correlated with the effectiveness of traditional adverts, but not non-traditional adverts except for Hindrance with PI.

articles.title: When Different Relational Experiences with AI Become Visible in Conversation: Linguistic and Dyadic Evidence from Naturalistic ChatGPT Interactions
articles.authors: Nadine Nicole Schmitt; Lennart Seizer; Fanny Alexandra Dietel; Lea Grimm-Keßler; Björn Schuller; Johanna Schuller
articles.abstract: People may experience large language models (LLMs) as therapeutically allied, emotionally close, or socially substitutive, but whether these relationships become visible in conversations is unknown. We distinguished what users discussed, what unfolded relationally, and how they experienced the AI relationship. We linked self-reports from 94 adults to donated, personally meaningful ChatGPT conversations using 21 outcome-blind frozen topics, blinded triple annotation of 500 sequences, and participant-grouped machine learning frozen before outcome access. Digital Therapeutic Alliance (DTA) and AI Attachment were related but showed different conversational correlates. Validation (R²_CV = .423) and uptake (R²_CV = .260) were recoverable out of sample, yet, neither formed a generalizable DTA signature. Conversely, a post-registration multivariate analysis identified a distributed Social Substitution fingerprint beyond conversation length and 21 topics (ΔR²_CV = .070) and improved prediction in 98% of repetitions. Ruptures were rare and consistently repaired; their association with DTA was fragile. Thus, different human–LLM relationships leave different—and sometimes no readily observable—conversational traces.

articles.title: Adolescents’ Economic Circumstances and their Mental Health: Identifying Candidate Causal Mechanisms through Review and Expert Consultation
articles.authors: Thomas Steare; Kelly Rose-Clarke; Sara Evans-Lacko; Gemma Lewis; Praveetha Patalay
articles.abstract: Living in poorer economic circumstances is routinely associated with poorer mental health throughout the life course. In adolescents, explanatory theories have almost exclusively focused on the role that economic circumstances have on parenting behaviors, and the resources families can provide for their children, which in turn influence adolescents’ mental health outcomes. Through a systematic search of mediation studies and expert consultation we propose candidate causal mechanisms through which economic circumstances might impact adolescents’ internalizing mental health outcomes such as anxiety and depression. Most of the candidate causal mechanisms we identified have not been considered in adolescent-specific theories of health inequalities to date and many have not been empirically investigated within mediation studies, indicating clear limits in current awareness of the processes through which economic circumstances affect adolescents’ mental health. We propose a conceptual model that highlights how economic circumstances may shape environmental and material factors, which we theorize in turn influences an interconnected set of behavioral, biological, psychological and social mechanisms linked to mental health outcomes.

articles.title: The Associations between Social Network Size and Preschool Children’s Visual Perspective-Taking and Non-Verbal Cue Understanding
articles.authors: Esmee Miron Aalders; Stephanie Wermelinger; Moritz M. Daum
articles.abstract:
Exposure to diverse communicative environments fosters a broader, more flexible
repertoire of communicative behaviour. Children’s social networks may constitute a
meaningful, yet underexplored, factor contributing to environmental diversity. In a
cross-sectional study, we examined whether social network size in preschool children
(N = 128, Mage = 4.06, SDage = 0.29) is associated with their communicative behaviour
indicated via three aspects: visual perspective-taking, non-verbal cue understanding,
and theory of mind (ToM). We ran two different types of analysis: first, the
conventional weekly contact threshold to operationalise social network size. This
analysis revealed no significant associations with the outcome variables. Second, we
conducted a data-driven grid search to identify the contact frequency threshold that
best predicted each outcome. The results suggest distinct candidate thresholds across
the three communicative behaviours assessed, indicating that each behaviour is
associated with a different relevant level of contact frequency. Visual perspective-taking
was positively associated with social network size calculated using a threshold of
approximately monthly contact. For non-verbal cue understanding, the best-fitting
threshold was about four interactions per week, at which social network size was
negatively associated with task performance. We found no significant associations
between social network size and children’s ToM. The findings show associations between
children’s social networks and pragmatic communication behaviour, but these
associations are sensitive to how social network size is operationalised.

articles.title: Early intervention for young children with motor learning impairments: the approach and processes of Dame Vera Lynn Children’s Charity
articles.authors: George Horne; Antonina Pereira; Glenys Creese; Benjamin T Sharpe
articles.abstract: Early intervention is widely viewed as important to improve functional outcomes in children with motor learning impairments. According to existing recommendations, early intervention should be holistic and target different areas of development such as sensorimotor, attention, and communication skills. Currently though, no guidelines or examples describe how to do this. This study presents Dame Vera Lynn Children’s Charity’s early intervention services as an example. Produced as part of a critical realist ethnography, this article outlines how the charity integrates allied health and educational approaches to support children and their families. Our reflexive thematic analysis then identifies processes of family-led, collaborative, and flexible support that underly DVLCC service provision, and principles of care and pragmatism that underly these processes. This ethnography adds context to the charity’s preliminary positive research results and provides an example model of UK-based early intervention for future development and critical engagement.

articles.title: Aging and Hearing Loss in Emotional Prosody Processing: Divergent Neural Adaptation and Behavioral Performance
articles.authors: Yi Lin; Yangfan Lu; Hongwei Ding; Yang Zhang
articles.abstract: Emotional prosody perception is vulnerable in later adulthood, yet the contributions of central aging and peripheral hearing loss remain unclear. Across two experiments, we combined event-related potentials (ERPs) , time-frequency analyses and behavioral measures to examine how aging and hearing sensitvity shape emotional prosody processing. Experiment 1 used acoustically matched speech and nonspeech stimuli in a passive oddball paradigm to assess preattentive processing. Experiment 2 examined explicit emotion identification and implicit stimulus judgment to evaluate goal-directed performance and its associations with neural responses. Aging was associated with reduced neural differentiation between emotions and lower behavioral efficiency, alongside enhanced P3a amplitude. Older adults also responded more slowly than younger adults during emotion identification. Hearing sensitivity showed no significant main effect on accuracy or reaction time, despite associations with delayed early neural processing and stronger theta- and alpha-band activity. Hearing-related neural effects were most evident in older adults and varied across emotions and stimulus types. Brain–behavior associations were selective: reduced mismatch negativity (MMN) was associated with slower responses during stimulus identification, whereas longer MMN latencies were associated with lower accuracy and slower responses during emotion identification. These findings indicate that aging and hearing loss have distinct yet interacting associations with emotional prosody processing, with neural responses not necessarily corresponding to behavioral performance. We propose an “asymmetric adaptation” account in which neural responses to degraded auditory input reorganize selectively across processing stages and contexts, potentially explaining this neural-behavioral divergence and informing more sensitive assessment of socioemotional communication in later adulthood.

articles.title: Effects of a Web-Based Debiasing Intervention on Brazilian Psychologists’ Accuracy on Major Depressive Disorder Diagnostic Tasks: A Randomized Training Intervention
articles.authors: Kalil Maihub Manara; Eric A. Youngstrom; Joshua A Langfus; Clarissa Marceli Trentini
articles.abstract: This randomized experimental study evaluated a web-based debiasing intervention designed to improve clinical judgment in the assessment of adult major depressive disorder (MDD) in Brazil. The intervention, adapted from prior work on pediatric bipolar disorder, taught Bayesian probability estimates and other debiasing strategies. Brazilian psychologists (N = 535) were assigned to either the intervention or an active control condition featuring a brief educational video, and were assessed post-intervention (n = 299). Outcomes were decision-making errors and diagnostic accuracy in response to vignettes, which depicted diagnostic challenges that could elicit cognitive biases. Assignment to intervention was associated with significantly fewer decision-making errors and greater diagnostic accuracy. Intervention effects were stronger for the vignette involving diagnostic risk estimation, as supported by intervention-by-vignette interaction effects. Intervention effects across vignettes were not statistically significant when only categorical diagnostic tasks were considered. Years of clinical practice and postgraduate training were largely unrelated to outcomes, and decision-making errors were not associated with treatment decisions. Overall, findings provide preliminary evidence of the transferability of this brief, web-based debiasing intervention to a distinct clinical and cultural context, although effect sizes were substantially attenuated compared with those observed in the original intervention.

articles.title: Polarity and the speed of scalar implicature processing
articles.authors: Michael Vrazitulis; J E Loy; Vera Demberg
articles.abstract: Scalar implicatures (SIs) such as the inference from 'some' to 'some but not all' are known to vary in processing cost. According to the Polarity Hypothesis (van Tiel et al., 2019; van Tiel & Pankratz, 2021), this cost depends on the polarity of the scalar term: SIs from positively polar expressions (e.g., 'some' implicating 'some but not all') are expected to be slower to compute than literal interpretations, while the reverse should hold for SIs from negatively polar expressions, sometimes referred to as indirect SIs (e.g., 'not all' implicating 'not all but some'). We tested this prediction in a sentence–picture verification experiment with 538 English-speaking participants. Each participant judged whether sentences containing weak or strong scalar terms matched a corresponding picture, allowing us to measure response times as an index of processing effort. Our results showed no clear evidence for the Polarity Hypothesis effect. Specifically, we found that the effect strongly varies across the different scales included in our experiment. We additionally conducted a meta-analysis pooling our estimate with all existing evidence so far: the pooled effect is small and in the predicted direction, but the study-specific estimates behind it vary widely in magnitude. Surprisingly, our results do also not clearly validate the traditional assumption of a B&N effect (Bott & Noveck, 2004), i.e., a general polarity-independent processing slowdown under SIs: a subsequent analysis including trial order revealed that the B&N effect was present in early trials of our study, whereas later trials do not show the effect. Overall, we conclude that polarity may influence the speed of scalar implicature processing, but that this effect is not robust across all types of scales.

articles.title: PRELIMINARY FRAMEWORK FOR A DYNAMIC SOCIO-ACOUSTIC MODEL OF SPEECH PERCEPTION
articles.authors: Meghan Sumner
articles.abstract: Listeners store detailed acoustic information and access social information cued by variation fast and early. Yet, how we understand all we understand remains an open question. I propose a Dynamic Socio-Acoustic Model that frames perception as a continuous, multidimensional tracking system where speech variation functions as primary cognitive information. This listener-driven model includes the fluid topological stretching of cognitive space, an acoustic exemplar space that is untethered to linguistic units and allows for multidimensional cross-context categorization. Listeners maintain a sub-lexical, macro-exemplar landscape where incoming acoustic-kinematic trajectories drive real-time resonance. Rather than matching signals to static templates, listeners construct ad-hoc categories on the fly, dynamically scaling an active grid in response to immediate environmental contrasts. By uniting continuous sensory tracking with fluid, experience-dependent spatial restructuring, this framework offers an ecological account of perception and memory that rethinks structural variation from a hurdle into a pathway to social meaning.

articles.title: The Impact of Multilingualism on Self-esteem and Linguistic Identity
articles.authors: Subhangi Roy
articles.abstract: This study explores the effects of multilingualism on self-esteem and linguistic identity among individuals living in the UK. Although the cognitive advantages of multilingualism are extensively proven for children and adolescents, its impact on socio-emotional aspects, especially self-esteem and identity in adults, is inadequately investigated. The current study aims to fill this gap using a quantitative methodology, utilising data gathered from 50 participants representing diverse age, gender, ethnic, educational, and linguistic backgrounds, implementing the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES) and a Linguistic Identity Questionnaire (LQ). The primary argument put forward was that, multilingualism would improve self-esteem and foster a richer distinctive language identity. Descriptive statistics, correlation analyses, ANOVA, and independent sample t-tests were employed to investigate the relation among multilingualism, self-esteem, and linguistic identity, including differences among different language groups and sub-constructs of the assessments. The findings suggested no significant direct correlation between multilingualism and self-esteem; however, a noteworthy inverse relationship was identified between the ‘Language and Social Status’ sub-domain of linguistic identity and self-esteem, inferring that, individuals who associated higher social status to a language other than their native language experienced reduced self-esteem. These results indicate that societal perceptions of a language’s prestige can negatively impact self-esteem, especially for native speakers of languages deemed less socially valuable. The hypothesis that multilingualism improves self-esteem was not entirely proven; nonetheless, the study elucidates the impact of linguistic identification on self-esteem, especially for the subcategories that constitute Linguistic identity. The limitations encompass the restricted sample size and reliance on self-reported data. Future study may investigate these processes longitudinally with bigger, more varied samples to further understand the socio-emotional implications of multilingualism.

articles.title: Beyond Initial Crisis Recognition: Suicide-Risk Responses of ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini Across 14-Turn Ukrainian-Language Conversations
articles.authors: Hryhorii Kuzyk; Oleg Salamon; Liliia Andreieva; Kateryna Drozdova
articles.abstract: Nine deployed conversational systems mostly recognised the crisis, but it disappeared from their behaviour once the conversation moved on. We ran 16 scenarios in ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini as 14-message conversations (48 dialogues): crisis signals alternated with distraction, turn 13 introduced a new person at risk, and turn 14 was sent a day later. Coding was binary, as in the previous study, with clinical verification; two crisis-contour specifications were tested separately. New crisis signals drew a reaction in 87, 95, and 76 of 96 responses, respectively; the crisis stopped being mentioned mainly at an everyday message. The new person at risk drew a reaction in 44 of 48 responses; after a day, 29 retained crisis content. All 14 turns drew a 'yes' code in 4, 7, and 0 of 16 conversations. Reacting to the new person did not guarantee correct allocation of roles and actions. Both contour specifications produced safety-relevant errors. Neither hypothesis was supported: the systems behaved differently, and the same rule, introduced as a single package, did not stabilise their behaviour. Recognition, retention, and reconfiguration at a transition are distinct properties; the weakest is retention of the prior state and tracking of each person's trajectory.

articles.title: Likert Versus Visual Analogue Scales in Ecological Momentary Assessment: Initial Evidence That Likert Scales Come With Reduced Capacity to Sustain Attentiveness
articles.authors: Esther Ulitzsch; Dominik Vollbracht; Lijin Zhang; Alberto Jover Martínez; Benjamin Domingue; Jonas M B Haslbeck; Tanja Lischetzke; Leonie V. D. E. Vogelsmeier
articles.abstract: Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) prompts participants to report on their current emotions, cognitions, or behaviors multiple times per day across several days, yielding rich, high-frequency data. However, the high frequency of measurement can burden participants, leading to disengagement in the form of non-compliance or careless/insufficient effort responding (C/IER), which compromises the validity of conclusions drawn from EMA data. To minimize these effects, it is crucial to understand how EMA design factors influence respondent disengagement. This study investigates how response format, a comparatively subtle design choice, affects C/IER as an important but hard-to-detect aspect of disengagement. We re-analyzed data from two experimental EMA studies, in which surveys were administered either in a Likert or a visual analogue scale (VAS) format in between-subjects designs. Each dataset was analyzed with one of two state-of-the-art confirmatory mixture modeling approaches to examine whether response format affects (a) the overall level of C/IER and (b) its associations with two fatigue- and attention-related contextual factors: the cumulative number of EMA study days and time of day. Across datasets and analytical approaches, we found indications that Likert scales yield up to 3 percentage points higher rates of C/IER than VASs, though the temporal patterns varied across studies. In Study I, differences were observed in overall C/IER levels, with parallel increases across EMA days. In Study II, initial C/IER was comparable between formats, but the Likert format showed a steeper increase over time. Implications for EMA design are discussed.

articles.title: Assessing User-Subjective Experience with Conversational Agents for Behavioral and Mental Health Interventions: Design and Psychometric Evaluation of CUE-Chat
articles.authors: Esther Mertens; Janis Butz; Jean-Louis van Gelder
articles.abstract:
While AI-conversational agents are increasingly integrated into behavioral and mental health interventions, standardized instruments to assess their performance remain scarce. To address this gap, we developed an instrument to measure user-subjective experience with AI-driven agents in the healthcare domain. We focused on user perception due to its direct contribution to intervention effects, and on healthcare given that the rapid adoption of AI-agents in this domain continues to outpace the development of validated evaluation instruments. 
Across four studies, we developed and tested the Chatbot User Evaluation instrument (CUE-Chat). First, we identified relevant assessment domains and items through literature review, existing instruments, input from AI-driven agents, and the research team’s domain expertise. Following this, we requested feedback on draft subscales, definitions, and items from expert and laypeople panels. We then tested the structure of the instrument’s concept version. Finally, we conducted a psychometric evaluation and finalized the instrument.
CUE-Chat consists of four factors: Perceived Efficacy (4 items), Usability (4 items), Intelligence (4 items), and Safety and Risk Management (4 items). Reliability and validity of the total score and each subscale was good to excellent (Cronbach’s α = .73-.92; Ω = .74-.93). Predictive validity was strong with all scales predictive of users’ overall rating of an AI-agent’s performance.
We conclude that CUE-Chat’s strong psychometric properties are promising, and that it is particularly useful for researchers integrating AI-driven agents into behavioral and mental health interventions in both developmental and evaluative stages.

articles.title: Familiar Content Changes Performance and Processing in Matrix Reasoning in Early Adolescence
articles.authors: Paulo Guirro Laurence; Marcela M. Weiss; Elizeu Macedo
articles.abstract: Matrix-reasoning assessments commonly use abstract geometric figures, although familiar content may change both performance and processing. This within-participants study compared accuracy and gaze-defined patterns of visual exploration for abstract and contextual items requiring corresponding relational rules. Participants were 56 children and adolescents recruited from a public school in São Paulo, Brazil, aged 11 to 15 years. Each participant completed six abstract and six contextual 3 × 3 matrices while gaze was recorded. Trial-level transition matrices were constructed from fixation sequences across nine matrix cells and the response alternatives, and k-means clustering identified two recurring patterns. Contextual items were answered more accurately than abstract items, with 2.44 times higher odds of a correct response. Completion time, fixation count, and fixation duration were similar between conditions. Cluster 1 was characterized by localized transitions involving the final row and response alternatives, whereas Cluster 2 involved broader, more sequential exploration across the matrix. Contextual items had lower odds of Cluster 1 classification, indicating that representational format modestly altered the distribution of gaze patterns. A significant condition-by-cluster interaction further showed that Cluster 2 was associated with higher accuracy for abstract items, but no cluster difference was detected for contextual items. These exploratory findings suggest that familiar content changes how matrices are explored, indicating that abstract and familiar matrix items should not be treated as interchangeable.

articles.title: What is there to explain about free will? An “easy problem” of consciousness downstream of agency
articles.authors: Nicolas Rouleau
articles.abstract: Free will is one of the most enduring problems in philosophy and cognitive science, yet what, exactly, requires explanation remains unclear. The most tractable target is the experience of free will – the vivid sense of self-authorship, control, and a felt capacity to have done otherwise. As with the scientific study of mystical experiences, this phenomenology can be investigated without resolving the metaphysical claims implied by its content. Here, I argue that free will is an “easy problem” of consciousness: a phenomenon that can be measured, manipulated, predicted, and mechanistically explained. Taking causal determinism as a working postulate, I consider whether prediction and reinforcement could generate the experience of controlling one’s own actions through causal misattribution and superstitious conditioning, without granting consciousness independent causal power. If the experience can be explained under deterministic constraints, the core scientific explanandum of the free will phenomenon has been addressed. Free will can then be distinguished from agency, which remains a causally consequential, graded capacity for goal-directed, adaptive, and self-regulating action across living systems, machines, and hybrids thereof.

articles.title: Making good decisions with counterfactuals
articles.authors: Ma Ricky; Scott Mueller; Thomas Icard; Tobias Gerstenberg
articles.abstract: Making a good decision often requires knowing something counterfactual: whether a person would be better off if we acted than if we didn't. Formal work shows how both experimental and observational data ought to be combined to inform good decisions. Here, we ask whether people's intuitions follow this normative standard. In three experiments (N = 354), participants decided whether or not to act based on observational and experimental data. Participants performed better than chance but far from optimally. Trial-by-trial feedback about the consequences of their choices, including what would have happened had they chosen otherwise, didn't improve performance. The breakdown was at the inference step: participants' estimates of whether a person would benefit from the treatment, be harmed by it, or be left unaffected were almost unrelated to normative predictions. Yet, participants' decisions followed coherently from those (incorrect) estimates. Experts in statistics, economics, and data science made better decisions than novices, but their counterfactual inferences were no more accurate. Counterfactual reasoning is critical for making good decisions from experimental and observational data, but its logic doesn't come naturally to people.

articles.title: Breaking Common Ground through Reciprocal Misalignment
articles.authors: Siham Abu Ali; Tatiana Philippova; Isaac Fradkin
articles.abstract: Establishing shared meaning is widely considered the normative, almost ubiquitous trajectory of linguistic interaction, while moments of misalignment are typically viewed as temporary interruptions that individuals attempt to repair. However, it is not uncommon to experience communication breakdowns that actively escalate rather than resolve. This raises a fundamental question: does interaction inherently lead people toward shared meaning, or is semantic alignment a reciprocal, socially contingent process?
