We conducted four experiments using a novel multiplayer word association task, where participants generated semantic associations while interacting with either human or simulated partners varying in semantic typicality. Our results show that, in general, social interaction motivates individuals to produce more conventional associations to support alignment. However, this tendency depended on partner’s behavior: when interacting with an atypical or difficult-to-align-with partner, individuals actively reduced their own typicality and tendency to match partner’s associations, effectively sacrificing semantic alignment. Such ‘reciprocal misalignment’ persisted even when participants were incentivized to maximize alignment. Our findings suggest that semantic misalignment may reflect a reciprocal, socially-motivated modulation of identity and differentiation, rather than solely a failure of coordination. This work sheds light on the interactional mechanisms underlying interpersonal distancing, communication breakdowns in neurodivergence, and potentially broader patterns of social polarization.

articles.title: Inconclusive prospective effects between technology acceptance, classroom distraction, and academic engagement among Chinese high school students: A reassessment of Li and Chen (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles.abstract: Li and Chen concluded reciprocal prospective associations between technology acceptance, classroom digital distraction, and academic engagement among high school students. However, significant cross-lagged parameters do not by themselves establish genuine prospective influence because similar estimates may arise through alternative statistical processes. Using simulated data that reproduced the sample size and correlation matrix reported by Li and Chen, I examined whether their conclusions were robust across several defensible analytic specifications. The pattern of results depended strongly on analytic choice: some models suggested positive prospective associations, whereas others indicated negative or null effects. When estimates from all specifications were combined using meta-analytic methods, no overall effect reached statistical significance. Accordingly, the available evidence does not provide a firm basis for concluding that technology acceptance, classroom distraction, and academic engagement exert reciprocal prospective influences on one another. In line with multiverse-analysis recommendations, conclusions should be drawn from the collective pattern across reasonable analytical alternatives rather than from a single model.

articles.title: “Oh No, the Robots Are Here”: AI identity labels, social uptake and sanctioning in mixed human–AI communities
articles.authors: Sara Major; Aleksandar Tomašević; Ana Vranić; Darja Cvetkovic; Dušan Vudragović; Boris Stupovski; Marija Mitrovic Dankulov
articles.abstract: Social media users can now encounter autonomous AI accounts that post, reply and vote alongside other users. In a longitudinal field experiment, we examined how labelling these accounts relates to whom people answer and how they evaluate AI contributions. YSocial is a Reddit-like hybrid platform for social media simulation, where people interact with language-model agents. On it, 36 participants discussed popular culture with 72 AI accounts powered by an uncensored language model over 21 experiment days. The AI accounts kept persistent personas and remembered previous exchanges. They were visibly labelled in one community and unlabelled in the other. Among 2,143 human replies, Bayesian models estimated that the probability of replying to an AI-authored post or comment was 3.5 percentage points higher in the hidden-label community, given the same earlier posts and comments available in the thread (95% credible interval 0.5–6.5). In both communities, participants were more likely to reply to an AI account after it had replied to them and less likely after they had replied to it. The gap in criticism, including polite disagreement, between replies to AI and human accounts was 13.3 percentage points larger in the visible-label community (95% credible interval 5.1–21.4). The toxicity difference was uncertain. Visible labels were associated with less engagement with AI contributions and more criticism of them.

articles.title: Impact of social affiliation and musical agency on movement and interpersonal coordination in adolescence
articles.authors: Martin Hartmann; Alessandro Ansani; Iballa Burunat; Marc Thompson; Pedro Neto; Joshua Silberstein Bamford; Patti Nijhuis; Rita Mustonen; Matias Hämäläinen; Toivo Niemi
articles.abstract: Dancing together to music is a common social activity in which movement coordination emerges from the interplay of interpersonal relationships and a shared musical environment. While previous work on dyadic dance movement has focused on individual differences, third-party judgments of synchrony, and disentangling partner- from music- driven coordination, relational and situational determinants of coordination have received less attention. This motion capture study investigated how social affiliation and agency over the music influence movement characteristics and social coordination in young people. A total of 164 adolescents danced in dyads with both a friend and a stranger, and to self- and researcher-selected music in a counterbalanced design. Extracted kinematic features included head and hand movement magnitude, movement complexity, fluidity, interpersonal distance, mutual orientation, and synchrony. Results showed greater, more complex and less fluid movements when participants danced with friends compared to strangers. Head and hand movement magnitudes were larger for self-selected than researcher-selected music, but only when self-selected music followed researcher-selected music. Friends also exhibited higher interpersonal synchrony, danced closer, and looked more towards each other than strangers. These findings shed light on how social and contextual factors shape dance behaviour in adolescence.

articles.title: Inconclusive prospective effects between fear of failure, academic buoyancy, and academic procrastination among Chinese primary school students: A reassessment of Fang et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles.abstract: Fang et al. concluded reciprocal prospective associations between fear of failure, academic buoyancy, and academic procrastination among primary school students. However, significant cross-lagged parameters do not by themselves establish genuine prospective influence because similar estimates may arise through alternative statistical processes. Using simulated data that reproduced the sample size and correlation matrix reported by Fang et al., I examined whether their conclusions were robust across several defensible analytic specifications. The pattern of results depended strongly on analytic choice: some models suggested positive prospective associations, whereas others indicated negative or null effects. When estimates from all specifications were combined using meta-analytic methods, no overall effect reached statistical significance. Accordingly, the available evidence does not provide a firm basis for concluding that fear of failure, academic buoyancy, and academic procrastination exert reciprocal prospective influences on one another. In line with multiverse-analysis recommendations, conclusions should be drawn from the collective pattern across reasonable analytical alternatives rather than from a single model.

articles.title: Registered Report: Does the valence-dominance model apply to deepfake faces? Validation and its impact on deepfake detection
articles.authors: Gianmarco Convertino; Mara Stockner; Michela Marchetti; Danilo Mitaritonna; Luca Corvitto; Luca Maiano; Lorenzo Papa; Irene Amerini; Giuliana Mazzoni
articles.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has given rise to increasingly more realistic fake contents such as deepfake faces, hardly distinguishable from real faces. However, evidence has shown that social evaluations of real faces are also able to impact the detection of deepfake faces. The present study aimed at applying for the first time the valence-dominance model for face evaluation on deepfake faces. Moreover, the impact of its thirteen attributes on deepfake detection performances was investigated. Specifically, 311 participants categorised 120 faces (50% real, 50% deepfake created ad hoc by Diffusion Model technology) and rated faces in regards to one of the attributes. Principal Component Analysis was applied in order to validate the valence-dominance model on deepfake faces, and a Brunswikian lens model was  applied to understand how each attribute contributes to a face being judged as deepfake. Results replicated the valence-dominance model on real faces as well as on faces categorized by participants as deepfake, but not on actual deepfake faces. Finally, the indirect effects of the Brunswikian model revealed caringness and intelligence to impair detection of deepfake stimuli, whilst weirdness was revealed to be a positive indirect predictor, being positively associated with higher detection accuracy of deepfake faces. Our results shed, for the first time, light into the differential cognitive processing of deepfake faces and their social evaluation whilst also providing novel insight into underlying mechanisms associated with deepfake detection. Interdisciplinary implications regarding the theoretical and applied contribution are discussed.

articles.title: Predict to Resist: A Mixed-Method Evaluation of a Prediction-Based Impulse Control Intervention
articles.authors: Tilia Linthout; Lieke Reintjes; Pieter Van Dessel
articles.abstract:
Impulsive behaviors often persist despite people’s intentions to act in line with personally valued goals. A recently developed intervention based on the Goal-Directed Predictive Processing (GDPP) framework aims to change such behaviors by helping people construct and practice inference chains in which personally relevant risk situations lead to predictions of goal-consistent behavior. The present study was designed as a replication and qualitative extension of a previous study testing this intervention. Ten Dutch-speaking adults with self-reported impulse control difficulties were allocated to a GDPP-based intervention condition or a waitlist control condition. Participants reported the frequency of their personally selected target behavior daily across baseline, training, and post-training phases. Participants in the GDPP condition also completed semi-structured interviews after the intervention. Single-case analyses showed heterogeneous response patterns. Two participants in the GDPP condition showed reliable reductions in impulsive behavior, but other participants did not, and reliable change was also observed in the waitlist control condition. The quantitative results therefore did not provide strong evidence for a uniform intervention effect. The qualitative results identified three main themes: intervention experience, perceived factors contributing to intervention effects, and perceived barriers to intervention effects. Participants described the rationale as recognizable and reported that the intervention increased awareness of impulsive and alternative behaviors, but also identified barriers such as mismatch between the rationale and the target behavior, persistent risk situations, insufficient repetition, motivational barriers, and strong craving. These findings suggest that GDPP-based impulse control interventions require further refinement and careful personalization before larger-scale efficacy testing.
Keywords: impulse control; behavior change; goal-directed predictive processing; single-case design; qualitative methods

articles.title: A Three-Domain Framework for Trust in Digitally Mediated Social Life
articles.authors: anonymous; YUAN SHEN; Ke Shen; Jinliang Qin
articles.abstract: Digital technologies increasingly mediate information access, social interaction, and institutional participation, raising the question of how trust in digital systems is organized in relation to trust in people and institutions. Across three independent samples of Chinese young adults, we tested a three-domain framework of trust in digitally mediated social life and developed a concise measure distinguishing interpersonal trust, institutional/rule trust, and digital system trust. Study 1 (N = 1,495) identified a three-factor structure using parallel analysis and exploratory factor analysis. Study 2 (N = 1,333) confirmed this structure: the three-factor model outperformed a unidimensional model and all pairwise-collapsed two-factor alternatives, although the three domains remained strongly correlated. Study 3 (N = 901) provided evidence consistent with measurement invariance across gender and initial nomological differentiation. Learning-oriented digital engagement was more strongly associated with institutional/rule and digital system trust, everyday/relational engagement with interpersonal and digital system trust, and digital information judgment with institutional/rule trust. Sensitivity analyses reproduced the primary patterns. Together, the findings support a three-domain framework in which digital system trust is strongly interconnected with, but not reducible to, trust in people or institutional arrangements.

articles.title: Temporal choice dynamics track opponent-dependent adaptation in autism
articles.authors: Tahmineh Godazgar; Rana Ghamari; Abolfazl Nadi; Atiye Sarabi-Jamab
articles.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder involves differences in social communication, interaction and behavioral flexibility, yet conventional single-response Theory-of-Mind tasks rarely capture the trial-by-trial dynamics of social adaptation. We examined how autistic and non-autistic young people organized recent choice history, how they adjusted it across opponents, and how these patterns related to task performance. Twenty-seven autistic children and adolescents and 24 healthy controls completed the same two-choice hide-and-seek task under social and non-social framing against artificial opponents of graded sophistication. We compared aggregate performance, Bayesian model-based estimates of latent strategy use, and model-free history kernels measuring how current choices depended on recent self-actions and opponent actions. History kernels showed that autistic participants switched away from their previous choice more strongly against every opponent, whereas controls added lag-2 and opponent-coupled structure when the opponent adapted to them and reconfigured their kernels across opponents more. Within the same dataset, replaying participants’ kernels against empirically fitted opponents reconstructed accuracy (r = .86) and the direction of the group difference against the first-order opponent, against which switching provided less benefit than against the zero-order opponent. Against the first-order opponent, controls were more often described by first-order opponent modelling (influence learning) and autistic participants by heuristic policies. These findings suggest that autism-related differences in repeated interaction are expressed in how choice history is organized and reconfigured across opponents, beyond categorical differences in inferred strategies.

articles.title: When Are Less Precise Predictions More Credible?
articles.authors: Eitan David Rude; Amin Shiri; Felipe M. Affonso; Hal Hershfield; Craig R. Fox
articles.abstract: People expressing uncertain values frequently offer point predictions or intervals of varying widths (e.g., “I’d say your investment will be worth $6,000” versus “I’d say your investment will be worth $5,000–$7,000”). Interestingly, prior research has drawn conflicting conclusions concerning the credibility of more versus less precise predictions. We resolve this inconsistency by identifying a key moderator: the perceived nature of uncertainty. Specifically, we find that under epistemic (“knowable”) uncertainty, predictions are seen as conveying experts’ degree of confidence, and more precise predictions are seen as more credible. Under aleatory (“random”) uncertainty, however, predictions are seen as conveying experts’ assessments of the degree of outcome variability, and less precise predictions are seen as more credible (provided they are within reasonable bounds). These results inform literatures on both the communication of uncertainty and the interpretation of confidence intervals.

articles.title: Intrusive and voluntary memory from a single system: A retrieved-context account of selective interference in the trauma-film paradigm
articles.authors: Jordan Gunn; Richard Henson; Emily A Holmes; Tommy Mcconnell; Deborah Talmi
articles.abstract: Memory theory must explain why interference can affect deliberate and involuntary remembering differently. Studies using distressing films show that a film reminder followed by an imagery-competing task such as Tetris can reduce later spontaneous memories of the film (intrusions) while leaving voluntary memory relatively intact. This selective interference effect is often interpreted through clinical theories of traumatic memory in which intrusive and voluntary remembering depend on different memory representations. We develop an alternative account in an emotional Context Maintenance and Retrieval (eCMR) model that predicts sequences of film and non-film recall events. Events become associated with context, a changing internal representation of experience. A film reminder reinstates film-associated context, so mental imagery generated during the subsequent task becomes associated with that context. During later retrieval, task memories compete with film memories cued by the same context, reducing film recall without weakening the original film associations. During deliberate recall, however, we propose that people pursue the goal of remembering the film by constructing and maintaining a retrieval cue that distinguishes film from task material. In simulations, sustained support from this cue was required to reproduce the selective-interference pattern across reminder and task conditions, protecting deliberate recall relative to involuntary retrieval. These results suggest that competitor learning and retrieval cueing can produce selective interference within a shared memory system, motivating tests in other memory tasks.

articles.title: Expertise Diversity Enhances Information Sharing in Wiki settings: Evidence from Sequential Collaboration
articles.authors: Maren Mayer; Joachim Kimmerle
articles.abstract: Online collaborative projects such as Wikipedia and OpenStreetMap rely on sequential collaboration, where contributors iteratively revise a shared product over time. While previous research has examined wikis for computer-supported collaborative learning and sequential collaboration for numerical judgment tasks, little is known about the cognitive mechanisms underlying information sharing in such settings. The present study bridges research on computer-supported collaborative learning, group information sharing, and cognitive models of sequential collaboration. Drawing on a computational model of sequential collaboration, we tested the prediction that higher variation in contributors' expertise facilitates the integration of information into a shared product. In an experimental study with 413 participants we demonstrate that information accumulation increased throughout the sequential chain but at a decreasing rate. Consistent with model predictions, higher expertise variation significantly increased the likelihood that information was incorporated into the shared text. Contrary to expectations, expertise variation did not affect the timing of information inclusion across chain positions, nor did it increase information deletions. These findings demonstrate that predictions derived from a cognitive model of numerical judgment formation generalize to information-sharing contexts. More broadly, the results suggest that diversity in contributors' knowledge can improve collaborative knowledge construction in sequential environments. This research adds to evidence that sequential collaboration is an effective mechanism for integrating distributed knowledge in online collaborative systems.

articles.title: Visual Deprivation Alters Parent-Specific  Autonomic Tuning During Infancy
articles.authors: GIULIA CAPPAGLI; Marta Guarischi; Guido Catalano; FEDERICA MORELLI; gori monica; Sabrina Signorini
articles.abstract: Parents' touch regulates infants' physiology, and vision may be essential for identifying social partners, but whether the absence of visual feedback affects this physiological effect has never been tested. We examined whether visual deprivation alters infants' autonomic responses to affective touch from a parent versus a stranger. Eighteen infants aged 8–13 months (9 with peripheral visual impairment, 9 sighted) received slow stroking (3 cm/s) on the right shin while the parent or an unfamiliar adult sat in front of them as the apparent source of touch. Typically developing infants showed a larger heart-rate deceleration during parent than stranger touch. Infants with visual impairment did not differentiate between adults and showed higher heart-rate responses than typically developing infants in the parent condition (Group × Parent Identity interaction). Visual experience may help link affective touch to its social source. The small, clinical sample limits generalizability, and replication is needed.

articles.title: Techno-Optimism Reduces Willingness to Address Climate Change
articles.authors: Jonas M B Haslbeck; Maien S. M. Sachisthal; Fabian Dablander
articles.abstract: Technological innovation is essential for mitigating climate change, but so are wider socio-economic transformations as well as lifestyle changes. Techno-optimism, the belief that technological innovation alone is sufficient to address climate change, may reduce public willingness to engage in climate action. Here we use a structural causal model to estimate the causal effect of techno-optimism on willingness to contribute 1\% of one's monthly household income to address climate change using a large, population-weighted sample from the Netherlands (N = 23, 395). We find that being a techno-optimist reduces the probability of being willing to contribute by 18.7% (95% CI: 15.6, 20.7). In addition, we find that the causal effect is much smaller for respondents on the political right, where overall willingness is already very low. We close by discussing the importance of adequately framing the role of technology when discussing climate change mitigation.

articles.title: Synchrony under uncertainty. The effects of auditory context on the perception of the temporal location of quasi-musical sounds
articles.authors: Anne Danielsen; Sabine Leske; Justin London
articles.abstract: Auditory perception and sensorimotor synchronization always occur within a specific auditory context, a fact that is often overlooked when they are studied in the laboratory. Here we address the question of how our perception of a given sound's temporal characteristics is modulated by the sounds surrounding it. Previous research has highlighted the importance of acoustic factors like attack and duration in defining both a sound's perceived temporal position ("P-center") and the temporal range in which it is heard as synchronized with another sound ("beat bin"). Our experiment investigated whether the same probe/target pair is perceived differently when situated in contexts of sounds with different acoustic features, from contexts of mostly clear, sharply defined sounds to contexts of mostly “muddy,” noisy ones. Our findings reveal that the P-center of the target sound shifts progressively later as the context becomes dominated by sounds with softer onsets, and the variability of P-center location—indicative of the width of the beat bin—also increases under such conditions. These results significantly advance our understanding of how sonic environments influence the perception of a sound's temporal characteristics, and shed light on its underlying neural mechanisms. The study offers new insights into the intricate nature of temporal perception in complex auditory environments and sets the stage for further exploration of the mechanisms underlying auditory processing and synchronization.

articles.title: Real-time Associations Between Psychological States and Context in University Students with Suicidal Ideation: An Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
articles.authors: Ana Portillo-Van Diest; Gemma Vilagut; Laura Ballester; Johan Bjureberg; Paula Carrasco; Raquel Falcó; Margalida Gili; Mathilde Husky; Glenn Kiekens; Francisco H. Machancoses
articles.abstract: Suicidal ideation (SI) is dynamic and linked to emotion regulation difficulties that may be reflected in associations between momentary psychological states and context. In a 2-week ecological momentary assessment (EMA) study, 476 students reported passive daily SI, momentary psychological states (affect, stress, tiredness, concentration difficulties) and contexts four times per day. Multilevel network analysis compared contemporaneous, temporal, and between-person networks across three groups: one without SI or psychopathology (No-MD/SI), and two with low and high 14-day passive SI (Low- and High-SI). Low- and High-SI groups showed more temporally self-reinforcing negative affect and weaker affect-context connections. No-MD/SI students showed stronger positive affect recovery following negative affect. High-SI students spent less time with loved ones and were more likely to engage in conversation after stress than after positive emotions. Findings suggest that passive SI is associated with greater negative emotion rigidity and a shift in social connectedness from enjoyment to distress-driven coping.

articles.title: fMRI hyperscanning reveals widespread neural coupling during natural conversations
articles.authors: Laetitia Mwilambwe-Tshilobo; Lily Tsoi; Sebastian Speer; Zaid Zada; Shannon M. Burns; Emily B. Falk; Diana Tamir
articles.abstract: Conversation is one of the most powerful tools that people have for building and maintaining social connections. How does conversation bring two minds together? Here we tracked the neural dynamics between dyads during real-time conversation using fMRI hyperscanning, where both people were scanned simultaneously, to explore whether and how conversation aligns brains. Dyads engaged in natural, free-flowing conversation as they co-constructed the content of their dialogue. In a control condition, partners read aloud scripted dialogue from another dyad’s conversation, preserving the turn-taking structure while removing the co-construction. To examine neural alignment, we compared whole-brain intersubject correlation between partners in each condition, assessing both synchronous and predictive neural dynamics. Results showed that naturalistic conversation led to significant widespread neural alignment across brain regions implicated in attention, audition, affect, executive control, and social cognition, compared to scripted conversation. Temporally refined analyses showed that during naturalistic conversation, relative to scripted conversation, both speakers and listeners anticipated each other within a short temporal window, with brain activity preceding their partner’s in the same neural systems. These findings show that live, turn-taking conversations align neural activity well beyond passive or asynchronous communication, providing a foundation for future research examining how spontaneous, co-constructed dialogue allows people to communicate effectively.

articles.title: When Habits Dominate in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: Tracking the Temporal Dynamics of Habitual and Goal-Directed Control
articles.authors: Chenyu Yuan; Yinqing Fan; Chaoyi Wu; Jingyi Zhang; Binxin Huang; Tingyue Bai; Trevor William Robbins; Tristan Bekinschtein; Zhen Wang
articles.abstract: Patients with Obsessive–Compulsive Disorder (OCD) often struggle to suppress maladaptive habitual behaviours, yet the temporal dynamics of habit–goal arbitration remain unclear. Here we address this question using an intensive four-day training protocol followed by a time-resolved forced-response test, combined with computational modelling. OCD patients and healthy controls (HCs) showed comparable learning trajectories, indicating intact basic associative learning and perceptual–motor speed in OCD. Critically, when previously learned stimulus–response mappings were remapped, OCD patients exhibited a selective increase in habitual errors, but only within an early time window. At longer preparation times, differences disappeared. Computational model comparison showed that OCD patients were more likely than HCs to be best described by a habit model. Within this model, OCD patients showed reduced variability in habitual preparation latency, reflecting more temporally consistent, sharply tuned habit behaviour. Exploratory analyses linked greater symptom severity to more variable goal-directed preparation. Together, these findings suggest that precisely timed habitual responses are more likely to be expressed during early preparation in OCD. This early-expression bias offers a possible account of ego-dystonic compulsions as a biased race in response preparation, without treating the task as a direct test of competition between independent systems

articles.title: Developing an adolescent self-report measure of social media experience: Insights from cognitive interviews
articles.authors: Jo Hickman Dunne; Louise Black; Jade Davies; Frederick Jones; Molly Anderton; Pratyasha Nanda; Felicitas Beissel; Lauren Burke; Reihaneh Farzinnia; Margarita Panayiotou
articles.abstract: Despite a rapid increase in research exploring the relationship between adolescent social media use and mental health, the field is hindered by poor quality tools that lack the validity and precision to assess this relationship. The current study presents findings from cognitive interviews that aimed to refine a multidimensional measure of adolescents’ social media experiences relevant to their mental health and wellbeing. We conducted 20 individual, paired or group interviews with 35 adolescents aged 11-16, across three rounds of interviews, testing 83 of a possible 107 items. Through iterative testing, issues relating to comprehension; inapplicability and assumptions within items; and items not addressing their intended experience, were identified and addressed. The interviews also highlighted two wider conceptual issues: (1) the impact of parental restrictions on adolescents’ experiences, and (2) difficulties in responding to items about abstract, identity-based experiences. In addition, the interviews supported an understanding of preferred response options and format. Findings from this study informed specific revisions to measure items to enhance validity, as well as broader considerations for assessing adolescent social media experience. Our study also reinforces the importance of cognitive interviewing in refining adolescent measures more broadly. We identify the need for the development of a set of general recommendations to guide item writing for adolescents, and further work to understand optimal response label options and wording for longer recall periods. Development of such guidance, alongside the greater use of cognitive interviews to pre-test measures, is crucial for improving instrument validity in the field of adolescent mental health.

articles.title: Citation Fabrication and Accuracy in AI-Generated Psychiatric Research: A Comparative Evaluation of Four Contemporary Large Language Models
articles.authors: Jake Linardon; Cleo Anderson; Tayarna Bolger; Claudia Liu; Olivia Marie Soliman; Zoe McClure
articles.abstract:
Objectives. LLMs are increasingly used to support academic writing, but their tendency to hallucinate citations raises concerns about the integrity of AI-assisted scholarly work. This study provides a timely snapshot of citation reliability in LLM-generated academic reviews by testing whether citation fabrication and accuracy differ across four LLMs and review topic specificity.  

Method. ChatGPT-5.4 Plus, ChatGPT-5.3 Free, Gemini-3, and Claude Sonnet-4.6 were tasked with generating 16 literature reviews on mental health, divided into general topics (broad areas with substantial evidence bases) and specialised topics (narrower areas with smaller evidence bases). 

Results. Only 6.1% of the 825 LLM-generated citations were fabricated, with fabrication absent for ChatGPT-5.4 Plus (0%), very low for Claude Sonnet-4.6 (0.5%) and ChatGPT-5.3 Free (5.5%), and highest for Google Gemini-3 (20.2%). A similar model-level pattern emerged for citation accuracy (real citations containing no bibliographic errors). Review topic specificity was not associated with citation fabrication or accuracy. 

Conclusion. Findings suggest possible improvements in citation reliability relative to estimates from prior studies testing older model iterations, while also showing that current performance is strongly model-dependent. These findings highlight the need for rigorous human verification of LLM-generated references and stronger safeguards to protect research integrity as LLMs are integrated into research.

articles.title: Understanding the role of generative artificial intelligence in mental health support: Survey of user experiences, engagement patterns, and perceived risks and benefits
articles.authors: Jake Linardon; Zoe McClure; Cleo Anderson; Claudia Liu; Olivia Marie Soliman; Mariel Messer
articles.abstract: Generative AI – especially ChatGPT – is increasingly used for mental health purposes, but users’ subjective experiences of these tools remain unclear. We characterized how individuals utilize ChatGPT for mental health support through a web-based survey completed by 308 adults (Mage=31.5, SD=5.3; 54% men) who reported prior use of this tool. Around half reported use of ChatGPT for mental health support more than once a week, 80% have used it for more than 3 months, and a third reported increased use over time. Depression (55%), anxiety (74%), stress (66%), and relationship conflict (49%) were the problems most frequently discussed with ChatGPT, with the severity of these problems typically rated as mildly or moderately severe. Endorsed reasons for use were its on-demand availability (71%), free cost (69%), and anonymous nature (54%), while common functions the platform served included obtaining advice (71%), providing a safe space for expression (63%), and to learn coping strategies (61%). Experiences were largely positive, with 8 in 10 agreeing that ChatGPT helped them feel understood, better process their emotions, and improve their mental health literacy. Concerns were also evident, with around half expressing worry about data privacy, and a quarter feeling overly reliant on the platform and reducing their motivation to seek help. Few indicated that ChatGPT had replaced professional help (7%) or discouraged help-seeking (12%). Findings shed light on how users are engaging with generative AI for mental health support and highlight the importance of rigorous research designed to evaluate its safety and long-term efficacy.

articles.title: In AI Do We Trust? Comparing a Transformer-Based Natural Language Processing Model Against a Traditional Content Analysis Approach to Qualitative Research
articles.authors: Matthew Baron; Catherine Stein
articles.abstract:
Central to debates about the use of artificial intelligence (AI) models for qualitative
research are concerns about comparability and trust in AI generated findings. The present
methodological study compared findings from a transformer-based Natural Language Processing
(NLP) model, BERT, against a traditional content analysis approach to qualitative research using
the same text data. We examined claims that AI models generate findings that are identical or
similar to traditional qualitative approaches. The study assessed three aspects of comparability
between the BERT model solution and human-coded findings that included topic labeling,
classification overlap, and AI replicability. Results indicated broad similarity in the semantic
meaning of topic categories generated by the BERT model and themes from content analysis.
There was low overlap in the classification of individual participant responses between BERT
and content analysis categories, even for categories similar in semantic meaning. Running the
BERT model a second time on the same input data resulted in differences in topic categories and
document classification between the two approaches. Study implications and research
recommendations for the use of NLP models are discussed.

articles.title: Yes, ChatGPT (and other models) need a psychiatrist: parallels between experimental neuropsychiatry and AI alignment science
articles.authors: Karthik V Sarma
articles.abstract: AI chatbots (such as ChatGPT or Claude) sometimes state false information with confidence, a behavior popularly termed “hallucination.” In their recent perspective, de Boer et al. [1] compared these errors to confabulation in patients with memory disorders, and asked whether ChatGPT needs a psychiatrist. I argue that it does, but for different reasons. False statements from chatbots may be better explained by how they are trained: first to produce contextually consistent text rather than true text, and later by being rewarded to produce answers. The more meaningful parallel lies elsewhere: because these systems learn to simulate human characters, they may also reproduce human personality traits and patterns resembling the symptoms of mental illness. Understanding them may require the methods of experimental psychiatry and psychology, and could advance our understanding of the human mind.

articles.title: Social Support among LGBTQ, Cisgender, and Heterosexual Undergraduate Students:  An Ego-Centric Social Network Study
articles.authors: Allyson Marie Blackburn; Nathan Todd; Nicole Allen
articles.abstract: While the population and acceptance of LGBTQ people are growing, there are persistent mental health disparities for LGBTQ individuals, especially for emerging adults. Social support is critical for the promotion of well-being. Yet, who receives support and the nature of the support provided can vary based on social identity, including sexual orientation and gender identity. In this study, we demonstrate the benefit of using ego-centric social network analysis (ESNA) to advance research about emotional support for sexual minorities. Using a sample of 1,215 undergraduate students (253 sexual minorities) from a large Midwestern university, we show that sexual minorities reported a greater proportion of LGBTQ people yet a lower proportion of family in their social network. We also show that sexual minorities reported that they were less likely to receive support but were more likely to be nominated by both heterosexuals and sexual minorities as network members who provide support. Finally, sexual minority participants relied more on friends than parents for emotional support, whereas the opposite was true for heterosexual students. These (and other) findings show how ESNA allows for testing hypotheses that capture the interconnected context of relationships. We discuss how findings advance the literature along with limitations and implications. Overall, we show that ESNA is a valuable tool to use to understand social networks as a critical context for development and well-being.

articles.title: Cross-country variation in early childhood family digital media ecology: A ManyBabies 8 registered report
articles.authors: Nevena Dimitrova; Sarah Kucker; Joscelin Rocha-Hidalgo; Koeun Choi; Lucas Gago-Galvagno; Elizabeth Jessica Goldman; Louisa Kulke; Lauren J. Myers; Sarah Pila; Catarina Vales
articles.abstract: Digital media use during early childhood is widespread yet unevenly documented globally, with most evidence drawn from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD; i.e., Minority World) societies. This registered report examines cross-country and context-specific variation in digital media exposure among children 6-36-months-old. Guided by the Dynamic, Relational, Ecological Approach to Media Effects Research (DREAMER) framework, the ManyBabies 8 consortium investigates: (1) age of first direct media use; (2) amount of direct media use and indirect media exposure; (3) social context of media use (joint media engagement, caregiver media disruptions); and (4) caregiver motivations and rule-setting practices. Caregivers from 58 countries will complete standardized surveys in 2027. Countries will be grouped into empirically derived country-clusters based on country-level indicators. Preregistered linear and logistic mixed-effects regression models will examine differences across country-clusters, accounting for participants nested within countries and family structural characteristics included as covariates. It is hypothesized most children will experience direct use and media exposure before 2-years, and that direct media use, indirect exposure, caregiver practices, and motivations will vary across countries and family contexts. By harmonizing measures across countries, this study will provide the first comprehensive characterization of early childhood direct digital media use and indirect exposure.

articles.title: Questionable mediated effect of care-resistant behavior in dementia patients on nurses’ occupational burnout: A comment on Ding et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Ding et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking care-resistant behavior in dementia patients to nurses’ occupational burnout. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported care-resistant behavior, psychological detachment, professional calling, and occupational burnout are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles.title: Cross-linguistic affective iconicity
articles.authors: José Antonio Hinojosa; Daniele Gatti
articles.abstract: Whether relationships between word form and affect reflect shared human constraints or language-specific conventions remains largely unresolved. Addressing this, here we tested whether affective mappings learned in one language zero-shot predict estimations for the emotional dimensions of valence and arousal in another using 85,375 lexical entries from ten languages diverse in origin and culture across eight (sub)lexical representations spanning orthographic, phonological, articulatory, and distributional semantic information. Results revealed a strong semantic transfer, greater for valence than arousal, while form-based transfer was smaller but consistently above zero across all seven representations for arousal, with the strongest effects for articulatory features. Language-distance analyses further revealed that valence-related orthographic and phoneme-bigram transfer was stronger between more closely related languages, particularly genealogically and the modest correspondence between fitted form coefficients indicated that transferable prediction coexisted with differences in feature weighting across languages. These findings characterize affective iconicity as graded and representation-dependent: valence generalizes most strongly through distributional meaning, whereas arousal leaves a more consistent cross-linguistic trace in word form. This pattern motivates an account in which culturally and historically shaped evaluative mappings coexist with activation-related mappings that may draw more broadly on shared embodied constraints, connecting linguistic form with the conceptual organization of affective experience.

articles.title: Using conversational artificial intelligence to dissect the psychoneuroimmunology of social safety and threat
articles.authors: Julian Packheiser; Sigrid Elsenbruch; Harald Engler; Dirk Scheele
articles.abstract: Human health is profoundly shaped by the quality of our social environments, yet the mechanisms through which social experiences become biologically embedded remain poorly understood. Social Safety Theory (SST) proposes that perceived social safety and threat influence health through neuroendocrine and immune pathways, but it remains unclear which features of social interaction engage these pathways. Here, we argue that conversational artificial intelligence (AI) provides a powerful experimental tool to address this mechanistic gap. Synthetic agents allow researchers to systematically vary core social signals, including responsiveness, reciprocity, empathic cues, agency, and multimodal information, while holding other features of the interaction relatively constant. This controllability creates a unique opportunity to identify which social signals are necessary or sufficient to generate perceived safety or threat and to engage downstream biological responses. Building on SST, we propose a psychoneuroimmunological framework linking experimentally controlled features of synthetic social interaction to neuroendocrine and immune processes and derive testable hypotheses concerning perceived humanness, social-signal strength, and multimodal embodiment. By enabling the causal decomposition of social interaction, conversational AI could help reveal what makes an interaction biologically social and clarify the mechanisms linking social disconnection to health.

articles.title: Sleep Helps You Make Good Social Decisions, Even If You’re Not Sure Why
articles.authors: Lewis Vincent Ball; Yicheng Qiu; Heather Jane Ferguson; M. Gareth Gaskell
articles.abstract: Memory supports trust decision-making in social encounters. We investigated whether this support is influenced by sleep, given the beneficial effect of sleep on episodic memory. Participants encountered images of cooperative and cheating partners during exposure. Item (is this person old/new?) and source memory (did they cooperate/cheat?) were then measured, before participants chose whether to cooperate with old and new partners. Experiment 1 ruled out time-of-day influences on our measures. In Experiment 2, a ~12 hr delay separated exposure and memory/cooperation phases. The Sleep group slept overnight in between whilst the Wake group experienced a day awake. Experiment 3 replicated the paradigm and measured trust in a contextually-novel task relative to exposure, measuring the extent to which participants would accept each partner as their neighbour. In a combined analysis across Experiments 2 and 3, participant-level item and source memory correlated with the frequency of adaptive decisions. Recognition of cheating partners was enhanced in the Sleep group (item memory), but there were no group differences in recalling the past behaviour of partners (source memory). Participants were more likely to cooperate with cooperators than cheaters and more likely to accept cooperators than cheaters as their neighbours (Experiment 3). Importantly, both effects were enhanced in the Sleep group. These findings are consistent with sleep promoting socially-adaptive decision-making. Given there was no significant evidence that sleep influenced explicit memory for behaviours, sleep may facilitate decision-making by integrating new memories into generalised knowledge structures in long-term memory, supporting more flexible decision-making.

articles.title: Arousal by Any Other Name? Testing the Specificity of Sexual Arousal in Men’s Cue-Based Judgments of Potential Flirt Partners
articles.authors: Ingo Landwehr; Alexander F. Schmidt
articles.abstract: Inferring whether a woman is showing romantic or sexual interest can be challenging, especially when multiple cues conflict or cue integration is influenced by physiological states such as arousal. Building on research linking sexual arousal to men’s overreliance on global cues (OGC) when assessing women’s sexual interest, this preregistered study tested whether a similar cue-weighting bias would emerge under nonsexual arousal. Heterosexual men (N = 275) completed a decision task judging which of two women was more likely to be flirting with them. Stimuli from a validated image set combined global sexual (clothing) and specific affective (facial) cues in congruent versus incongruent pairings. Error rate (ER) indexed OGC, whereas reaction time (RT) captured complementary decision dynamics. Incongruent trials yielded longer RTs and higher ERs, but nonsexual arousal did not reproduce the OGC-related performance pattern previously observed under sexual arousal. Findings suggest that sexual arousal may exert distinct effects on cue weighting and conflict-related processing, highlighting the importance of specifying the conditions under which arousal alters the integration of global sexual and specific affective cues in social judgments.

articles.title: The Cultural Logic of Honor and Antisocial Punishment in Social Dilemmas: A Multi-Lab Study Across Three World Regions
articles.authors: Shuxian Jin; Dina Rabie; Jinkwon Lee; Jinkyung Na; Rania Miniesy; Vivian L Vignoles; Ayse K. Uskul
articles.abstract: Punishment can sustain cooperation by targeting free riders (prosocial punishment), but it may also backfire by triggering retaliation; and when punishment is directed at cooperators (antisocial punishment), it can lead to a decline in cooperation. Samples exhibiting greater antisocial punishment in previous research have tended to come from societies where honor is believed to play a stronger role in shaping social behavior. Here, we tested the role of honor in antisocial punishment through a preregistered multi-lab experiment conducted in Egypt (n = 266), South Korea (n = 212), and the United Kingdom (n = 192), using public goods games with and without punishment. While the level of antisocial punishment was higher among the Egyptian sample, compared to the South Korean and British samples, individual-level honor values and norms were not associated with antisocial punishment across all three samples. Nevertheless, individuals with stronger personal honor values exhibited heightened retaliation, particularly targeting cooperators after being punished unfairly. These findings suggest that honor is not a cultural aspiration that provokes, nor a norm that prescribes, aggression toward cooperators, but rather a cultural logic that shapes when and for whom punishment becomes a tool of harmful retaliation rather than cooperation enforcement.

articles.title: Jargon as a Psychological Construct? A Multidecade Analysis of Communication Failure in Evaluation Reports
articles.authors: John Hite
articles.abstract: For seven decades, studies have asked whether the people who receive psychological evaluation reports understand what they say. Existing research has largely measured reader satisfaction rather than what readers comprehend, recall, or interpret. This narrative synthesis identified six studies, conducted between 1984 and 2025 in school psychology and, most recently, child neuropsychology, in which 253 readers were assigned to a standard-format report and had their comprehension scored directly. Comprehension ranged from 46.6% to 61.1% (weighted mean = 55.2%) and showed no detectable change across four decades. In every study that also scored an accessible version of the same report, readers understood it better, with scores from 60% to 82%. Recent evidence from pediatric neuropsychology shows the same gap: parents rated their understanding of their child's report highly, yet almost half could not state the child's diagnoses without error. Effective formats combined plain-language wording with one or more of domain-based organization, concrete behavioral examples, and elaborated recommendations. These findings suggest that jargon-related comprehension failure is a persistent, measurable, and modifiable problem spanning specialties within psychology. Implications for training, supervision, and evidence-based communication practice across school and clinical psychology are discussed.

articles.title: Formal training in a visual aesthetic domain increases shared taste in a domain-specific manner
articles.authors: Edward A. Vessel; Claire Reymond; Nancy Etcoff
articles.abstract: Although there is strong agreement for aesthetic preferences (“shared taste”) for natural kinds such as faces and landscapes, preferences for cultural artifacts such as artwork and architecture are more individual. These differences in aesthetic tastes may reflect differences in how individuals parse their perceptual world. We examined the aesthetic preferences of students enrolled in training programs for visual communication and architecture and hypothesized that formal training in an artistic domain would lead to shifts in which features individuals use to aesthetically evaluate that domain, causing changes in which images are preferred and to an increase in shared taste (convergence) across individuals. In a longitudinal study, 27 architecture and 21 visual communication students viewed images of buildings, posters, and artworks and rated them for both understanding and aesthetic appeal at 3 timepoints spread over two years. A single set of ratings were also collected from 69 online control participants. After two years of training (T3), a double-dissociation pattern emerged: architecture students agreed more on which buildings were aesthetically pleasing and understood, but visual communication students agreed more on which posters were aesthetically pleasing and understood. Average aesthetic ratings, on the other hand, were higher for the domain of study only at T1. These findings demonstrate a clear link between the development of expertise, a key form of learning, and aesthetic appeal. Rather than solely being a function of stimulus-computable features, aesthetic appeal is a function of how a person understands their visual world, reflecting personal biographies of visual experience and knowledge.

articles.title: Young Children Make Rapid Behavior-to-Behavior Inferences from Costly Social Choices
articles.authors: Bill Pepe; Lindsey J Powell
articles.abstract: People’s actions provide insights into their motives and traits. Adults can use just one observed action to make social inferences that guide predictions for how the actor will behave in the future. However, previous work suggests young children require significantly more evidence than older children and adults before they will make such generalized inferences. Here we test whether young children can make rapid behavioral generalizations when a single observed action provides diagnostic evidence about a social motive relevant to later behavior. Building on evidence that children employ a naive utility calculus to understand the values underlying others’ choices, children were introduced to a protagonist who could choose to provide costly, non-obligatory help to a needy target. The protagonist either helped, pursued their own goal, or hindered the target. When asked if the protagonist would help the same target (Exp 1) or a new person (Exp 2) in new scenarios, children were more likely to predict help, toward both same and new targets, from the protagonist who previously helped, and less likely to predict help from the hinderer, relative to a neutral protagonist who did not intervene. These findings provide novel evidence that children can use a single instance of prosocial or antisocial behavior to guide predictions about a person’s future actions, and connect this evidence to current theories of social cognitive development. Overall, results suggest children can rapidly infer motives or traits that guide their expectations for people’s future actions.

articles.title: Morpho-phonetic adaptation is realised in multiple cues: evidence from articulography
articles.authors: Motoki Saito; Jessie S. Nixon
articles.abstract: A critical issue in models of speech production concerns the modularity of processing: for example, can information from morphology influence the articulation of phonologically identical segments? A phenomenon that has the potential to help shed light on this question is what we term morpho-phonetic adaptation: systematic phonetic differences in identical segments patterning with morphological differences. Previous studies have been largely inconclusive, finding longer (enhancement) and shorter (reduction) duration of affixes, as well as null effects. The occurrence of morpho-phonetic adaptation for affixes suggests that morphological information can indeed influence segment articulation. However, to date, most studies have involved acoustic realisations in English. If it is the case that morphology interacts with phonetics, such morphological effects should also be observed in languages other than English. We also hypothesise that effects should also occur in articulatory realisations such as tongue movements. In the present study, we compared acoustic duration and tongue movements between two German suffixes -er [ɐ] and -t [-t]. We found that the suffixal -er [ɐ] was significantly longer in duration and significantly lower in tongue positions than its segmentally identical non-suffixal counterpart, and the lower tongue position could not be simply attributed to longer duration. Importantly, however, no effect of morphological status was found for -t [-t] for either duration or articulatory trajectory. These findings show that morpho-phonetic adaptation manifests in multiple cues and may depend on segment identity, with implications for models of speech production.

articles.title: Assessing psychological, neural and AI-based representational geometries across multiple similarity properties
articles.authors: Johan Alejandro Gamba; Megan A. K. Peters; Vincent Taschereau-Dumouchel; Brian Odegaard
articles.abstract: Assessing similarity between objects is a fundamental cognitive process, and similarity judgments can assess many different attributes, including objective properties (color, shape) or subjective appraisals (preference, scariness). Here, we investigated how psychological similarity across eight different properties relates to neural representational geometries and artificial models. We first collected large-scale pairwise similarity ratings for 280 objects. Using representational similarity analysis (RSA) and multidimensional scaling, we identified three mental representational spaces: one defined by multiple object features and general similarity, a second by affective evaluations, and a third by color. Combining fMRI and RSA in 80 participants, we found that object feature ratings significantly correlated with representational structures in visual and prefrontal cortices. Unexpectedly, affective ratings also correlated with patterns in visual cortices. Crucially, regional variability strongly shaped these correspondences: visual cortices exhibited high noise ceilings and consistent alignment with behavior, whereas associative regions showed greater across-subjects variability and weaker correlations. Finally, algorithms and neural networks with high classification performance on specific properties strongly correlated with behavioral and fMRI RSA matrices. Together, these results demonstrate that similarity is a multidimensional construct that comprises multiple representational spaces whose neural correspondence is shaped by representational content, regional variability, and modeling methodology.

articles.title: Synthometricon: A search engine to identify conceptual overlap in measures in the behavioral sciences
articles.authors: Björn Erik Hommel; Annika Iris Külpmann; Ruben C. Arslan
articles.abstract: Every month, scores of new measures and constructs enter the behavioral science literature. Researchers struggle to keep an overview of their subfields, let alone the wider field, with an estimated number of allegedly different constructs now exceeding 30,000. Proposing constructs is easy, finding redundancies and overlaps is not. The effort of finding redundancies using participant responses grows quadratically with the number of measures. This cost motivates the use of language models, which can simplify and speed up the process without requiring new data collection. Earlier work employed latent semantic analysis (LSA) to make use of the textual nature of questionnaires in the social and behavioral sciences. However, LSA treats sentences as bags of words and ignores word order, syntax, and negation, all of which shape how respondents interpret items. Recent advances demonstrate that transformer-based sentence embedding models offer a more viable solution for predicting empirical relatedness between survey items. In the presented work, we use a fine-tuned language model, the SurveyBot3000, to introduce the Synthometricon, an open-access web application for systematic detection of conceptual overlap. The application indexes over 570,000 items across more than 97,000 scales from approximately 28,000 instruments in the APA PsycTests database and other sources.

articles.title: Understanding Medical Invalidation from the Patient Perspective: A Qualitative Interview Study Across Diseases and Healthcare Settings
articles.authors: Seraina Petra Lerch
articles.abstract:
Objective 
Research on patients feeling that their symptoms are not taken seriously (medical invalidation) has predominantly focused on individual diseases. This study explored patients' experiences across different medical conditions and healthcare contexts to identify common characteristics, contributing factors, consequences, and opportunities for prevention. 
Methods
The study was conducted in Germany between January and March 2025 using interviews undertaken remotely or in person. Data were analysed using qualitative content analysis following Kuckartz and Rädiker. Thirty-one adults (≥18 years) with self-reported experiences of not being taken seriously in healthcare were purposively recruited through patient organisations and social media to achieve maximum variation regarding symptoms and diagnoses.
Results
Participants described not being taken seriously as a cross-cutting healthcare phenomenon occurring across diverse symptoms, diagnoses, medical specialties, and healthcare settings. Experiences ranged from isolated encounters to cumulative processes that developed over repeated interactions with healthcare professionals (HCPs). Contributing factors were perceived at multiple levels, including healthcare system, HCPs, patient, disease, and interactional factors, which frequently interacted. Consequences extended beyond the initial consultation and included psychological distress, loss of trust, delayed or inappropriate diagnosis and treatment, reduced healthcare utilisation, occupational consequences, and impaired social well-being. Participants identified opportunities for prevention at different levels, highlighting structured feedback mechanisms. 
Conclusions
Medical invalidation is a multifactorial phenomenon that extends across diseases and healthcare settings. Patients emphasized that medical invalidation depends not only on clinical decision-making but on being heard, having their illness perceptions acknowledged, and receiving transparent communication. Strengthening these elements of patient-centred care may improve healthcare experiences.

articles.title: Congenital visual impairment does not impede the development of infants’ ability to reach to the self
articles.authors: GIULIA CAPPAGLI; Matej Hoffmann; Lisa K Chinn; Jason A.M. Khoury; Jeffrey J. Lockman; Sabrina Signorini; gori monica
articles.abstract: While early visual deprivation can hinder some spatial skills, it can also lead to sensory enhancements. Evidence from visually impaired infants is sparse but suggests preserved unisensory orienting and greater reliance on touch alongside reduced multisensory spatial integration and delayed spatially guided action.1,2 Reaching to touch on the body is a spatial task requiring touch to be remapped relative to body posture. Visual impairment could therefore delay this ability if vision calibrates spatial representations, or preserve or enhance it if attention to somatosensory input supports compensation. We tested sighted, low-vision, and blind infants (6–24 months) reaching to vibrotactile targets. Reaching success was comparable across groups and increased with age. Low-vision infants reached more slowly than sighted infants, whereas blind infants did not differ from sighted infants. Thus, body-centered tactile localization can develop without typical visual experience, although degraded visual input may selectively slow somatosensory guidance of action.

articles.title: A Megastudy of Behavioral Interventions to Increase Voter Registration Ahead of the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
articles.authors: Katherine Anne Mason; Kayley Okst; Don Green; Robb Willer; James Druckman; Jan G. Voelkel; Yash Patel; Claire Robertson; Wooyoung Choi; Jasmine Sanchez
articles.abstract: In the United States, voter registration is required for participation in most elections, yet many eligible individuals remain unregistered. Relatively little is known about how to increase the likelihood that an eligible adult registers to vote. We evaluated 10 expert-crowdsourced interventions among eligible but unregistered U.S. voters (N = 12,927) in an online survey experiment conducted before the 2024 presidential election. The study was powered to detect small attitudinal effects and effects on voter registration and turnout of roughly 3 percentage points. Nine interventions increased self-reported voting intentions, and five increased clicks on the official voter registration website. Escalating Commitment, a social pressure strategy, produced the largest absolute effect on these proximal outcomes. However, none of the interventions significantly increased voter registration or turnout. These findings highlight the challenge of translating shifts in intention into registration behavior, but also identify potentially promising messaging strategies for future large-scale field evaluation.

articles.title: The eyes have it: Perceived ocular vitality as a unifying account of eye-region dominance in social perception
articles.authors: Shiyun Zhang Isabelle
articles.abstract: The eye region has an outsized influence on first impressions of faces. Its surface features, however, have been studied one cue at a time. This narrative integrative review proposes perceived ocular vitality as a unifying construct: an observer-side inference of youthfulness, health, and alertness drawn from the eye and periocular region. Five cue domains are evaluated: periocular contrast, scleral coloration, scleral exposure, limbal ring prominence, and iris luminance and framing. Evidence ranges from strong (periocular contrast; limbal ring health effects) to contested (the direction of the pupil-size effect). Two experimentally confirmed interactions, one so far shown only with non-human primate faces, suggest that the cues work jointly. Together they also expose confounds that single-cue designs miss. Chief among them, the limbal ring health effect appears to be carried substantially by scleral brightening. Within cue-based overgeneralization theory, the construct has two channels with pre-specified routing. Photometric cues carry youth and health to the valence dimension of face evaluation. Structural cues make the eye legible, which observers read as alertness, and are predicted to reach the dominance dimension as well. The construct is specified precisely enough to be falsified, and an analysis of an existing normed corpus could decide it.

articles.title: Caregiver prosody coincides with infant sustained visual attention
articles.authors: Manash Sahoo; Valerie Bambha; Chen Yu; Linda B. Smith; Jeremy Isaac Borjon
articles.abstract: Prosodic modifications in caregiver speech are related to infant attention, word learning, and long-term language development, yet how moment-to-moment caregiver prosody relates to infant attentional dynamics during naturalistic interaction remains unclear. Here, we used unsupervised learning to categorize 12,311 caregiver utterances produced during free play across the second year of life (12-24 months) into four prosodic contour types: fall, hill, rise, and valley. Infant visual attention was measured using head-mounted eye-tracking. Proportions of contour types were stable from 12 to 24 months. Despite this stability, specific contours were temporally coordinated with the onset and offset of infant sustained visual attention (SVA). Rise contours coincided with the initiation of SVA in older infants, beginning approximately one second before onset, and valley contours coincided with the period following SVA offset in both age groups. At the dyad level, two patterns emerged. Caregivers who produced higher levels of vocalizations that coincided with the onset or offset of SVA had infants with more SVA episodes and total SVA time overall. Further, caregivers who exhibited a specific prosodic pattern in the two seconds following SVA disengagement, a fall contour in the first second and a valley contour in the following second, had infants with longer average SVA episodes.  These results dissociate two facets of dyadic temporal coordination: a broad association between caregiver prosody and the quantity of SVA episodes, and a specific post-disengagement prosodic pattern linked to the duration of SVA.

articles.title: Validating the Chinese Version of the Manifestation Scale (CVMS): Translation, Cultural Adaptation and Psychometric Extension
articles.authors: Jiaqi Guo; Lucas J Dixon; Kehan Mei; Mei Shi
articles.abstract: The Manifestation Scale assesses belief in metaphysically attracting success through positive self-talk, visualization, and symbolic actions. We translated and validated a Chinese version (CVMS) in 1,901 Chinese-speaking adults and compared it with data from 1,023 English-speaking participants. Analyses supported correlated Personal Power and Cosmic Collaboration dimensions within a broader general manifestation construct. Cosmic Collaboration was more distinct in the CVMS, and one item contributed more clearly to the general factor than to specific factors. Findings supported an 11-item Total scale, a six-item Personal Power subscale, and a four-item Cosmic Collaboration subscale, with high internal consistency and three-month stability. Partial scalar invariance supported cross-language latent comparisons. Associations with positive thought-action fusion, hope, perceived success, risk propensity, and get-rich-quick beliefs broadly replicated validity, alongside some cross-language differences in how the scale dimensions were related to metaphysical belief. The CVMS provides the first evidence that manifestation belief can be measured beyond Western contexts.

articles.title: Orthographic retrieval unfolds in parallel with single-word production
articles.authors: Jens Roeser; Pablo Aros Muñoz; Markus Damian; Gary Jones; Mark Torrance
articles.abstract: Written word production is often assumed to begin after the relevant spelling has been retrieved. We challenge this pre-onset assumption by asking whether spelling-related processing can continue during output. Across four picture-word interference experiments (Ns = 60, 72, 96, 93), participants typed or spoke picture names while ignoring pronounceable non-word distractors. Distractors either preserved the target-compatible spelling pattern or introduced a phonologically plausible alternative spelling; only the latter should disrupt writing if phonology makes alternative spellings relevant during orthographic retrieval. Bayesian mixed-effects mixture models estimated the probability that response-onset latencies and post-onset intervals came from a longer-duration component. Spelling-mismatch distractors sometimes facilitated onset responses but increased long-duration probability at later timings and within typed words. These late mismatch effects disappeared for spoken responses. These time-course data challenge the classical assumption that written words are mentally prepared as complete spellings before output begins; instead, orthographic retrieval can remain vulnerable to phonologically plausible alternatives during written production.

articles.title: Questionable mediated effect of artificial intelligence anxiety on academic burnout: A comment on Long et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Long et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking artificial intelligence anxiety to academic burnout. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported artificial intelligence anxiety, perceived stress, rumination, and academic burnout are conceptualized as negative indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles.title: Spatial Aspects of Felt Presence and the Phenomenon of Childhood Imaginary Companions: Peripersonal Space, Embodied Perspective, and Continuity of Agent Propensity
articles.authors: Burak; Bigna Lenggenhager
articles.abstract:
Felt presence (FP) refers to the experience of sensing another agent nearby despite the
absence of corresponding sensory evidence, and has been reported across neurological,
psychiatric, and non-clinical populations. However, its potential phenomenological similarity and
continuity with the common childhood experience of imaginary companions (ICs) have received
little attention. The present study characterizes the spatial and perspectival features of
retrospectively reported childhood IC experiences, evaluates their parallels with the
phenomenology of FP, and interprets these convergences within the theoretical framework of
bodily self-consciousness (BSC) and peripersonal space (PPS). Three theory-driven predictions
were tested using retrospective self-reports from a healthy adult sample (N = 185; IC+ = 45; IC−
= 140) excluding participants with psychiatric or neurological diagnoses. First, we examined
whether IC representations were spatially anchored within PPS (Peripersonal Anchoring). Second,
we assessed whether IC experiences were predominantly reported from an embodied, first-person
or third-person perspective. Third, we tested whether individuals reporting childhood ICs show a
greater adult propensity for presence-related experiences (Continuity of Agent Propensity).
Results supported all three predictions. Most spatial distance reports (76.1%) fell within 70 cm of
the body, with an overall median distance of 12 cm, consistent with PPS anchoring. IC experiences
were primarily reported from a first-person perspective (55.6%) and referenced to the body
(88.9%). Furthermore, individuals with childhood ICs reported higher scores on the Sensed
Presence Questionnaire (SenPQ; 15 items, excluding Item 7 due to cross-loading) during
adulthood, whereas dissociative tendencies did not differ between groups. Exploratory logistic
regression identified perceived presence proneness as the only significant predictor of IC history.
Together, these findings suggest that both adult FP and childhood IC experiences may be grounded
in the spatial organization of the bodily action field and reflect a stable disposition for internally
generated social-agent representations.

articles.title: When attention turns inward: Mind wandering reduces perceptual sensitivity across visual fields
articles.authors: Bianca de Haan
articles.abstract: We all mind wander from time to time, where instead of being focussed on our task, we start thinking about task-unrelated personal events or concerns. In daily life, however, mind wandering is often associated with reduced processing of external information. This is commonly explained by the decoupling hypothesis, which posits that processing of external sensory information is attenuated when attention turns inward. However, it remains unclear whether perceptual decoupling reflects a global, uniform attenuation of sensory processing, or a spatially-specific reduction linked to lateralised attentional mechanisms. In the current, pre-registered study, we used an online signal detection task to assess the impact of mind wandering on perceptual performance in the left and right visual fields. While performing the task, participants periodically reported whether they were mind wandering or on task. Consistent with the decoupling hypothesis, perceptual sensitivity (d′) was significantly reduced on trials during which participants reported mind wandering compared to on-task trials. However, this reduction in sensitivity did not differ between stimuli presented in the left and right visual field. These findings suggest that perceptual decoupling during mind wandering reflects a global attenuation of sensory processing, and that attentional systems involved during mind wandering may be distinct from those associated with slower fluctuations of attentional resources such as reductions in alertness.

articles.title: First Frequency, then Transitional Probability: Insights from primate statistical learning
articles.authors: Andreas Lazartigues; Thomas Chartier; Frédéric Lavigne; Joel Fagot; Arnaud Rey
articles.abstract: Statistical learning is a fundamental cognitive capacity, whereby humans and other species extract the structure of sequences based on statistical cues. Among these cues, Transitional Probability (TP) quantifies the probability of the next stimulus given the preceding one(s), while Frequency quantifies the relative occurrence of local sequences. Mechanistic explanations have generally considered TP the prevalent cues, but a role of Frequency cannot be ignored. Yet, the specific contributions of each, and their interaction, are not well understood. Here, we report a simple serial reaction time experiment that 1) provides online, trial-by-trial learning data, 2) allows a clear dissociation of Frequency and TP, 3) excludes the involvement of internal verbalized rules by testing non-human primates (Guinea baboons, Papio papio).
