Our results show that, contrary to the traditional view, Frequency can be the main cue influencing statistical learning. Indeed, we found learning to be primarily determined by Frequency in the first 2,000 trials of the learning phase, while the usual prevalence of TP emerged only later on. These data provide a better understanding of the interactions between statistical factors involved in sequence processing. They also constitute new constraints for computational models of statistical learning and challenge existing results.

articles.title: A multidimensional normative database of experiential ratings for German nouns
articles.authors: Cristina Cara; Christian Bellebaum; Laura Bechtold; Marta Ghio
articles.abstract: Theories of semantic representation propose that concepts are grounded in multiple forms of experience, yet normative resources capturing this multidimensionality remain scarce, especially in German. We present a database of experiential ratings for 1,985 German nouns, with particularly broad coverage of abstract concepts (a 3:1 ratio of abstract to concrete nouns). In total, 354 native German speakers rated the extent to which the meaning of each word is associated with 16 experiential dimensions spanning perceptual, motor, affective, cognitive, social and magnitude-related domains, complemented by concreteness and familiarity ratings. The database additionally provides the dominant experiential dimension of each word and an exclusivity score quantifying how strongly its profile is dominated by a single dimension relative to the others. Cross-database validation against existing German norms showed strong convergence with our concreteness, valence, and arousal ratings. Longitudinal test-retest assessment of all experiential dimensions, as well as concreteness and familiarity, in a subsample of 36 participants showed moderate to high temporal stability across ratings. To characterize the multidimensional structure captured by the database, we further applied exploratory factor analysis followed by hierarchical clustering in the factor-derived semantic space. These analyses identified three broad factors interpreted as socioemotional, perceptual, and magnitude-related, and four clusters of words with distinct experiential profiles. Summary-level and participant-level data are freely available through the project website, which also provides an interactive interface for exploring the norms. The database provides a resource for research on conceptual representation in psycholinguistics, cognitive neuroscience, and computational semantics.

articles.title: Intentions to Help Friends Across Cultural Groups: The Role of Emotional Connectedness
articles.authors: Arzu Karakulak; Michael Bender
articles.abstract: Across five studies (N = 1,859), we examined cross-cultural variation in emotional connectedness and intentions to help a family member, a friend, and a stranger. Samples included a nationally representative Dutch panel (Study 1), Turkish and Dutch students (Study 2), Turkish and German working adults (Study 3), culturally primed Turkish-German biculturals (Study 4), and bilingual Turkish students (Study 5). Contrary to the traditional view that collectivists prioritize in-group ties more strongly than individualists, we hypothesized greater intentions to help friends among participants from relatively individualistic contexts or primed with an individualistic cultural frame. Results consistently supported the hypothesized differences for intentions to help friends, while differences in intentions to help a family member and a stranger were less consistent and generally not reliable. Study 1 further suggested that emotional connectedness statistically accounted for group differences in intentions to help friends, and Study 5 provided tentative converging evidence that an English-language prime was associated with greater connectedness with friends than a Turkish-language prime. Together, these findings suggest that considering the role of particular relational targets within their cultural context may provide a more differentiated account of cross-cultural variation in helping than broad individualism–collectivism or in-group–out-group classifications alone.

articles.title: Vocal Evaluation of Classical Singing in a Concert Hall: Perceptual and Acoustic Associations with Overall Scores in Male and Female Singers
articles.authors: Haruka Kondo; Sotaro Kondoh; Shinya Fujii
articles.abstract:
Introduction. In classical vocal competitions, judges reduce a performance to a single overall score, yet what that score reflects is unclear. Research has separately identified the perceptual attributes experts use and the acoustic features of trained singers. Few studies link these to expert evaluation, and those that do have used playback of sound-treated recordings and rarely tested for sex differences. Yet classical singing is judged live in halls, and male and female voices differ acoustically. We asked which attributes and acoustic features are associated with the overall score in a concert hall, and whether they differ by sex.
Methods. Twenty-two classical singers (10 males, 12 females) performed Caro mio ben a cappella in a concert hall. Five singer-instructors rated each performance on a 100-point overall score and 7-point scales for six vocal attributes. Singing power ratio (SPR), loudness units full scale (LUFS), vibrato rate (VR), and vibrato extent (VE) were computed from annotated vowel segments of close-microphone recordings. Linear mixed-effects models related the overall score to the ratings or acoustic features, with sex interactions and a random judge intercept.
Results. Higher ratings of vibrato, resonance, and expressiveness were associated with higher overall scores, whereas timbre, diction, and intonation were not. Higher SPR, greater VE, and lower VR were associated with higher overall scores, whereas LUFS was not. Sex interacted with VE and VR but not with SPR or LUFS: the VE association was stronger in females, the VR association in males.
Conclusion. Overall scores were associated with perceived vibrato, resonance, and expressiveness, and with spectral prominence at 2–4 kHz. Vibrato associations were sex-dependent: a faster rate accompanied lower scores in males, a greater extent higher scores in females. These findings give expert evaluation a measurable basis under realistic conditions and indicate that vibrato should be interpreted with reference to singer sex.

articles.title: Divided attention during encoding constrains the benefits of interim testing for subsequent learning
articles.authors: Bernhard Pastötter; Karl-Heinz Bäuml
articles.abstract: Retrieval practice can enhance learning of subsequently studied target information, a phenomenon known as the forward testing effect or test-potentiated new learning. The present study examined whether this effect depends on attentional engagement during encoding. In two experiments, participants studied three lists of unrelated words (Experiment 1) or three educationally relevant prose passages (Experiment 2). After the first two learning blocks, they either restudied the material or were tested on it. Attention during encoding of the final target material was manipulated by a concurrent secondary task. Under full attention, interim testing enhanced recall of the final target material in both experiments and improved performance on a final knowledge transfer test in Experiment 2. Under divided attention, these effects were reduced in Experiment 1 and eliminated in Experiment 2. The findings indicate that the beneficial effect of interim testing depends critically on attention during encoding of the latter studied information.

articles.title: Music as Emotional Regulation in the Climate Crisis: Relationships with Eco-Anxiety, Eco-Guilt, and Eco-Grief
articles.authors: Friederike Koehler; Dana Swarbrick; Suvi Saarikallio
articles.abstract:
Background: Climate change increasingly evokes complex emotional responses, yet little is known about how everyday practices, such as music listening, relate to these emotions. Given that music is one of the most common tools people use to manage affect in daily life, examining its role in the climate context offers huge potential for insights into eco-emotional experiences. 
Methods: 312 adults completed an online survey on music‑based mood regulation and eco‑anxiety, eco‑grief, and eco‑guilt. Associations were examined using structural equation modelling.
Results: Zero-order bivariate correlations indicated positive correlations between eco-emotions and all music-based mood regulation strategies except for entertainment. Structural equation models further revealed two distinct patterns: using music for mental work, discharge, solace, and strong sensation were associated with higher levels of eco‑distress, whereas entertainment, revival, and diversion were linked to lower distress. This suggests that when distressing climate emotions arise, individuals who experience them more intensely may immerse themselves more deeply in their emotional processing through music, while those who experience less distress may use music in lighter, recreational ways. Qualitative responses showed that individuals use music in diverse ways to navigate climate emotions, including calming listening, engaging with climate‑themed lyrics, creative expression, community, and nature‑evoking soundscapes, while others reported no connection. 
Conclusions: Findings highlight music as a meaningful yet heterogeneous context in which people relate to climate emotions, offering new insight into the emotional dimensions of the climate crisis. Through integrating music psychology and climate-emotion research, the study underlines the value of everyday cultural practices as part of individual and collective adaptation.

articles.title: Inhabiting digital ecologies: A qualitative approach to good digital practices
articles.authors: Esther Paniagua; Myriam Durán Vilches; Noemí Robles; Pepa Barral González; Manuel Armayones
articles.abstract:
The integration of digital technologies into everyday life has produced complex digital
ecologies in which platforms, algorithms, and social practices jointly shape experience,
identity, and emotional regulation. Although research on digital well-being has
increased significantly, little is known about how individuals reflect on their digital lives
and the practical criteria they develop to navigate these environments while preserving
well-being and autonomy.,This paper addresses these questions through qualitative
research conducted within a digital community of 100 adults residing in Spain whose
participation unfolded across four successive waves. Fieldwork combined individual
journals, thematic forums, and an open social space, generating a longitudinal corpus
on the everyday experience of inhabiting digital spaces. Results were interpreted
through discourse analysis to reconstruct shared patterns of meaning and discursive
positions.,Findings reveal an ambivalent relationship with digital environments: the
same tools that enable connection, communication, and access to information are also
described as sources of noise, overstimulation, attention fragmentation, and loss of
control. Alongside these discomforts, participants describe daily repertoires of
adjustment that crystallise into distinct discursive positions from which they inhabit
digital ecologies and develop good practices.,We propose that good digital practices
should not be understood as a universal list of self-regulatory norms, but as relational
competencies developed through reflection and experience. Methodologically, the
study shows that a digital community is a particularly suitable tool for examining
everyday, complex, largely automated phenomena, since it enables participants to
observe, compare, and transform their digital experience into practical criteria guiding
their relationship with digital ecologies.

articles.title: Questionable mediated effect of family functioning on college students’ differentiation of the self: A comment on Luo et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Luo et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking family malfunctioning to decreased differentiation of self. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported family malfunctioning, loneliness, psychological security, and differentiation of self are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles.title: Made in the Culture, Not the Voice: Lyrical Camp, Production Texture, and the Queer Anthemization of Popular Songs
articles.authors: Logan Barrett
articles.abstract: Why do some popular songs become queer anthems while others, including many by openly queer artists, do not? We tested musical affordance and historical contingency accounts in a purposive corpus of 100 songs (69 artists) designed to dissociate queer authorship, explicit queer lyrical content, and community adoption. Adoption was measured as an evidence-coded anthemization score from URL-verified documentation of Pride, drag, ballroom, club, activist, and queer-media use. Anthemization was unrelated to whether artists were publicly queer (rs = −.02) and only weakly related to explicit queer lyrics (rs = .22). Among 16 language-model-coded lyrical themes, camp potential predicted anthemization after family-wise correction and controls for era, genre, authorship, and explicit content (partial r = .40, n = 55). The association replicated with masked lyrics, among songs the coding model could not identify, with a second coding model, and with two independent outcome coders (partial r = .45–.54, n = 46), although it was not robust when the model's own anthem judgements were also partialled out. Full-mix acoustic descriptors related to formant energy and voicing predicted anthemization (|rs| = .38–.43, family-wise p < .05) but vanished when computed on Demucs-separated vocal stems (n = 80), locating the acoustic signal in production texture rather than the singer's voice; spectral brightness was confounded by genre and era. Outcome reliability was moderate (weighted κ = .57). The results support reception-centred accounts of musical queerness. They implicate lyrical camp and production as affordances for queer adoption, not a characteristic queer voice.

articles.title: One Gender Axis, Two Vocabularies: How People Conceptualize Gendered Speaking and Singing Voices
articles.authors: Logan Barrett
articles.abstract: Gender-affirming voice care is organized around speech, yet many people also want to change how they sing. Whether the two rest on one concept of vocal gender is unknown. Participants (N = 2,536) described what makes a speaking voice and a singing voice sound feminine and masculine, rated their current and ideal voices in each modality, and named people whose speaking and singing voices they would like to have. I embedded the descriptions with a sentence encoder and analyzed them, together with word frequencies, in exploratory analyses. The feminine–masculine direction in speaking descriptions was nearly identical to the direction in singing descriptions (cosine = .967), and a classifier trained on one modality separated the other with almost no loss (area under the curve = .960 and .979). The shared direction was carried by register, softness, and depth words; singing descriptions added range, notes, and power, and speaking descriptions added softness, roughness, and monotony. Individuals’ own contrasts aligned only modestly across modalities (mean cosine = .362). Wanting a more feminine speaking voice predicted choosing a female singer but not a more acoustically feminine singer within gender category. Vocal gender appears to be a shared, category-level abstraction expressed in modality-specific vocabulary.

articles.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to estimate how common alcohol references and alcohol-related brand references are among influencers on Instagram
articles.authors: Jack Delmenico; Dan Anderson-Luxford; Emmanuel Kuntsche; Jingda Du; Zhen Du; Megan Cook; Charlotte Jonhston; Paula O'Brien; Simone Pettigrew; Benjamin Riordan
articles.abstract:
Background: Young people spend hours on social media every day, where following influencers is the norm. Influencers post frequently about alcohol and alcohol brands and there has been a rise in influencer marketing. However, prevalence estimates rely on manual analyses of only a small number of posts. We used a large language model (LLM) to estimate at scale how often top Australian Instagram influencers reference alcohol and alcohol brands, and whether this varies by influencer type.
Methods: We identified 988 of the most-followed Australian Instagram influencers and retrieved all 667,531 of their posts that were visible to all users, including those under 18 (i.e., not age gated). An LLM classified whether each post referenced alcohol and these were screened manually to record brand references. Influencers were coded into 14 types (e.g., athletes, actors).
Results: Most influencers (87.45%) referenced alcohol and 47.10% referenced an alcohol brand in at least one post. Overall, 20,448 posts (3.06%) referenced alcohol and 2,869 (0.43%) a brand (14% of alcohol-related posts). Food influencers posted the most alcohol and brand-related content, while athletes posted the least alcohol-related content but had the highest proportion referencing a brand.
Conclusions: Influencer alcohol-related and alcohol-related brand content is pervasive on Instagram and reaches audiences of every age, including those under 18 who should not see alcohol advertising.
So what: Given the link between exposure and use, health promotion should aim policies and strategies at reducing alcohol-related content, particularly branded content that likely reflects influencer marketing.

articles_hidden.title: Poor reliability in measuring habituation: Implications for clinical and translational research on exposure and extinction
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Dear; Gabrielle Rose Messner; Julia Levitan; Richie Ward Gray; Cheri A Levinson; Eric Lenze; Jaclyn Weisman; Thomas Rodebaugh
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: The purpose of this study was to investigate the reliability of change indices in exposure therapy. 
Method: We analyzed data from 119 adults with elevated social anxiety who participated in studies of public speaking exposures. Participants reported their distress using the Subjective Units of Distress Scale (SUDS) at regular intervals. The reliability of within-session habituation, between-session habituation, and expectancy change measures were estimated. 
Results: Commonly used measures of between-session habituation (BSH) typically demonstrated only moderate reliability, and commonly used measures of within-session habituation (WSH) typically demonstrated poor reliability. Exploratory tests in expectancy change indices suggests these findings apply to other measures of change during exposure.  
Conclusions: Our results indicate that measures underlying the study of habituation may be inadequate because of low reliability. This threatens the foundation of clinical and translational research, such that no substantive conclusions can be drawn from them.

articles_hidden.title: Reward Contingency Shapes Incidental Reward Effects on Cognitive Flexibility
articles_hidden.authors: Joseph M Orr; Beatrice Lomeo; Juan Balcazar; Daniela Porro
articles_hidden.abstract: Voluntary task switching (VTS) provides a useful paradigm for examining how recent reward outcomes are associated with the balance between cognitive stability and flexibility. We investigated whether reward-history effects on task choice varied as a function of cue–outcome contingency. Participants (N = 616) completed a VTS task with performance-contingent rewards. Reward contingency was manipulated between-subjects at probabilities of100\%, 80\%, 70\%, and 60\%. Switch probability was modeled using logistic mixed-effects regression. The relationship between prior reward outcomes and the current reward prospect in predicting switch behavior differed across probability conditions. Reward transition effects were larger at 100\% and 80\% than at 70\% and 60\%. Secondary analyses further indicated that outcomes that were unexpected given the cue–reward mapping were associated with subsequent switching in some comparisons, although evidence that these associations systematically varied with probability was mixed. Because task choices did not influence reward outcomes, the observed effects are more consistent with carry-over associations between reward history and task selection than with reward-guided exploration or reward maximization. Exploratory individual-differences analyses suggested that reward transition effects were more pronounced in males than in females; additionally, trait-level reward sensitivity moderated the magnitude of reward transition effects on switch behavior. Overall, the findings are consistent with the hypothesis that cue-outcome contingency modulates the extent to which recent rewards are followed by particular task-choice patterns, although further research is required to clarify the mechanisms through which reward uncertainty may contribute to these effects.

articles_hidden.title: Feeling the heat: How climate emotions shape trust in government and policy support across 68 countries
articles_hidden.authors: Jlenia Avellino; Fabienne Stucki; Omid Ghasemi; Viktoria Cologna; Theofilos Gkinopoulos; Niels G. Mede; Stylianos Syropoulos; Sebastian Berger
articles_hidden.abstract: Negative emotions related to climate change can adversely impact people’s mental health and wellbeing. However, they could also accelerate action on climate change by driving support for environmental policies. Using the TISP Many Labs data, we present results from a cross-sectional secondary analysis of survey responses from 69,534 participants across 68 countries worldwide. The survey included items on people’s emotional response to climate change, perceptions of government responses to climate change, and support for environmental policies. Participants experienced relatively low levels of negative emotions toward climate change (M = 2.79, SD = 1.01; 1 = not at all, 5 = very strongly), with relatively little variation across countries (SD = 0.27). Individuals reporting stronger negative emotions were less satisfied with their government’s climate action and expressed greater support for environmental policies. Our results thereby contribute to a global assessment of climate emotions and its correlates, crucially augmenting past research that has been more limited in global scope.

articles_hidden.title: Multilevel meta-analyses of emotional processing deficits associated with callous-unemotional (CU) traits: Do they differ by age and sex?
articles_hidden.authors: Emily C. Kemp; Paul Frick; Taylor Miller; Julianne Speck; David Gertz; Zeying Du
articles_hidden.abstract: Callous-unemotional (CU) traits, defined by deficient empathy and remorse, characterize a distinct subgroup of antisocial individuals with more severe behavioral problems and unique affective profiles. Two processes implicated in the development of CU traits are hyporeactivity to and inaccurate recognition of others’ emotions. Although many studies link CU traits to emotional processing deficits, findings have been inconsistent across age and sex. We conducted multilevel meta-analyses of emotional reactivity and recognition, accounting for age and sex as moderators, to clarify these discrepancies. A four-level meta-analysis indicated CU traits were negatively associated with emotional reactivity to both broad emotional stimuli (r = -.23, p < .0001; k = 106, n = 402) and distress-specific stimuli (r = -.22, p < .0001; k = 83, n = 234), with no moderation by age or sex. Similarly, a three-level meta-analysis showed CU traits were negatively associated with recognition accuracy for both broad facial emotions (r = -.09, p < .0001; k = 97, n = 437) and distress (e.g., fear, sadness; r = -.10, p < .0001; k = 60, n = 140). Sample age moderated broad (r = .003, p = .01) and distress (r = .004, p = .04) recognition deficits, such that effects diminished with sample age. These results have important implications for causal theories of CU traits and support emotional hyporreactivity as a core deficit that may cause delays in the development of emotion recognition abilities. Such developmental changes have implications for improving treatments for individuals with elevated CU traits.

articles_hidden.title: From Lab to Life: Stress Beliefs and the Stress Optimization Model in Everyday Stress
articles_hidden.authors: Lara Oeltjen; Susanne Fischer; Johannes Andreas Christoph Laferton
articles_hidden.abstract: Individuals’ beliefs about stress have been linked to health and performance. The stress optimization model proposes regulatory strategies through which these beliefs may shape stress responses, but evidence for these mechanisms comes largely from laboratory research.  We investigated whether these mechanisms generalize to everyday life in a 14-day ecological momentary assessment study of N = 173 university students (86% women, M_age = 22.6). Multilevel models examined associations of stress beliefs with stress regulation strategies, affect and somatic symptoms. Stress beliefs were associated with several regulation strategies on the between-person level, but explained little variability in how regulation changed with increasing stress intensity. Associations with affective and somatic responses were limited. Thus, laboratory-derived stress-belief mechanisms appear to generalize only partially to everyday life. We discuss advantages of laboratory and daily-life research on this topic. Interpretation is limited by a homogenous sample, potentially missed event-contingent assessments and independently modeling regulatory processes.

articles_hidden.title: Investigating the Possible Prevalence of AI Bots in Project Implicit Research Pool Studies
articles_hidden.authors: Imane Farah; Jordan Axt
articles_hidden.abstract: Due to an increased usage of AI agents in online behavioural research, several detection methods have been developed to ensure that data responses are from human participants. However, vision-enabled AI agents (e.g., ChatGPT, Perplexity Comet) are still able to complete studies that utilize traditional detection methods. Thus, the following study used the Cognitive Trap Framework introduced by Affonso (2026), which consists of six questions that are easy for human participants to complete but difficult for AI agents to process. A total of 410 participants on the Project Implicit platform completed the six "cognitive trap" questions. Participants failed an average of 0.78 questions, with only 5.61% of the sample failing three or more of the questions. Results indicate that the use of AI agents on the Project Implicit platform may be low at this time.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond the Child: Reframing Autism Research Through a Contextual, Transactional, Developmental Model
articles_hidden.authors: Judah Koller; Yonat Rum
articles_hidden.abstract: Heterogeneity in autistic development is usually attributed to variation in child-level characteristics. We argue that it is better understood as the output of a process. The child and family system continually calibrates the balance between environmental demands and available capacities, and those calibrations accumulate. When demand exceeds capacity, families lower demand, often through accommodation, or raise capacity through scaffolding and support. Each calibration changes what the system brings to the next encounter. Iterated across daily life and developmental transitions, this process pulls trajectories apart, producing what has been termed chronogeneity. The components of this account are established, but they have been invoked separately, and the field still largely models the child alone. This leaves basic questions unanswered, including why children who start in similar places diverge, why the same response helps in one family and constrains in another, and why divergence concentrates at developmental transitions. This paper is the first to specify a family-system mechanism that accounts for all three, and to establish that it cannot be described without three interlocking elements. Context defines the demands the system faces. Transactions are the operations through which calibration occurs. Development is how each calibration alters the terms of the next. The model identifies the fit between demands and capacities, rather than focusing on the child alone, as what assessment should measure, what intervention and policy should target, and what outcome measures should index, and it generates testable predictions about when and why trajectories diverge.

articles_hidden.title: CAVL: A Cognitive Architecture for Vigilant Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Jean-Sébastien Vayre
articles_hidden.abstract: Newell’s challenge remains: experiments often study cognitive mechanisms separately, although real learning requires their coordination. We present CAVL, a functional, multilevel, precomputational architecture of socially embedded vigilant learning. It links working memory, long-term knowledge, expertise, epistemic vigilance, source representation, metacognition, and social context. Structural embedding shapes knowledge, opportunities, and verification costs. Interactional embedding shapes how learners evaluate claims and their sources. CAVL makes three testable claims. First, valid prior knowledge and processing conditions alter the balance between content quality and attributed authority. Second, private acceptance can diverge from public expression when social costs are high. Third, unequal cognitive resources and allocated epistemic credit jointly shape participation and later learning. Six propositions specify critical tests and reasons to revise the architecture. CAVL treats ecological validity as a problem for research, not as a label attached to realistic settings. It proposes controlled and systematically varied experiments that preserve relevant person–task–environment relations. Its purpose is to connect experimentally established mechanisms with socially situated learning, not to replace controlled experiments or existing theories.

articles_hidden.title: Hyper-Expressions: AI-Generated Faces Emulate and Amplify Stereotypical Human Emotions
articles_hidden.authors: Chen Reshef; Hillel Aviezer; Ariel Goldstein
articles_hidden.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) models are capable of generating highly realistic human images with a tendency to stereotypically bias race and gendered features. These models also readily generate emotional faces, but little is known about the perceptual nature of these expressions. To examine if AI-generated facial expressions emulate similar characteristics to human posed stereotypical facial expressions, we compared the perception of emotions from AI generated facial images to classic sets of human actors posing facial emotions in a stereotypical manner. Across two experiments (total N = 648), participants rated AI-generated and human-posed facial expressions on multiple emotion scales. Study 1 focused on expressions generated by Midjourney (N = 498), and Study 2 replicated the experiment using Google’s Nano Banana 2 (N = 150 . Confusion patterns were remarkably similar across Human and AI-generated expressions, and exploratory factor analysis revealed that the underlying dimensional structure of emotion perception was nearly identical for AI-generated and human-posed expressions), demonstrating their generalizability across image-generation models. Interestingly, some AI-generated emotion categories were rated with higher accuracy and reduced confusability than human posed stereotypical expressions, a finding most robust in Nano Banana 2. This suggests that AI-generated expressions  are even more stereotypical and intense than stereotypically posed human expressions, a phenomenon we term Hyper-Expressions. Taken together, the findings suggest that generative AI not only captures stereotypical patterns of emotion expression, but also amplifies and biases them. Results are discussed in the context of current debates between basic emotion and constructional theories of emotion perception.

articles_hidden.title: Head-Mounted Augmented Reality Enhances Affective and Perceptual Responses to Simulated Vigorous Intermittent Lifestyle Physical Activity
articles_hidden.authors: Jonathan M. Bird; Henry Potts; Harold Kwong; Jingyi Zhang; John J Mitchell; Aidan Acquah; Joanna Blodgett; Abigail Fisher; Anthony Steed; Nikos Ntoumanis
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: Vigorous intermittent lifestyle physical activity (VILPA) refers to brief and sporadic (e.g., up to 2 min) bouts of vigorous physical activity performed as part of daily living (e.g., stair climbing, very fast walking). VILPA offers several accessibility advantages over structured exercise and confers substantial health benefits. However, there is a paucity of scalable interventions designed to enhance the VILPA experience. The primary aim of the study was to examine the effects of a novel head-mounted augmented reality application on affective and perceptual responses during and following a simulated VILPA bout. Methods: A counterbalanced within-subjects design was employed and 24 physically inactive adults (Nfemale = 14, Mage = 26.12 years, SDage = 3.56 years) completed 2-min bouts of vigorous-intensity incline walking under three experimental augmented reality conditions (i.e., motivational prompts, virtual pet, and gamification) and a no-technology control. Dependent variables included affective valence, arousal, perceived exertion, state attention, enjoyment, remembered pleasure, and heart rate responses. Data were analysed using linear mixed models. Results: The virtual pet and gamification experimental conditions elicited more positive affective valence (95% CI [0.41, 1.59], d = 1.13; 95% CI [0.33, 1.50], d = 1.03), greater attentional dissociation (95% CI [8.43, 21.99], d = 1.48; 95% CI [15.09, 28.66], d = 2.13), and higher ratings of enjoyment (95% CI [3.29, 8.62], d = 1.48; 95% CI [3.59, 8.91], d = 1.55) and remembered pleasure (95% CI [10.72, 39.12], d = 1.16; 95% CI [7.38, 35.78], d = 1.01), when compared to control. Motivational prompts did not enhance the VILPA experience relative to control. Conclusion: The findings provide initial evidence that augmented reality technology can enhance affective and perceptual responses to a simulated VILPA bout.

articles_hidden.title: Language-based Assessments for Experienced Well-being: Accuracy and External Validity Across Behaviors, Traits, and States
articles_hidden.authors: August Nilsson; Ryan Boyd; Adithya V Ganesan; Oscar Nils Erik Kjell; Syeda Mahwish; Haitao Huang; Richard N. Rosenthal; Lyle H Ungar; H. Andrew Schwartz
articles_hidden.abstract: Self-reported rating scales have been central to social science for decades, even though language is our primary form of communication. We used language analysis with machine learning to compare self-reported ratings with language-based responses of experienced well-being (i.e., daily emotions) linked with human traits, states, and behaviors.  In a sample of 764 U.S. service workers who reported their feelings daily for up to 12 weeks, responses were provided in 1) numerical ratings, 2) short essays, and 3) descriptive words. When predicting nine self-rated affective traits, essays were slightly less accurate than the ratings (r = .49 v .55, p < .001), while the word-based responses slightly outperformed the ratings (r = .53 vs .51, p < .001). For external predictive validity across 24 traits, demographics, and behaviors, both language formats doubled the ratings’ accuracy, with words reaching an average of r = .18 and essays r = .24 (p < .001). Beyond their greater accuracy, both language formats offered rich psychological insights, with words focusing on emotions and essays encompassing broader life domains. While both language-based formats showed advantages and disadvantages, each demonstrated greater information-richness than traditional rating scales.

articles_hidden.title: Achievement Goals for Teaching
articles_hidden.authors: Martin Daumiller; Markus Dresel
articles_hidden.abstract: This chapter synthesizes research on teacher achievement goals, highlighting teachers as a theoretically informative population within achievement goal theory. Unlike students, teachers occupy a dual role as both architects of learning and achievement environments for students and learners and achievers themselves. We review the historical development and taxonomy of the teacher goal concept, including teaching-specific refinements such as relational goals and the distinction between task and learning goals. The analysis extends to the antecedents, consequences, and temporal dynamics of these goals, with particular attention to professional learning, well-being, and instructional behavior. Drawing on research in schools and higher education, we examine the processes through which teachers’ personal achievement goals may become relevant for student motivation and learning through their student-oriented goals, instructional behavior, and classroom goal structures. Finally, we discuss how considering the reasons underlying goal pursuit can advance research on teachers’ professional learning. This goal-complex perspective connects teachers’ aims with the broader meaning of their pursuit and provides a basis for investigating how goals and reasons relate to learning behavior and competence development.

articles_hidden.title: Personality Differences among Men and Women of Various Sexual Orientations, Including Asexual and Pansexual Individuals
articles_hidden.authors: Jakub Fořt; Dominika Benešová; Petr Freudenfeld; Jaroslava Varella Valentova; Jan Havlicek
articles_hidden.abstract: Several theoretical approaches explain variance in personality related to sexual orientation. Drawing on the minority stress theory and the gender shift hypothesis, this study explores personality differences across people of various sexual orientations, including underrepresented groups, such as asexual and pansexual individuals. The minority stress theory posits that non-heterosexual individuals experience heightened social stressors, contributing to higher neuroticism. The gender shift hypothesis further suggests that prenatal hormonal influences may lead to sex-atypical development, explaining some personality variation in sexual minorities. Using a large Czech and Slovak sample (N = 6,476), we administered the Big Five Inventory (BFI-10) to heterosexual (N = 2,598), gay/lesbian (N = 1,943), bisexual (N = 1,412), pansexual (N = 389), and asexual (N = 165) cisgender individuals. We found that non-heterosexual men scored higher in neuroticism than heterosexual men, consistent with both the minority stress and gender shift hypotheses. Pansexual and bisexual individuals of either sex were higher in openness to experience than heterosexual individuals, and asexual individuals scored lower in extraversion than same-sex individuals of any other sexual orientation. We recorded mixed results for conscientiousness. No differences were found in levels of agreeableness. Effect sizes of the recorded differences are, except for few, generally small.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring Emotion Differentiation: A Systematic Review of Current Practices, Methodological Concerns, and Directions for Future Research
articles_hidden.authors: Ilaria Telazzi; Michela Zambelli; Stefania Balzarotti
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Emotion differentiation (ED) is the ability to represent emotional experiences with nuance and specificity. Because it is defined as an ability, ED requires performance-based measures, which makes its assessment particularly challenging and has led to highly heterogeneous operationalizations across the literature.
Objective: The present systematic review has three main objectives. First, it systematically maps how performance-based ED has been conceptualized and operationalized across literature. Second, it identifies the main methodological concerns associated with current operationalizations. Finally, it derives recommendations for transparent reporting and a research agenda to strengthen the ED measurement.
Methods: Following a preregistered protocol, we searched Scopus, PsycInfo, PubMed, and Web of Science from inception to January 2025. Three reviewers independently screened records and extracted data. Peer-reviewed empirical studies of non-clinical adult samples were included.
Results: Ninety-six articles (115 studies) met the inclusion criteria. The results showed high variability in ED conceptualizations and operationalizations within and across three main methodological dimensions: Measurement approach (ecological vs. nonecological), emotion vocabulary (predefined labels vs. natural language), and computational procedures to derive ED indices. Key methodological choices were frequently unreported.
Conclusions: Heterogeneity across methodological dimensions raises distinct concerns for the validity, reliability, replicability, generalizability, and cross-study comparability of ED measures. Critically, this heterogeneity reflects not only methodological variation but also different assumptions about what counts as evidence of the ability to differentiate emotions. Research requires aligning the theoretical meaning of ED, the information collected, and the assumptions used to derive scores. We propose reporting guidelines and future directions for refining the assessment of ED.

articles_hidden.title: The Memory We Miss: Exploratory Behavior as a Window into Developmental Recognition Processes
articles_hidden.authors: Eleanor G. Williamson; Jesse Cushman; Patrese A Robinson
articles_hidden.abstract: Recognition memory tasks are among the most widely used approaches for studying learning and memory across the lifespan, yet the behavioral measures used to assess memory performance, particularly during developmental studies, remain limited. In most rodent studies, recognition memory is inferred almost exclusively from discrimination ratios or discrimination indices that quantify preferential exploration of novel stimuli. While these measures have proven valuable, their widespread use may constrain our understanding of the behavioral and cognitive processes that support nuanced memory expression across ontogeny. Similar concerns have emerged in the fear conditioning literature, where expanding analyses beyond freezing behavior has revealed previously unrecognized differences in learning and memory. In this perspective, we argue that recognition memory research would benefit from a comparable expansion of behavioral analyses. Drawing on affordance-based approaches to object exploration, we discuss evidence showing that object properties influence both memory performance and exploratory behavior. More importantly, our recent findings indicate that juvenile (but not adult) rats exhibit task-dependent shifts in exploratory behavior, contingent on the object's specific affordance, which are not captured by traditional discrimination measures.  These findings suggest that developmental differences in memory may be expressed not only through recognition performance but also through the exploratory strategies animals employ during learning and retrieval. Expanding behavioral analyses in recognition memory tasks may therefore reveal developmental neurobehavioral mechanisms that remain hidden from conventional metrics, providing a more complete understanding of memory development. The challenge moving forward is not simply to determine whether young animals remember, but to identify how they remember and whether the behavioral routes to successful memory change across development.

articles_hidden.title: No Evidence that Retrieval Practice Facilitates Cortical Memory Integration: Insights from Novel Word Semantic Priming
articles_hidden.authors: Lewis Vincent Ball; M. Gareth Gaskell
articles_hidden.abstract: According to the Rapid Consolidation Hypothesis (RCH), retrieving new information from memory integrates the corresponding memory representations into cortical long-term memory, leading to longer-term memory benefits than restudy or rehearsal. However, this prediction has not been empirically tested. We explored this in the current study by comparing semantic priming effects between novel words taught under retrieval practice and restudy conditions. Words are more effective at priming (speeding up) the recognition of semantically related words once they have integrated with related knowledge in cortical language networks. According to the RCH, semantic priming should therefore be enhanced for novel words taught via retrieval practice. In a learning phase, participants learned 20 novel words and their definitions (e.g., blontack - a type of cat) under restudy conditions and 20 under retrieval practice conditions by retrieving part of the definition (e.g., blontack - a type of ___). The novel words, and a set of familiar words, then served as prime words for related (e.g., dog) and unrelated target words in a primed lexical decision task, both immediately after learning and ~48 hrs later. Familiar prime words successfully primed the recognition of related target words in both tasks. The definitions of novel words taught under retrieval practice were recalled more accurately ~48 hrs later than the restudy condition. However, we found no significant priming effects in either learning condition or task, with exploratory Bayesian analyses revealing moderate evidence in favour of the null hypothesis. Our findings suggest that retrieval practice facilitates the longer-term retention of novel words and their definitions, but may not support their integration with related knowledge in language networks. However, methodological factors could have attenuated the scope for semantic priming with novel words, with future research required to continue this investigation.

articles_hidden.title: Valence Automatically Elicits Vowel Articulation
articles_hidden.authors: Saru Parajuli; Charlotte Sophie Löffler; Ralf Rummer; Anita Körner
articles_hidden.abstract: The association between vowels and valence is known as valence sound symbolism. For example, the vowel /i/ (as in English "meet") is associated with more positive valence than the vowel /o/ (as in German “Boot”). The present experiment employs an implicit paradigm to determine whether valence sound symbolism, like size and shape sound symbolism, operates automatically. Participants (N = 47) classified valenced facial expressions by articulating the target vowels /i/ or /o/. Specifically, in the congruent blocks, participants were instructed to say /i/ for happy and /o/ for angry faces, and in the incongruent blocks, to say /i/ for angry and /o/ for happy faces. Response initiation times were faster in congruent compared to incongruent blocks. An additional analysis of acoustic parameters revealed a significant interaction between congruency and vowel type for pitch (f0). Specifically, /i/ was produced with higher pitch in the congruent blocks (happy faces) than in the incongruent blocks (angry faces), whereas /o/ was produced with higher pitch in the incongruent blocks (happy faces) than in the congruent blocks (angry faces). In sum, the present results indicate that the association between vowels and valence operates automatically, thereby contributing to our knowledge of cognitive processing during valence sound symbolism.

articles_hidden.title: Of Two Minds: A registered replication
articles_hidden.authors: Frederik Aust; Tobias Heycke; Benedek Kurdi; Pieter Van Dessel; Jeremy Cone; Melissa Ferguson; Xiaoqing Hu; Elsa Congjiao Jiang; Robert Rydell; Lisa Spitzer
articles_hidden.abstract: Several dual-process theories of social evaluation posit that implicit (or automatic) and explicit (or non-automatic) evaluations reflect distinct attitudes acquired via qualitatively different learning processes. Consequently, one may explicitly like a person but dislike them implicitly. Rydell et al. (2006) reported a striking demonstration of this dissociation: Briefly flashed negative words paired with a person described as behaving positively produced positive ratings of that person but negative Implicit Association Test scores. However, Heycke et al. (2018) could not replicate this dissociation. In two new replication attempts (N = 593) across four countries and three languages, with words flashed between 13 and 27 ms, we too found overwhelming evidence against the dissociation between directly and indirectly measured evaluations. We conclude that the dissociative evaluative learning effect reported by Rydell et al. (2006) is replicably non-replicable.

articles_hidden.title: The contribution of retrieval processes to behavioural markers of event segmentation
articles_hidden.authors: Qiying Liu; Jordan Gunn; Tobias Sommer; Deborah Talmi
articles_hidden.abstract: Event segmentation divides continuous experience into discrete events. Previous research suggests that poorer temporal order memory and higher temporal distance ratings for pairs of items that were encoded across a boundary, compared to those encoded within the same event, serve as behavioural markers of event boundary perception. Four pre-registered experiments challenge the widely accepted interpretation that these effects depend solely on processes that occur during the encoding of event boundaries. We found that temporal order memory and temporal distance judgments depend critically on associative and reconstructive memory at retrieval, specifically memory for each item's event-defining source and for the order of those sources. Retrieval processes determined both the magnitude and direction of effects typically attributed solely to encoding processes. We outline a new retrieved-context model variant that distinguishes object- and event-based contextual evidence for temporal judgments. Our findings suggest that greater caution is required when interpreting behavioural markers of event segmentation.

articles_hidden.title: Worry is underpinned by persistence in searching uninformative avenues
articles_hidden.authors: Alexis An Yee Low; Karl Friston; Michael Moutoussis
articles_hidden.abstract: Worry is common both in mental health and distress. What, then, distinguishes pathological worry? We hypothesized that what characterizes pathological worry is excessive internal search that fails to resolve uncertainty; i.e., is uninformative. In an information sampling paradigm, increased sampling was predicted both by trait (p = .018) and—more powerfully—state worry (p < .001). An information-poor environment significantly increased sampling in high worriers (p < 0.001, CrI 1.1% inside Region of Practical Equivalence defined as <0.2 SD), but not low worriers (p = 0.480, CrI 68.2% in ROPE). Crucially, this increase in sampling in high worriers did not increase their accuracy (CrI 97.5% inside ROPE). A ‘sampling until success’ heuristic was identified as a driver. Stimulus uncertainty and aversiveness had similar effects on sampling and worry, increasing both (p < 0.001). Persistent searching—in the face of irreducible uncertainty—may therefore be a key mechanism behind worry, differentiating high from low worrying.

articles_hidden.title: Can Knowledge of the CO₂ Emissions of Food Increase Meat Tax Support?
articles_hidden.authors: Hellen Temme; Mattis Geiger; Philipp Sprengholz; Cornelia Betsch
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose
Climate policy acceptance and sustainable behavior partially depend on accurate CO₂ estimates and perceived policy effectiveness. We tested whether seeding, an intervention in which people learn accurate CO₂ values for representative foods that serve as anchors for estimating other foods' emissions, can increase carbon numeracy (i.e., the ability to estimate carbon footprints of foods without explicit calculations). 
Method
Two pre-registered experiments examined whether increased carbon numeracy also enhances perceived effectiveness and acceptance of a value-added tax (VAT) reform on food and food choice. Study 1 (N = 974) tested whether seeding increased the effectiveness and acceptance of a VAT increase for meat. Study 2 (N = 1,023) extended this by explaining the policy mechanism. Food choice was assessed by asking participants to select a food box (vegan, vegetarian, or meat-based) in a lottery.
Results
Both studies found that seeding improved carbon numeracy (ηp² = .55−.58, p < .05). However, neither seeding nor policy explanations significantly increased policy acceptance or food choice, although explaining the policy increased perceived effectiveness (β = .21−.24, p < .05). In both studies, perceived effectiveness (r = .31−.41, p < .001) and policy acceptance (r = .30−.49, p < .001) were significantly related to selecting a non-meat food box. Exploratory analyses revealed that perceptions of a potential price change were the strongest predictor of policy acceptance (β = -.47, p < .001). 
Conclusion
These findings suggest that VAT policy changes could require both explaining environmental benefits and addressing perceived personal costs.

articles_hidden.title: The Effects of Nature Walk on Positive and Negative Affect and Perceived Restorativeness in Deaf Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Georgios Stavrinos; Elisavet Panagiotou
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Exposure to natural environments has been associated with positive affective responses and perceived restorativeness. However, these experiences have primarily been investigated in hearing populations, and little is known about deaf adults’ affective and restorative experiences in relation to natural environments.

Purpose: We examined whether deaf and hearing adults differed in post-walk positive and negative affect, perceived restorativeness, and nature relatedness. We also explored the sensory pathways associated with their affective and restorative experiences.

Methodology: We conducted a mixed-methods study with 15 deaf and 14 hearing adults who completed an outdoor nature walk in a national forest park in Cyprus. Participants completed the Positive and Negative Affect Scale, the Perceived Restorativeness Scale, and the Nature Relatedness Scale, alongside semi-structured interviews. Hierarchical multiple regressions examined group associations with the quantitative outcomes after adjusting for relevant covariates. Deductive content analysis then explored affective and restorative experiences and their associated sensory pathways.

Results: Deaf participants reported significantly higher post-walk positive affect than hearing participants (B = -3.82 for hearing relative to deaf group, 95% Confidence Interval [-6.89, -0.76], p = .017). No significant group associations were identified for negative affect, perceived restorativeness, or nature relatedness. Qualitative findings identified both high and low arousal positive affect experiences, alongside restorative experiences such as fascination and the feeling of being away. These experiences were linked to various sensory pathways in both groups, with visual pathways frequently described and auditory, tactile, and bodily/thermal experiences also contributing to participants’ accounts.

Conclusion: Our study provides preliminary evidence of differences in post-walk positive affect between deaf and hearing adults while highlighting the diverse sensory experiences linked to affect and perceived restorativeness in natural environments. Larger studies are needed to clarify these findings and investigate the role of sensory experiences in nature restoration.

articles_hidden.title: What difference do cash transfers make? Understanding impacts and mechanisms from cash transfer recipients and communities in Malawi and Lesotho.
articles_hidden.authors: Mirela Zaneva; Josphine Hapazari; Theodora Khofi; Christopher James Graham; Eunbi Han; Shruti; Aswathi Surendran; Rizwana Amin; Roseline Dzekem Dine; Hangala Siachiwena
articles_hidden.abstract: Cash transfers are a common poverty alleviation intervention, yet qualitative reports of recipients’ lived experiences are limited. Without these perspectives, policy frameworks risk reducing beneficiaries to passive inputs in programmatic equations. This means potentially overlooking the social meanings, moral negotiations, and relational dynamics through which transfers are actually received, used, perceived, and redistributed. To address this gap, we analyzed 74 in-depth interviews with cash transfer recipients and their household members in rural Malawi and Lesotho. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we created four themes: 1) “With my poverty it can’t work”: Enough to survive, not enough to change, 2) “I can’t be eating in my house while my children are hungry next door”: Grandmothers and the obligation to share, 3) “I am already worried as to what I will be doing”:  Psychological relief and stress intertwine, 4) “Sky-falling” and “satanic” money: Notions of deservingness produce stigma and jealousy. Recipients consistently noted improvement in food security, while effects on mental health and social relationships were more mixed. We argue that recipient-centered reports complement and strengthen quantitative evidence about the impacts and mechanisms of cash transfers. We discuss specific policy recommendations, such as larger and more predictable payments, better communication, and sensitive disbursement options, gender-sensitive support, and more active monitoring of psychosocial and community effects in order to mitigate potential negative impacts. Finally, we argue there is a need for a more ambitious focus on development as the key path to poverty eradication.

articles_hidden.title: From Green to Technology:  Age Group Variability in Conceptual Complexity and Concreteness
articles_hidden.authors: Ilenia Falcinelli; Chiara Fini; Claudia Mazzuca; Anna M. Borghi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Concepts are widely recognized as flexible and shaped by multiple factors. Here, we investigate how conceptual representations differ across age groups by focusing on four timely domains—ecological, geo, natural (which we labeled altogether green), and technological. Replicating a previous study, we collected ratings from 320 Italian older adults (aged >64) on 50 concepts per domain across 39 semantic dimensions targeting different conceptual aspects (e.g., sensorimotor, sociopolitical, inner, emotional). We then compared these ratings with those from younger adults (aged 18–35) collected in the earlier study.
Results revealed strong semantic proximity among green concepts and a clear separation between them (especially natural) and the technological ones. The internal semantic composition of each domain revealed clear age group differences. Within the green domains, older adults exhibited richer, more multifaceted, and more concrete conceptual representations than younger adults, with fine-grained divergences across green concepts. In contrast, no age group differences emerged in the complexity of technological concept representations; however, younger adults characterized this domain more concretely.
These differences were closely linked to self-reported domain experience and familiarity: older adults reported greater personal experience with ecological topics, whereas younger adults reported higher familiarity with technology.
Theoretically, our findings suggest that conceptual complexity and concreteness vary across domains and are shaped by age group membership and all that it entails. Scientifically, the resulting O-TECo database provides the first semantic norms tailored to older adults. Societally, results highlight the need for age-sensitive interventions to foster engagement with environmental policies and responsible technology use.

articles_hidden.title: The Verifiability of Recovered Memories of Abuse
articles_hidden.authors: Mirjam ter Beek; Henry Otgaar; Linsey Raymaekers; Corine de Ruiter; Paul Riesthuis; Tamara L. F. De Beuf; Anne Hoving; Meike Hogenkamp; Bruno Verschuere
articles_hidden.abstract: Different ways of remembering sexual abuse - continuous memories, spontaneously recovered memories, and recovered memories following an active search - have been shown to differ in the availability of case-level corroborative evidence. The present study examined whether memory types in delayed sexual abuse statements also differ in terms of verifiability, a statement feature previously associated with differences between truthful and deceptive accounts. Victim statements from archival police files (N = 140) were classified according to how the abuse was remembered. Confirmatory analyses showed that statements based on continuous memories contained more verifiable details than statements based on recovered memories following an active search. Exploratory analyses indicated that details reported following an active search were more often disconfirmed than those reported in continuous or spontaneously recovered memories. Verifiability may extend beyond deception detection paradigms to capture systematic differences associated with memory retrieval and reconstruction processes in delayed sexual abuse reports.

articles_hidden.title: Detecting the “We-Mode” in Observed Interactions:  Infants’ Increasing Selectivity to Cues of “Truly” Joint Attention From 9 to 18 Months
articles_hidden.authors: Maleen Thiele; Daniel Hanus
articles_hidden.abstract: Human social cognition is grounded in “we-mode” interactions, providing a psychological foundation for coordinating attention and knowledge, thereby facilitating human-specific cultural learning. While infants’ sensitivity to interpersonal sharedness is well-documented in participation-based “first-party” interactions, its ontogenetic origins in observed “third-party” settings remain poorly understood. Focusing on joint attention as a foundational mechanism of shared cognition, this study investigated when infants begin to appreciate the “we-dimension” within observed triadic interactions, addressing theoretical debates between leaner and richer accounts of joint attention. In a screen-based object-encoding task, 9-month-old infants and 18-month-old toddlers saw videos of two adults looking at an object. We systematically manipulated (a) partner-directed gaze (looking at partner vs. away) and (b) its temporal alignment (synchronously vs. asynchronously). This allowed us to contrast “truly joint attention” (coordinated mutual awareness, “we-mode”) with “parallel attention” (mere co-orientation) and a novel “social gaze” condition featuring uncoordinated partner-looks without sharedness. Results from a looking-time-based novelty-preference test revealed that 18-month-olds selectively encoded objects only when observing eye contact in the “synchronous–looking at partner” condition, indicative of “truly joint attention”. Conversely, 9-month-olds exhibited a broader sensitivity, encoding objects in all conditions featuring partner-directed gaze, including “social gaze” scenarios lacking markers of sharedness. These findings demonstrate that infants’ early sensitivity to third-party joint attention refines into a more selective appreciation of the observed “we-dimension” during the second year. This developmental progression marks a critical milestone in recognizing others’ collaborative engagement, providing the foundation for the specialized observational learning that underpins human-unique cultural transmission.

articles_hidden.title: Dissociation as a candidate mechanism in functional neurological disorder:  Evidence from digital remote monitoring in everyday life
articles_hidden.authors: Susannah Pick; L. S. Merritt Millman; Gabriela Crispim Baiocchi; Snigdha Bhuma; Sorawit Wainipitapong; Jemima Uloyok-Job; Jessica Davies; Yasmine Basamh; Lauren Blunstone; Rhiannon White
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Affective hyperarousal and dissociation are possible mechanisms underlying symptom occurrence in functional neurological disorder (FND), although evidence is limited by retrospective and cross-sectional measurement. We aimed to examine these mechanisms in everyday life with digital remote monitoring technologies in functional seizures (FS) and functional motor symptoms (FMS).
Methods: Smartphone-based ecological momentary assessment (EMA) tracked subjective functional neurological symptoms (FNS), subjectively significant daily events, affect, dissociation, and subjective arousal six times daily over 14 days, alongside wearable heartrate monitoring (Fitbit Charge 5). Participants were aged 18-65 years with FS (n=45) or FMS (n=48). Healthy (HC, n=45) and clinical controls with anxiety/depressive disorders (CC=47) were included for comparison. We used linear mixed-effects models to compare groups and to interrogate concurrent and time-lagged temporal relationships between variables. 
Results: FS and FMS groups reported elevated dissociation across the 14 days compared to CC/HC (p≤0.01), including depersonalisation, derealisation, and amnesia (p<0.05). Reduced event-related pleasantness was also reported by FS/FMS/CC groups compared to HC (p<0.05). At the day- and momentary-levels, dissociation was the most robust correlate and/or temporal predictor of FNS severity in the FS/FMS groups (p=0.02-<0.001), withstanding correction for confounds. Event-related stress/pleasantness ratings, negative affect, and subjective arousal significantly predicted FNS severity in some models.
Conclusions: Dissociation is a distinguishing feature in FS/FMS and a prominent correlate and momentary temporal predictor of FNS severity in both groups, indicating a possible shared mechanism. Future studies should examine the neurobiological basis of dissociation-FNS interactions and explore interventions that enhance management of dissociative states in this population.

articles_hidden.title: Comparing the temporal dynamics of top-down mindfulness and bottom-up reward systems in optimizing cognitive functioning
articles_hidden.authors: Preslava Hristova; Silvy Collin
articles_hidden.abstract: Optimizing human cognitive functioning requires a delicate balance between top-down self-regulation and bottom-up motivational reinforcement. However, the precise temporal trade-offs between these opposing trajectories (specifically, immediate reward-driven gains versus gradual mindfulness-based structural adaptation) remain poorly understood. Using a mixed longitudinal design, we assessed cognitive and psychological outcomes using the Mindful Attention Awareness Scale, Perceived Stress Scale, Stroop task (executive control), N-back task (working memory), and Rapid Visual Presentation task (sustained attention). Results showed that mindfulness meditation significantly improved working memory (in an N-back task). Interestingly, the Stroop task showed declined accuracy, but with faster reaction times, suggesting a speed-accuracy trade-off rather than genuine improvement for executive control. Moreover, while mindfulness did lead to an increase in the Mindful Attention Awareness Scale, it did not decrease perceived stress. The result patterns for the reward condition differed from mindfulness meditation. Explicit reward resulted in faster reaction times on the Stroop task, but these were accompanied by reduced accuracy, suggesting a speed–accuracy trade-off rather than genuine cognitive improvement for executive control (in line with mindfulness meditation). Reward did not lead to any significant changes over time in other cognitive tasks. Thus, the improvements in working memory over time were specific to mindfulness meditation and not shown for reward-based manipulations. Overall, these findings highlight the importance of distinguishing genuine cognitive improvements from changes in response strategies.

articles_hidden.title: Registered Report: Does the valence-dominance model apply to deepfake faces? Validation and its impact on deepfake detection
articles_hidden.authors: Gianmarco Convertino; Mara Stockner; Michela Marchetti; Danilo Mitaritonna; Luca Corvitto; Luca Maiano; Lorenzo Papa; Irene Amerini; Giuliana Mazzoni
articles_hidden.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has given rise to increasingly more realistic fake contents such as deepfake faces, hardly distinguishable from real faces. However, evidence has shown that social evaluations of real faces are also able to impact the detection of deepfake faces. The present study aimed at applying for the first time the valence-dominance model for face evaluation on deepfake faces. Moreover, the impact of its thirteen attributes on deepfake detection performances was investigated. Specifically, 311 participants categorised 120 faces (50% real, 50% deepfake created ad hoc by Diffusion Model technology) and rated faces in regards to one of the attributes. Principal Component Analysis was applied in order to validate the valence-dominance model on deepfake faces, and a Brunswikian lens model was  applied to understand how each attribute contributes to a face being judged as deepfake. Results replicated the valence-dominance model on real faces as well as on faces categorized by participants as deepfake, but not on actual deepfake faces. Finally, the indirect effects of the Brunswikian model revealed caringness and intelligence to impair detection of deepfake stimuli, whilst weirdness was revealed to be a positive indirect predictor, being positively associated with higher detection accuracy of deepfake faces. Our results shed, for the first time, light into the differential cognitive processing of deepfake faces and their social evaluation whilst also providing novel insight into underlying mechanisms associated with deepfake detection. Interdisciplinary implications regarding the theoretical and applied contribution are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Same Displays, Different Judgments: Numerical Ratio Effects in Quantity and Valence Tasks
articles_hidden.authors: Duru Başak Özbek; Melike Sefikoglu; Özce Cinoğlu; Merve Bulut; Ezgi Gür; Hakan Cetinkaya; Seda Dural
articles_hidden.abstract: Numerical ratio reliably predicts performance in explicit non-symbolic quantity comparison, but whether it also predicts performance when the same objects are judged by their valence remains unclear. We examined this question in 156 participants assigned to one of four instructions: select the group containing fewer or more bacteria, or select the group depicted as good or bad. All groups viewed the same paired displays, making numerosity relevant to quantity judgments and irrelevant to valence judgments. Mixed-effects models assessed the relationship between numerical ratio, defined as the smaller numerosity divided by the larger numerosity, and response times and accuracy. As ratio approached 1, responses became slower and less accurate in the quantity task. In the valence task, neither response times nor accuracy showed a reliable relationship with ratio. The average ratio slopes differed significantly between quantity and valence judgments for both outcomes. These findings indicate that the behavioral expression of numerical relations depends on whether quantity is relevant to the required judgment.

articles_hidden.title: Is Insomnia a Western-centered disorder? A cross-cultural study of sleep satisfaction and perceived sleep duration
articles_hidden.authors: Kevin Mammeri; Leela McKinnon; Ming Fei Li; David Samson; Lampros Perogamvros
articles_hidden.abstract: Insomnia disorder (ID) is highly prevalent in industrialized societies, yet it is primarily conceptualized and treated at the individual level, with limited consideration of sociocultural influences. This cross-sectional, cross cultural study investigated subjective sleep satisfaction and perceived sleep duration across groups differing in lifestyle, scale and degree of industrialization. A total of 1,389 adults from seven countries completed measures of sleep satisfaction and perceived sleep duration. Healthy participants included 37 individuals from the Hadza hunter-gatherer group in Tanzania (small-scale, non-industrialized group), 447 individuals from rural regions of Madagascar, Guatemala, and South Africa (mixed-scale groups) and 833 participants from large-scale, industrialized groups (United States and Mexico, large-scale). A separate clinical sample of 72 Swiss patients suffering from ID was included. Logistic regressions and Bayesian analyses were conducted on two dichotomous outcomes: sleep satisfaction and perceived sleep duration (<6 h vs. ≥6 h). Participants from the Hadza group showed a significantly higher probability of being satisfied with their sleep than participants from large scale groups and patients with ID. All non-clinical groups reported greater sleep satisfaction than the ID group. In contrast, no significant differences in perceived sleep duration were observed across groups. Sleep satisfaction, but not perceived sleep duration, varied across groups differing in levels of industrialization. These findings suggest that subjective sleep experience extends beyond perceived sleep duration and that sociocultural factors may play an important role in subjective sleep experience and should be considered in models of insomnia and sleep health.

articles_hidden.title: A Dynamic and Recursive Allocative Model of Talent Development and Expression
articles_hidden.authors: Rony Moortgat
articles_hidden.abstract: Talent development is increasingly understood as domain-specific, temporally extended, and shaped by interactions between persons and environments. Yet existing models remain underspecified regarding how structural and institutional conditions, together with prior developmental histories, become concrete developmental conditions for persons over time. This article develops a dynamic and recursive allocative model of talent development and expression. Person-specific allocation is conceptualized as an endogenous, multidimensional interface through which configurations of tasks, developmental resources and support, demands and constraints, recovery affordances, and recognition are generated. The model distinguishes allocated conditions from their person-level realization and embeds these processes within successive developmental windows separating available capacities, domain-directed focus, independently measured learning speed, realized goal-directed activity, proximal conditions, and domain-specific performance. Aptitude is represented as a latent person-by-domain component of the focus–learning relation. Prior performance and allocation configurations contribute to subsequent allocations, creating recursive pathways through which cumulative advantage and disadvantage may emerge. The model further distinguishes proximal fit from outcome-specific developmental functionality and recovery affordances from realized recovery, allowing the same configuration to have different consequences across outcomes. It yields falsifiable propositions and a multilevel, multimodal measurement architecture for domain-specific empirical evaluation. The framework offers a testable account of recursively reallocated developmental conditions.

articles_hidden.title: Memory and Cognitive Control in Hypothesis Sampling: Individual Differences in Resampling Rejected Hypotheses
articles_hidden.authors: Yoonsang Lee; Randall W Engle
articles_hidden.abstract:
Efficient hypothesis sampling requires avoiding resampling: returning to hypotheses that have already been rejected. Doing so could depend on maintaining information about which hypotheses have been ruled out, or on disengaging from previously activated hypotheses once they are no longer relevant. Participants (N = 302) completed a hypothe- sis sampling task in which they tested hypotheses from six alternatives until identifying the correct one, along with batteries measuring working memory capacity (WMC), fluid intelligence (Gf), and attention control (AC). In latent- variable models, higher WMC, Gf, and AC were each associated with less resampling when considered separately, but only Gf uniquely predicted resampling once their overlapping contributions were partialled out. Mediation anal- yses showed that AC accounted for the WMC association but not the Gf association. Separating AC into selective and sustained components, selective but not sustained AC predicted resampling, although not uniquely after ac- counting for Gf and WMC, and neither component mediated the Gf effect. Overall, this pattern is consistent with the idea that avoiding rejected hypotheses depends more on disengaging from outdated representations than on maintaining information in working memory. The unique Gf association beyond AC suggests that this contribution
is not fully reducible to domain-general attention control.

articles_hidden.title: Psychosocial interventions for school refusal in children and adolescents: a protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Akira Sato; Yan Luo; Satoshi Funada; Masatsugu Sakata; Motoki Kurumai; Ethan Sahker; Toshi A. Furukawa
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Attending school can be emotionally distressing for some children and adolescents. When school attendance becomes difficult for a child and is accompanied by emotional distress, the condition is called school refusal. Contextual factors at the individual, parental, and school levels that interfere with school attendance may complicate school refusal. A 2015 systematic review of psychosocial interventions, including both randomized and non-randomized studies, reported mixed results for treating anxiety in school refusal, while showing promising results for school attendance. No systematic review or meta-analysis restricted to randomized controlled trials, however, has been conducted. We will therefore conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials to determine whether psychosocial interventions reduce anxiety and improve school attendance among school-refusing children and adolescents. 

Methods: Our protocol followed the PRISMA-P guideline. We will include individually- and cluster-randomized trials in which most children and adolescents are aged 18 years or younger, are enrolled in primary or secondary education, have exhibited school absence, and received psychosocial interventions for school refusal. Our primary aim is to reduce anxiety and increase school attendance. We will search CENTRAL, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, ERIC, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the ICTRP. Two reviewers will independently assess the study selection, data extraction, risk of bias in included studies, and reporting bias.
