We will also investigate heterogeneity and conduct sensitivity analyses. We will present ‘summary of findings’ tables to show the estimated effects and the certainty of the evidence.

Discussion: This will be the first systematic review to include only randomized trials and to broaden the concept of school attendance to capture the child’s engagement with learning in education.

articles_hidden.title: Direct and Generative Retrieval and the Phenomenological Characteristics of Future Thinking Associated with Depressive Symptoms: The Relevance of Contrast Avoidance and Memories of the Future
articles_hidden.authors: Noboru Matsumoto; David John Hallford
articles_hidden.abstract: Depression is characterized by reduced future thinking specificity, yet the retrieval processes underlying this impairment remain unclear. We examined whether depressive symptoms are differentially associated with direct retrieval (i.e., effortless searches that immediately bring future thoughts to mind) versus generative retrieval (i.e., searches requiring cognitive effort or additional information) of specific and categoric future events, and whether contrast avoidance (i.e., maintaining a negative mood to avoid a sudden negative emotional shift) contributes to these patterns. In Study 1 (N = 80) and preregistered Study 2 (N = 113), Japanese adults completed a future thinking task in which they imagined personally-relevant future events for positive and negative cue words, classified each retrieval as direct or generative, and rated phenomenological characteristics. Drawing on preliminary results from Study 1, Study 2 clearly linked depressive symptoms to more frequent directly retrieved categoric futures for negative cues. In contrast, regressions (but not correlations) showed associations between depressive symptoms to reduced generatively retrieved specific futures for positive cues. Depressed individuals also reported lower emotional valence, likelihood, and similarity with past events for positive future thinking, suggesting limited memory resources for generating plausible positive events. In Study 2, a higher propensity for emotional contrast avoidance was linked to increased retrieval of negative categoric futures and decreased retrieval of positive specific futures. These findings suggest that increased accessibility to negative categoric futures and reduced accessibility to positive specific futures may be a distinct pathological process in depression, with contrast avoidance potentially maintaining these biases.

articles_hidden.title: Navigating Autistic College Students’ Career Development: A Capability-Oriented Perspective on Agency and Advocacy
articles_hidden.authors: Yilun Jiang; Karly Ball Isaacson; Bradley E. Cox; Brett Ranon Nachman
articles_hidden.abstract: Autistic college students navigate career development through their interests and strengths, while encountering deficit-oriented assumptions about autism. Research on autistic students’ career development usually focuses on career support and skill development, while limited studies have examined how they pursue career pathways from a strengths-based perspective. Drawing on a secondary analysis of semi-structured interviews from a national mixed-methods study (n = 36), we examined how autistic college students in four-year U.S. colleges navigate career development. Applied thematic analysis identified three themes: participants developed purpose-driven career goals through long-standing interests, lived experiences, and community exposure; navigated judgments about capability and professional fit across academic and career contexts; and assembled career support across career centers, faculty, and autism support groups. Our findings highlight autistic participants’ capability to explore career pathways that reflect their interests and goals and suggest an agency-beyond-advocacy interpretation, in which agency refers to broader forms of action through which students shape their career development and advocacy represents one important form of agency. Finally, we offer suggestions for universities and employers to develop resources more tailored to autistic students’ career goals and needs.

articles_hidden.title: Echoes of Thought: Task Complexity, Inner Speech Analogs, and Prompt Design Shape LLMs’ Response Behavior in the Two-Step Task
articles_hidden.authors: Franziska Usée; Daniel Schad
articles_hidden.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance across a wide range of tasks, yet the mechanisms behind their response behavior remain poorly understood. Drawing on insights from cognitive science and the computational framework of model-free and model-based reinforcement learning (RL), we examined conditions under which GPT-3.5 and four open-weight LLMs can exhibit behavioral signatures of model-based RL in the two-step task, a well-established paradigm for studying human learning and decision-making. Across nine simulation studies, we varied the task complexity and prompt design to examine conditions under which previously reported model-based RL signatures could be replicated. We found that GPT-3.5 showed model-based RL signatures in simplified task settings, but that these effects disappeared under de-simplified task versions. Crucially, model-based reasoning signatures could be re-established when incorporating an inner speech-analog prompt, requiring the LLM agent to reflect on previous trials and anticipate consequences of future actions. For the open-weight LLMs tested, we observed diminished signatures of model-based reasoning under both de-simplified and facilitative task conditions. Our fine-grained analyses of behavioral learning dynamics highlight the role of structured reflective and anticipatory linguistic processes in enabling complex response patterns in LLMs and reveal both similarities to and differences from human decision-making patterns.

articles_hidden.title: How Self-Location Predicts the Degree and Quality of the Felt Sense of Connection
articles_hidden.authors: MARIE SESTER; Glenn Hartelius; Michaël Dambrun
articles_hidden.abstract: Research has typically examined how self-location in the head or heart is associated with traits and behavior, yet its link to relationality—specifically the felt sense of connection—remains underexplored. This study investigated how dispositional self-location predicts the embodied experience of being relationally linked to others and the world. We initially developed the Dispositional Self-Location Questionnaire (DSLQ), an association-based instrument designed to minimize potential subjective bias in participant reporting of self-location. Using this measure, we categorized a U.S. sample of 218 adults who had reported a strong experience of connection as head-locators or heart-locators and assessed them on self-construal, self-expansiveness, connectedness, and perceived qualities of connection. Head-locators reported firmer self-boundaries, emphasizing independence, rationality, and decision-making. In contrast, Heart-locators scored significantly higher on connectedness to both self and world, and on metapersonal self-construal, describing their connections as close, warm, caring, and authentic. These findings suggest that self-location functions as a somatic attentional stance that anticipates the experiential boundary between self and other: the head favors separation and autonomy, while the heart favors openness and expanded belonging.

articles_hidden.title: The successor representation in high-risk drinking and alcohol-related contexts
articles_hidden.authors: Milena Philomena Maria Musial; Sam Hall-McMaster; Kanji Shimomura; Ayaka Kato; Erik Lukas Bode; Clarissa Grundmann; Claudia Ebrahimi; Kenji Morita; Samuel J. Gershman; Tanja Endrass
articles_hidden.abstract: The successor representation (SR) is a reinforcement learning strategy which has been suggested to underlie nuanced forms of habitual behavior, rendering it a candidate mechanism for mental health conditions thought to involve habitual control, such as addiction. However, paradigms used to assess habits in humans cannot detect SR use. Together with the fact that they are usually conducted in disorder-irrelevant contexts, this may explain why the evidence for a hypothesized shift from goal-directed to habitual behavior in addiction is inconsistent. Here, we tested whether individuals with high-risk (n=260) compared to low-risk drinking behavior (n=260) rely more on SR or a rigid goal-based dimension-reduced SR variant, particularly in alcohol-related contexts. An online multi-stage decision-making task performed in either a virtual bar or apartment context allowed us to dissociate (red)SR from model-based and model-free learning strategies by testing how well participants adapted their choices to different types of distal changes in the environment. Findings suggest that a particular type of SR, namely a (reduced) random-policy SR-like strategy, contributes to human behavior, but that high-risk drinkers do not differ from low-risk drinkers in their use of this strategy. Instead, both groups seem to rely less on what is likely a (reduced) random-policy SR strategy in alcohol-related contexts – and instead more on model-free control. Results suggest that the use of an adaptive, resource-efficient decision-making strategy is selectively downregulated in substance-related contexts. This study highlights the importance of considering contextual modulation and nuanced decision strategies in understanding habitual and goal-directed behavior in mental health conditions such as addiction.

articles_hidden.title: Learning Children’s Conceptual Spaces using Deep Metric Learning.
articles_hidden.authors: Pablo Leon-Villagra; Isaac Ehrlich; Christopher G. Lucas; Daphna Buchsbaum
articles_hidden.abstract: Children learn to represent the world around them in meaningful categories that allow them to generalize past experiences. Understanding how these categorical representations develop is fundamental to cognitive science. However, capturing the structure of human conceptual knowledge is a challenging experimental task. The most prominent approach, Multidimensional Scaling (MDS), usually requires participants to produce many similarity judgments, leading to long experiments. Moreover, the representations found by MDS are limited to the fixed set of experimental stimuli and have to be reconstructed for every new item. In contrast, we present a more flexible machine-learning method that can generalize to novel stimuli. This method uses a child-friendly task that allows researchers to uncover the development of categories with fewer participant judgments. We evaluate our approach on simulated data and find that it can accurately reveal representations even when trained on data generated by groups that categorize differently. We then analyze data from the World Color Survey and find that we can recover language-specific color organization when aggregating languages that only share the same number of basic color terms. Finally, we use the method in a developmental experiment and find age-dependent differences in how complex fruit stimuli are organized. These differences were consistent with participants' reasoning and additional experimental measures. Our results suggest that our approach is applicable in psychological tasks and opens the possibility of examining children's developing psychological spaces in new detail.

articles_hidden.title: Psychological therapy for auditory verbal hallucinations: A qualitative assessment of voice-hearers’ experiences and preferences
articles_hidden.authors: Sanne Brederoo; Gerda van Ittersum; Francisca Goedhart; Ingrid Tewelde-Kampert; Wim Veling; Chris Geraets
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Psychological therapy for voice-hearing is increasingly recognized as an important component of care for people who hear voices. However, relatively little is known about voice-hearers’ experiences and preferences regarding psychological interventions for voice-hearing. The present study aimed to examine this in a transdiagnostic sample of voice-hearers.
Methods
An online survey was completed by 178 voice-hearers, who were recruited through multiple community-based and clinical channels. The survey assessed experiences with psychological therapy and discussing voices with therapists, asked about treatment preferences and goals, and experiences and wishes with regard to peer support.
Results
Three-quarters of respondents had previously sought help for voice-hearing, and about half reported having been offered psychological therapy. Among those who had followed therapy, overall satisfaction was moderate to high and respondents generally reported a positive relation with their therapist. With regard to treatment goals, out of eight options respondents prioritized reducing negative consequences and distress from voice-hearing over reducing voice frequency. Understanding voices and developing coping strategies were the most highly prioritized treatment foci out of nine options. Among reasons to decline psychological therapy were having no confidence it would be helpful, it not being the right time, and not trusting the therapist. Relatively few respondents had received peer support, but a larger proportion reported a current or past need for such support.
Conclusions
Respondents emphasized the importance of individualized care, a trusting therapeutic relationship, and shared-decision making. Incorporating questionnaires similar to the present survey at the start of psychological therapy may help facilitate shared decision-making and strengthen the therapeutic alliance.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable mediated effect of a positive attitude toward AI on AI literacy: A comment on Wang and Niu (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles_hidden.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Wang and Niu, I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking a positive attitude toward AI to AI literacy. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, a positive attitude toward AI, AI self-efficacy, motivation to use AI, and self-rated AI literacy are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles_hidden.title: French Validation of the Team Flow Monitor:  Factor Structure and Validity Evidence in Student Teams
articles_hidden.authors: Victoire Vallier; Nicolas Verger; Rebecca Shankland; Roxane Turgon; Quentin Hallez
articles_hidden.abstract: Teamwork is central to addressing tasks whose complexity exceeds the capabilities of any single individual, and the shared optimal experience known as team flow has been linked to collective performance. Validated instruments to measure team flow are, however, only available in Dutch and English. This research aimed to validate a French version of the characteristics subscale of the Team Flow Monitor (TFM). In Study 1 (N = 225), the scale was translated and adapted, and its factor structure, reliability, and convergent and discriminant validity were examined. Confirmatory factor analyses supported the original structure of four facets (sense of unity, sense of joint progress, mutual trust, and holistic focus) loading on a second-order team flow factor (CFI = .971, RMSEA = .071), with excellent internal consistency. Scores correlated positively with work engagement and self-rated task performance and were unrelated to grit, a trait-level individual disposition that is conceptually distinct from the situational and collective nature of team flow. Study 2 (N = 92) examined the scale in student teams completing collaborative coursework. Team flow scores correlated strongly with perceived team performance and satisfaction with team performance (rs ≥ .68) and only weakly with perceived individual performance (r = .28), a difference that was statistically significant for the total score and for each facet, which supports convergent validity with group-level outcomes and discriminant validity with individual-level self-assessment. This research provides a reliable and valid French TFM, suitable for measuring team flow and its association with collective outcomes in French-speaking settings.

articles_hidden.title: Measurement Invariance of the Externalizing Construct by Racial and Disadvantaged Contexts in System-Involved Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Kendall Donovan Smith; Keanan Joyner; Edelyn Verona
articles_hidden.abstract: Externalizing psychopathology is shaped by environmental and contextual factors, particularly those tied to disadvantaged backgrounds. There is insufficient work examining how broader contextual variables affect measurement models of latent externalizing. The current research examined the degree to which indicators traditionally used to model externalizing are similarly indicative of the latent construct across racial and contextual factors (i.e., metric and scalar invariance), using data from two studies of system-involved adults (Study 1: Mage=36.5, 67% male; Study 2: Mage=32.1, 62% male). In both studies, metric invariance generally held but not scalar invariance as a function of race/ethnicity and community-level racialized contexts, particularly for drug use, antisocial behavior and criminal justice-related indicators. Results suggest that contextual factors influence not only externalizing level but affect the measurement of the construct itself.

articles_hidden.title: “Puzzling, Yet So Refreshing”: Experiencing the Value of Neurodiversity Within an Inclusive Choir
articles_hidden.authors: Nicolas Petit; Géraldine Dessertenne; Fanny Aprile; Lucie Jurek
articles_hidden.abstract: The social challenges encountered by autistic people are increasingly understood as a double empathy problem: a mutual misunderstanding between autistic and non-autistic individuals, rather than an autistic deficit. It is thus critical to cultivate inclusive spaces that foster mutual understanding, where autistic people can fit in while allowing the general population to experience high-quality neurodiverse contacts. Choral singing offers a promising medium to do so and to facilitate cross-neurotype dynamics, as it is thought to have evolved as a biological mechanism to foster social bonding. Accordingly, this qualitative study explored how 12 general population adult choristers experienced a 6-month neurodiverse choir shared with 8 autistic adolescents and 3 autism specialists. We used a two-stage qualitative design, first capturing individual experiences through a thematic analysis of an open-ended online questionnaire, and subsequently deepening our results through a discussion with a community stakeholder panel. The findings revealed an intrinsically demanding experience, especially emotionally and cognitively, counterbalanced by important benefits, as it was also described as joyful and powerful, encouraging personal growth among the choristers and a shift in their perceptions of autism. These findings support the neurodiversity paradigm and suggest that choral singing may support double empathy experiences, facilitating intergroup contact in the social majority, to reduce prejudice and thereby remove social barriers to the inclusion of autistic voices.

articles_hidden.title: Teacher Help and the Development of Socioeconomic Ability Stereotypes: Longitudinal Evidence From Real Classrooms
articles_hidden.authors: Jonne Bloem; Iris Boer; Jellie Sierksma
articles_hidden.abstract: Teacher help is crucial for learning and boosts children’s development. Receiving help may also have unintended negative consequences as it may signal that recipients are not competent enough to solve tasks independently. Teachers often provide more help to children from lower-socioeconomic status (SES) backgrounds, and lab-based studies show that when help is distributed unequally it can reinforce negative ability stereotypes. In this preregistered study, we examined whether children (7-13 years) perceive differences in who receives help in their own classrooms and whether perceived SES-based differences in help lead to stronger SES stereotypes over time. At three time points across one school year Dutch children (N= 565, 65 classrooms, 49.5% boys, 49.5% girls, 1.1% other/prefer not to say; 65.2% native Dutch; mixed SES backgrounds) identified which classmates most often received help from their teacher and how much they endorsed ability stereotypes about SES groups. Across all time points, children perceived that teachers helped lower-SES classmates more than higher-SES classmates. This pattern emerged for two types of help, and was more pronounced among children from lower-SES backgrounds and older children. Moreover, perceived SES-based differences in teacher help at the start of the school year predicted stronger SES-based ability stereotypes halfway through the year, although this association was limited to one type of help. These findings suggest that everyday classroom practices intended to support children who need additional help may inadvertently shape which children and societal groups are seen as less capable. This has important implications for how SES-based stereotypes take root.

articles_hidden.title: Competition, concurrence, and cooperation between external and internal attention
articles_hidden.authors: Sam Verschooren; Tobias Egner; Mariam Aly
articles_hidden.abstract: Attention can be selectively directed to both external sensory inputs and internally generated representations. The relationship between these external and internal attentional states is not fixed but varies between competition, concurrence, and cooperation. However, the conditions that allow for each of these relationships to occur remain poorly understood. We distinguish between the level of brain states and behavior and synthesize evidence for each of these relationships at both levels. Our review shows that shared, capacity-limited mechanisms and opposing computational modes (e.g., encoding vs. retrieval) often produce competitive dynamics, particularly in the presence of simultaneous and incompatible demands. At the same time, several studies have revealed partially independent substrates that permit concurrent selection of internal and external information, especially when controlled, intentional processing is not required. More recently, researcher have started exploring conditions under which external and internal can support or facilitate each other, enabling cooperative integration in the service of a single goal. We argue that task demands, degree of control, representational overlap, and the considered timescale jointly determine whether external and internal attention compete, co-occur, or cooperate, and we outline key directions for future work aimed at a more nuanced understanding of how these states jointly shape cognition.

articles_hidden.title: The role of neuroscience for psychological causal explanation
articles_hidden.authors: Beate Krickel; Markus Werkle-Bergner
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychology provides causal explanations of behavior but it remains contested whether such explanations are scientifically legitimate without grounding in neuroscience. Two prominent arguments have been put forward to argue for the dependence of psychology on neuroscience: the classical causal exclusion argument argues that higher-level causes are excluded by lower-level causes; According to a more recent line of argument, variables and relations postulated by psychological models must correspond to variables and relations in neuroscientific models – otherwise the psychological model can only provide how-possibly explanation but not how-actually explanation. In this article, we defend the independence of psychological causal explanation. Based on an interventionist account of causation, we argue that a psychological model is causally explanatory when it identifies variables that serve as points of intervention. Still, we show that neuroscience sometimes has a crucial role for validating psychological models: when a psychological model identifies points of interventions that cannot be intervened on at the psychological level.

articles_hidden.title: Tools for Helping Identify Behavior Disorders: From Parsimonious Nomograms to Machine Learning Models
articles_hidden.authors: Yinuo Liu; Eric Arden Youngstrom; Caroline Bodary; Zhuoyu Shi; Jennifer Youngstrom; Ekaterina Stepanova; Robert L. Findling
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Disruptive behavior problems like Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD) and Conduct Disorder (CD) are high burden conditions where accurate diagnosis is crucial for effective treatment. We evaluated probability nomograms and machine learning (ML) algorithms (logistic regression, LASSO, SVM, random forest) on accuracy, calibration, and generalizability for detecting current ODD or CD diagnoses.
Method: Youth aged 5–18 receiving outpatient care were recruited from academic (n=622) and community (n=506) clinics. Predictors included demographics, comorbid diagnoses, mood and behavioral indicators. The criterion was K-SADS diagnoses of ODD/CD. Models were trained in the academic sample, using the community sample for external validation. AUC quantified accuracy, Spiegelhalter's z indexed calibration, and cross-site performance measured generalizability.
Results: For ODD diagnostic prediction, the nomogram selected CBCL Aggression as the strongest predictor and reached AUC≈.70 in both samples. ML models achieved good discrimination (AUC≈.86) with good-to-moderate calibration in the academic sample, deteriorating to fair accuracy with severe miscalibration in the community setting. For CD diagnostic prediction, the nomogram built on CBCL Rule-Breaking showed good accuracy (AUC≈.82) in both samples. ML models showed near-excellent accuracy (AUC≈.88) in the academic sample but underperformed in the community sample (AUC=.73-.76), though LASSO, SVM, and random forest maintained good calibration.
Conclusion: Across both disorders, nomograms demonstrated lower accuracy but strong cross-site stability, while ML using more predictors achieved superior accuracy that did not generalize. The nomogram offers a low-cost and parsimonious tool. Machine learning is best suited for well-resourced clinics where model training data closely resemble the new cases encountered in practice.

articles_hidden.title: Mapping the Dynamics of Depressive and Anxiety symptoms in Coronary Artery Disease  over two years: A Network Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Stefana Vida; Heidi Hermans; Joris Mulder; Mihai Alexandru Constantin; Nina Kupper
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Coronary artery disease (CAD), a leading cause of morbidity and mortality 
worldwide, negatively impacts psychological well-being. Depressive and anxiety symptoms are 
commonly reported by patients with CAD, but little is known about symptom 
interconnectedness in this population. Insight into this interconnectedness may improve our 
understanding of how comorbidity arises and persists. Therefore, our aim was to gain new 
insights into the comorbidity of anxiety and depression symptoms in patients with CAD by 
estimating psychological networks at multiple time points. 
Methods: 2241 patients who had undergone percutaneous coronary intervention (22.2% 
women; mean age = 65.0, SD= 10.3) were included. With five cross-sectional psychological 
networks measured at five timepoints over two years, the symptom-level dynamics of 
depressive and anxiety symptoms were studied. Besides the overall network structure, network 
communities, centrality measures and sub-group differences were explored.  
Results: The estimated Bayesian Gaussian graphical models showed predominantly positive 
associations, and symptoms were mostly connected within their own domain of depression or 
anxiety. Two symptom clusters remained relatively stable: Depressed mood, feelings of 
worthlessness, and suicidal ideation consistently clustered together, while in the first month 
post PCI, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and appetite disturbance tended to co-occur. Fatigue, 
depressed mood, difficulty relaxing, and restlessness showed high connectivity and acted as 
bridging symptoms between different symptom groups.  
Conclusion: These findings suggest that both symptoms related to depression and to anxiety 
should be targeted within cardiac rehabilitation programs to reduce patients' psychological 
burden.

articles_hidden.title: LGBTQIA+ Family-Making Through Assisted Reproduction (ART): A Narrative Review
articles_hidden.authors: António de Pádua Jesué Oliveira; Henrique Pereira
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: LGBTQIA+ people and couples increasingly pursue parenthood through assisted reproductive technologies (ART), yet the psychological, relational, and institutional processes
involved remain dispersed across reproductive health, family studies, psychology, sociology, and LGBTQIA+ scholarship.
Objective: This structured narrative review synthesizes recent literature on how LGBTQIA+ individuals and couples construct parental projects through ART, with attention to reproductive
aspirations, route selection, relational negotiation, minority stress, institutional encounters, and family narrative construction.
Methods: PubMed and Scopus were searched for publications from 2016 to 2026. After deduplication, 260 unique records were screened, 126 underwent refined relevance appraisal,
and 49 articles were retained as the mapped corpus. From these, 17 index studies were purposively selected for in-depth discussion as they offered particularly rich evidence on
psychosocial, relational, and institutional processes. The review followed a structured narrative synthesis approach guided by the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles
(SANRA).
Results: Three family-making domains structured the synthesis: lesbian couples’ donor conception, IVF, and reciprocal IVF pathways; gay fatherhood through surrogacy and thirdparty reproduction; and transgender, gender-diverse reproductive planning, including fertility preservation and institutional barriers. Across domains, LGBTQIA+ ART family-making
involved six recurring psychosocial tasks: aspiration, feasibility appraisal, route selection, relational negotiation, institutional navigation, and narrative integration.
Conclusion: ART is not only a set of reproductive techniques but a psychosocial and institutional context in which LGBTQIA+ parental aspirations are translated into reproductive
pathways, negotiated through relationships, shaped by clinical and legal conditions, and incorporated into family narratives. These findings support cautious, pathway-sensitive, LGBTQIA+-affirmative fertility counselling.

articles_hidden.title: The Same Memory Retrieved Differently: Competition Enables Flexible Generalization in Hippocampus-like Networks
articles_hidden.authors: Robby Ralston; Brandon Turner; Vladimir Sloutsky
articles_hidden.abstract: Hippocampus supports the retrieval of richly detailed episodic memories from sparse cues. However, an event can be detailed and also lead to generalization. To explain both phenomena, researchers have proposed multiple memory systems or distinct memory traces for specific and general content. In contrast, we argue that a single system can support both specificity and generalization. To do this, we present ATHENA, a formal framework that reinterprets cognitive memory models as recurrent neural networks. We show that many episodic memory models are single-step approximations of dynamic networks with competitive retrieval mechanisms, similar to Modern Hopfield Networks. Notably, under a cognitive interpretation, the intensity of the competitive process is a psychologically-meaningful parameter that shapes generalization in the network. Through simulations, we demonstrate that modulating this parameter during retrieval leads the same traces to produce qualitatively different forms of generalization over the same memory traces. We then extend our analysis to sequential memory, and show how the same competitive retrieval process can be combined with known hippocampal circuits to achieve more sophisticated forms of generalization. These results demonstrate the flexibility of single-system memory retrieval and highlight the interplay of specific and general mnemonic content.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable necessity effects on patient safety competency among nursing students: Re-examining Yang et al. (2027)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Using Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA), Yang et al. concluded that adequate levels of organizational support, patient safety culture, adverse event risk perception, professional identity, and self-efficacy constitute necessary prerequisites for achieving high patient safety competency among master's-level nursing students. However, NCA-derived necessity effects may arise solely from associations between variables rather than reflecting genuine necessity relationships. In the present reanalysis, we evaluated whether the necessity effects reported by Yang et al. exceeded expected levels attributable to correlation alone. All reported effects were found to fall within or below estimated ranges of spuriousness, indicating that they were not stronger than would be anticipated in the absence of true necessity. Accordingly, the evidence presented by Yang et al. does not provide robust support for the claimed necessity relationships. We recommend that researchers employing NCA routinely assess ranges of spuriousness and only interpret necessity effects as substantive when they exceed these benchmarks.

articles_hidden.title: Higher Objective Physical Activity Attenuates the Association Between Daily Stress and Rumination
articles_hidden.authors: Alfiannisa Shelma Wikenza; Justin Hachenberger; Sakari Lemola
articles_hidden.abstract: Rumination is commonly experienced in response to stressful events and has been linked to adverse psychological outcomes. However, research has predominantly examined rumination as a predictor or consequence of psychological functioning, whereas less is known about factors associated with its day-to-day fluctuations. The current study addressed this gap by examining factors associated with rumination using an intensive longitudinal design. A total of 91 young adults (81,5% female; 14,1% male; 4,3% diverse or preferred not to disclose their gender; aged 18–30 years) participated in a 28-day experience-sampling study. Daily self-reported rumination, stress, and subjective sleep quality (SSQ), as well as accelerometry-derived total sleep time (TST), sleep efficiency (SE), and physical activity, were assessed. Multilevel analyses showed that daily stress was associated with greater rumination. Although physical activity was not directly associated with rumination, it moderated the association between stress and rumination. Higher-than-usual physical activity levels were associated with a smaller difference in rumination between stressful and non-stressful days. Better SSQ was independently associated with lower rumination, whereas TST and SE were not. Higher baseline depressive symptom severity was also associated with greater rumination but did not moderate the stress–rumination association. These findings highlight physical activity as a potential protective factor in stress-related rumination and demonstrate the value of examining rumination as a dynamic outcome in everyday life.

articles_hidden.title: Asymmetry in self-comparisons: Focal self bias in comparative judgment
articles_hidden.authors: Jareef Martuza; Esra Aslan
articles_hidden.abstract: Logical symmetry implies that if X is better than Y, then Y must be worse than X. Does this hold when people compare different versions of themselves? Nine main and three supplemental studies (N = 9,207 US- and UK-based adults) reveal a “focal self” bias—the self that is the subject of comparative judgments is perceived more favorably than the referent or compared self, over and above the content of the selves. When participants compared their present selves to their past or future selves on morality, warmth, and competence, they generally rated whichever self was focal more positively (Studies 1A-C)—contradicting logical symmetry. The focal self bias also extended to role-based self-comparisons between personal versus professional selves (Studies 2A-B), demonstrating it can shape evaluations beyond temporal selves. This pattern persisted even when the same participants made both reciprocal comparisons (Study 3), suggesting that the opportunity to reconcile judgments does not eliminate the bias. Across studies, because focal selves were rated lower on negative attributes, our data favor a selectivity account over a valence-independent extremity account. We also found that self-enhancement is not necessary for the focal self bias, as it emerged also when participants compared other people’s selves (Studies 4-5B). Finally, in direct self-other comparisons, making a peer focal largely eliminated the better-than-average effect (Studies 5A-5B), suggesting focality can partly account for this classic effect. These findings extend comparison asymmetries from distinct entities to comparisons of the same person, suggesting that which self occupies the focal position systematically shapes evaluations.

articles_hidden.title: What Do People Dream About? Themes and Emotions in 400,000+ Dream Reports Shared on Weibo (2018–2023)
articles_hidden.authors: Yanqi Lyu; Wuwei Tang; Huanyu Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: Dream research has traditionally relied on small samples and retrospective self-reports, which are vulnerable to memory decay. The present study combines big data with natural language processing to investigate dreams that users spontaneously shared on Weibo, a major Chinese social media platform. Using the keywords “dream of,” “dream about,” and “in a dream,” we collected posts from April of each year between 2018 and 2023 and, after five rounds of screening, obtained 418,961 dream reports. We analyzed the demographic characteristics of the posters, the thematic content of the dreams (via word-frequency analysis and a co-occurrence semantic network), and the emotional tone of the reports (via lexicon-based sentiment scoring). Women shared dreams more often than men; users aged 20–35 predominated; posting peaked in the early morning. Six broad themes emerged—family, school, romantic relationships, work, danger, and body—covering a broader range but occurring at lower frequencies than typical-dream themes assessed by questionnaire. Themes related to danger and death moved in the opposite direction to the national urban unemployment rate after 2019, suggesting that dreams may buffer waking emotional states. Negative emotion scores consistently exceeded positive scores, indicating that negative content dominates dream sharing. We discuss the implications of these findings for understanding the emotion-regulation function of dreams and outline directions for future research.

articles_hidden.title: Does machine learning generalize across political change? Predicting approval of political violence four years later
articles_hidden.authors: Oskari Lahtinen
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examined whether approval of political violence could be predicted from individual characteristics and whether models developed in one political context would still work four years later. Logistic regression and XGBoost models using 18 demographic, political, and psychological predictors were developed in a Finnish adult sample collected in 2022 and applied without refitting to an independent 2026 sample. Cross-validated ROC-AUC was .676–.677 in 2022. Despite a decline in violence approval from 12.6% to 7.9%, discrimination remained similar or better in 2026 (ROC-AUC = .751 for logistic regression and .707 for XGBoost). The political distribution of violence approval, however, changed markedly. Midpoint-or-higher responses remained nearly unchanged in the left-party bloc (17.4% to 16.8%) but fell from 18.0% to 3.8% in the right-party bloc. Thus, models trained in 2022 continued to predict violence approval in 2026 even though its relationship with political orientation had changed substantially.

articles_hidden.title: Individual differences in the computational processes that support face recognition
articles_hidden.authors: Fournier Raphaël; Paul Downing; Richard Ramsey
articles_hidden.abstract: Face recognition ability varies substantially across the population, yet the cognitive and computational processes that give rise to this variation remain poorly understood. Here, we combined approaches from experimental, differential and mathematical psychology to test how individual differences in face recognition ability relate to latent parameters of the decision-making processes involved in face recognition. Participants (N = 300) completed a face memory task with learned and novel faces, together with independent measures of face recognition ability (Cambridge Face Memory Test) and general object recognition ability (car recognition). We modelled task performance with an evidence-accumulation model that translates accuracy and response times into latent parameters, including drift rate (the signal-to-noise ratio of the evidence) and threshold (response caution). Higher face recognition ability was associated with greater drift rate discrimination between correct and incorrect response accumulators in the face memory task, for both learned and novel faces and to a similar degree, consistent with expertise effects in other domains. This association remained largely unchanged when accounting for car recognition ability, suggesting that it is at least partly tied to face processing itself. Higher face recognition ability was also associated with greater response caution, which may reflect better calibration to task demands. Although the associations were modest in size, these findings suggest that individual differences in face recognition ability are reflected in distinct computational mechanisms, namely more efficient extraction of information from faces and a more cautious decision policy. This approach enables a more explicit and computational basis for cognitive theories of face recognition to be developed, as well as for testing whether these mechanisms operate similarly across the full spectrum of face recognition abilities.

articles_hidden.title: Examining the Relations Between Self-Construal, Culture, and Cognitive Dissonance Using the Induced Compliance Paradigm
articles_hidden.authors: Tim Figureau; Daniel Priolo; Willem W. A. Sleegers; Kenneth G DeMarree; Omid Ghasemi; Amélie Gourdon-Kanhukamwe; Maxime Mauduy; Asil Ali Özdoğru; Robert M Ross; Bjørn Sætrevik
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive dissonance, traditionally conceptualized as a fundamental psychological process involving discomfort from inconsistent cognitions, may vary across cultures. These variations could be attributed to self-construal, or how individuals define themselves in relation to others. Although previous cross-cultural research has predominantly used the free-choice paradigm, significant concerns have been raised regarding its procedural validity and the robustness of its findings. To address this issue, this registered report presents secondary analyses of a large-scale international dataset. We investigated the moderating role of cultural variables on dissonance effects within the induced-compliance paradigm across 18 countries (N = 3,804). We hypothesized that dissonance effects would be stronger for participants with higher individual-level self-construal scores (H1), in more individualistic countries (H2), and in countries with higher country-level self-construal scores (H3). Our results did not support these hypotheses, suggesting that cultural moderation may not generalize to the induced-compliance paradigm. We discuss the necessity of reassessing the procedure’s reliability and clarifying the theoretical role of choice.

articles_hidden.title: Ulyssean Self-Control: Pre-commitment is effective, but choosing it freely requires good self-control
articles_hidden.authors: Hallgeir Sjåstad; Mathias Ekström
articles_hidden.abstract: Can pre-commitment strategies be a solution to self-control problems, or do they mainly help those who are already successful at regulating their behavior? In Study 1 (N=1,012), pre-commitment causally improved effort performance in an incentivized matrix-solving task. However, in Study 2 (N=1,010) participants with low (vs. high) self-control as a general trait were 35 percentage points less likely to choose the pre-commitment strategy, which in turn was associated with worse performance and earnings. Information about strategy effectiveness led to a small increase in uptake, whereas a “paternalistic” policy with forced pre-commitment led to superior performance. Study 3 (N=1,037) found that participants with high trait self-control were more likely to choose pre-commitment strategies across work, education, and health domains, mediated by higher future focus, strategy familiarity, and temptation avoidance. Pre-commitment is an effective strategy, but it is most often chosen by those who are already doing well: Individuals with good self-control.

articles_hidden.title: Associations Between Global Emotion Beliefs and Three Stages of Emotion Regulation in Everyday Life
articles_hidden.authors: Valentina Bianchi; Imogen Smith; Felicia Semple; Amy S G Lee; Eeske van Roekel; Peter Koval
articles_hidden.abstract: Everyone experiences emotions, but people vary in their orientations to and beliefs about emotions. Research has linked global beliefs about the controllability and usefulness of emotions with psychological functioning and well-being, but the mechanisms through which those beliefs shape people’s well-being remain unclear. Ford and Gross (2019) proposed emotion regulation as a candidate mechanism, such that emotion beliefs influence whether people initiate emotion regulation (identification), which strategies people use to regulate their emotions (selection), and how successfully people are able to implement their selected emotion-regulation strategies (implementation). We tested predictions based on Ford and Gross’s (2019) framework in everyday life in a seven-day experience sampling study (Australian community sample recruited in 2024; N = 326; 80% female; MAge=26.11, SDAge=8.52). At the identification stage, neither controllability nor usefulness beliefs were associated with initiating emotion regulation. In terms of strategy selection, stronger beliefs about the usefulness of negative emotions were associated with greater use of situation selection and lesser use of expressive suppression, as predicted. Finally, at the implementation stage, controllability beliefs did not moderate the hedonic effects of any regulation strategy, whereas usefulness beliefs about negative emotions predicted a weaker positive association between cognitive reappraisal and negative affect, and believing positive emotions to be more useful predicted a stronger inverse association between rumination and positive affect. Our findings suggest that individual differences in global emotion beliefs may play a smaller role than theorised in daily emotion regulation processes.

articles_hidden.title: Now I See Me, Now I Don’t: A Replication and Psychometric Exploration of the Invisible Face Illusion
articles_hidden.authors: Lucy Stafford; Catherine Preston; Paul Mark Jenkinson
articles_hidden.abstract: Current theories of multisensory integration explain how conscious feelings of body ownership arise, at least in part, from the integration of simultaneously felt and observed touch. The same principles apply to illusory ownership of another face and even to the experience of having an invisible body or body parts. D’Angelo et al., (2021) demonstrated how a sense of invisibility can extend to the face. However, no attempts have been made to independently replicate the so-called Invisible Face Illusion (IFI), and the underlying phenomenological components of the illusion experience remain unknown. The aim of this preregistered study was to replicate the IFI and explore its underlying psychometric components. Participants (n=152) viewed a video of an invisible face being stroked in- or  out-of-synchrony with touches applied to their own face, and completed an IFI questionnaire after each condition. Separate exploratory factor analyses on the synchronous and asynchronous conditions found the same 14-item, two-factor model to be the best fit to the data, with the factors capturing 1) facial disembodiment and 2) feelings of touch referral. As expected, overall factor scores were significantly higher in the synchronous versus asynchronous condition, and significant increases were evident for eleven of the fourteen individual questionnaire items. This is the first study to replicate the IFI, suggesting that the illusion involves experiencing referral of touch on one's own face as arising from the invisible face, and a sense of disconnection or disembodiment from one's own face. We suggest possible therapeutic benefits of the IFI which require further exploration.

articles_hidden.title: Identifying the Critical Period of Academic Burnout: A Computational Simulation Approach Based on Large-Scale Assessment Data
articles_hidden.authors: Xin Tang; Xiaofeng Wen; Jianxiao Jiang; Danhua Lin; Yiqun Gan; Yu Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding student engagement and burnout has long been a central concern in educational research. While prior studies have extensively examined levels and correlates of them, far less is known about the timing at which students transition into amotivation (i.e., burnout) state from motivated state. In present study, based on Cox proportional hazards modeling and using large-scale data from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), we develop a computational simulation model to infer individual- and group-level distributions of academic burnout onset across study weeks. Results demonstrate systematic variation in the timing of academic burnout onset as a function of weekly study time, with longer study hours associated with an earlier increase in burnout risk. To facilitate practical application, we further implement an interactive ShinyApp that allows users to estimate academic burnout onset periods at the individual, classroom, and school levels. This study contributes a novel methodological framework for temporally locating motivational breakdown and offers a scalable tool for translating large-scale assessment data into actionable educational insights.

articles_hidden.title: Continuative Development of Traditional Psychology: Rethinking Inheritance and Innovation through Traditional Chinese Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Xianglong ZENG
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychological research increasingly draws on resources inherited from historical traditions, with the potential both to advance contemporary psychological knowledge and to sustain and further develop those traditions. Existing methodological discussions have often emphasized fidelity to inherited meanings in reconstructing and transforming traditional resources. Yet when contemporary research substantially revises inherited responses, can such work still count as inheritance, and if so, where does the boundary between continuation and departure lie? Focusing on traditional Chinese psychology, this conceptual article identifies a shared developmental logic across theoretical, practical, and methodological cases that go beyond the reconstruction of inherited responses. On this basis, it conceptualizes continuative development as a mode of inheritance distinct from reconstructive transformation. Its central argument is that continuity lies at the level of inquiry rather than in the preservation of particular inherited responses. The inquiry itself may even develop to address new questions under changing conditions. What distinguishes continuation from mere influence or use of traditional resources is an intelligible developmental relation to an inherited inquiry. The article further argues that, compared with reconstructive transformation, continuative development opens a broader space for ongoing knowledge generation by allowing new answers, practices, methodological approaches, and questions to emerge beyond the historical repertoire. This also means that contemporary psychology need not treat inherited traditions only as repositories of existing intellectual resources, but can also feed back into and further develop those inquiries. In turn, such development may contribute to cultural continuity while enabling inherited traditions to generate new psychological knowledge that may extend beyond their original cultural contexts. In sum, the article articulates the principles and potential contributions of continuative development as a distinct, methodologically defensible research orientation and clarifies the relationship between inheritance and innovation in traditional psychology.

articles_hidden.title: The emergence of language-specific biases in visual attention in pre-reading toddlers from two cultures
articles_hidden.authors: Christine Potter; Nadeen Kherbawy; Christopher Sepulveda; Sagi Jaffe-Dax
articles_hidden.abstract: Skilled adult readers show biases in their visual attention that reflect the direction of their native writing systems (e.g., English readers scan left-to-right while Hebrew readers scan right-to-left), but it not yet clear when these biases develop. We tested the hypothesis that language-specific patterns of behavior precede the ability to read by testing how toddlers (2.5-4 years) exposed to different writing systems allocated their attention in a picture naming task. Across two communities, children tended to name objects in the direction that matched their native language. Hebrew-learning toddlers labeled objects from right-to-left, while English- and Spanish-learning toddlers showed the reverse pattern, and language-specific tendencies strengthened with age. These results demonstrate that children have begun to discover directional regularities associated with their language even before they receive literacy instruction and illustrate how cultural conventions exert a direct influence on children’s attention from a very young age.

articles_hidden.title: Revealing the latent geometry of dream content with language models
articles_hidden.authors: Daniele Gatti; Tomaso Vecchi; Pietro Pietrini; Emiliano Ricciardi; Giulio Bernardi; Luca Rinaldi
articles_hidden.abstract: Dreams provide a unique window into human cognition, as their content may reflect individual and collective experiences. Here, we use language models to analyze 21,607 dream narratives, representing each report as a vector in a high-dimensional semantic space that enables continuous comparison without predefined categories. We ask whether different sources of information are organized within the same representational space and across multiple levels of semantic representation; we also tested how dream representational geometries evolve over time. We find that dreams produced by different individuals, as well as by individuals of different genders, occupy distinct regions of this space, particularly in abstract semantic representations. Similarity among descriptions of dreamers also predicts similarity in their dream content. Finally, we show how the semantic geometry of dream content evolves over time, with its trajectory shaped by the cumulative history of past reports. Together, this study provides evidence for the semantic structure of dream content and its evolution over time.

articles_hidden.title: A Critical Epistemological Audit of Early Evidence Syntheses in Generative AI Educational Research: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Tim Fütterer; Nina Peltzer; Peter Gerjets; Detmar Meurers; Tamara Powell Tate; Mark Warschauer; Valentin Emslander; Lisa Bardach; John hattie; Michael Sailer
articles_hidden.abstract: The rapid emergence of ChatGPT in education was accompanied by an equally rapid proliferation of meta-analyses synthesizing its effects on educational outcomes. We conducted a systematic epistemological audit of the first wave of these meta-analyses, evaluating both their methodological and reporting quality and the primary evidence they synthesized. We included meta-analyses published after the release of ChatGPT that quantitatively synthesized its effects on educational outcomes. Five meta-analyses comprising 87 unique primary studies met our inclusion criteria. We also reconstructed their quantitative evidence base and conducted exploratory three-level random-effects meta-analyses to examine effect magnitude, heterogeneity, and robustness, and how these varied with theoretically and methodologically relevant characteristics. The five meta-analyses generally searched multiple databases, specified eligibility criteria, and examined heterogeneity and potential publication bias, but showed limitations in independent screening and coding, preregistration, open data and code, and transparent reporting. The underlying primary evidence likewise showed methodological and reporting limitations and substantial conceptual heterogeneity. Among 69 classifiable primary studies, 79.7% assessed performance exclusively, whereas only 11.6% assessed learning exclusively. The reconstructed meta-analysis yielded a positive average effect (g = 0.83, 95% CI [0.68, 0.97]), but heterogeneity was substantial (I² = 94.06%; 95% prediction interval [−0.75, 2.41]), and estimates were markedly attenuated in sensitivity analyses addressing small-study and selection effects. Although positive effects remained among stronger studies assessing learning, increasingly stringent quality criteria rapidly reduced the evidence base, limiting the certainty and generalizability of conclusions about learning effects. Overall, our findings caution against interpreting a single pooled estimate as a stable general effect of ChatGPT on learning and highlight the need for more rigorous, conceptually precise, transparent, and reproducible research.

articles_hidden.title: Trait or Bias? Why item keying is indispensable when comparing language model responses across languages
articles_hidden.authors: Qing Li
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychological scales designed for humans are increasingly administered to language models, and differences between their responses in two languages are read as evidence of cultural tendency. Such comparisons presuppose that the two language versions measure the same thing. This study tests that premise. Three established social orientation scales were administered to four models built by United States and Chinese developers in Chinese and English under two temperature settings. Responses were then decomposed, using a psychometric model that separates a latent trait from a directional response bias, into the component that tracks what the instrument is meant to measure and the component that does not. The cross-linguistic difference is not one quantity. On scales with balanced keying, every estimate showed a higher trait and a lower bias under Chinese prompting, the bias moving further than the trait in most conditions. Because the two components run in opposite directions, they offset one another on scales containing no reverse-keyed items, where they also cannot be separated. A difference reported on such a scale therefore does not establish that models differ in the construct, only that they answered differently. Two further manipulations show that the difference is produced by item wording, though not by negation, and that the stability of a model identifier over four weeks varies by an order of magnitude between vendors. We set out three checks that would make cross-linguistic comparison interpretable: balanced keying, decomposition to the item level, and a contemporaneous control whenever collections are compared across time.

articles_hidden.title: Statistics Anxiety and Data Literacy for Sustainable Development: Preliminary Psychometric Evaluation of the Indonesian Statistics Anxiety Rating Scale
articles_hidden.authors: Dina Nazriani; Anang Dwi Santoso; Vena Jaladara; Suri Mutia Siregar; Rahma Fauzia
articles_hidden.abstract:
Education for sustainable development (ESD) emphasizes critical and systems thinking, and both depend on students' ability to read and interpret data such as Sustainable Development Goal indicators. Statistics anxiety is a documented barrier to this kind of data literacy, yet few multidimensional measures of it are available for Indonesian higher education. This study reports a preliminary psychometric evaluation of an Indonesian version of the 51-item Statistics Anxiety Rating Scale (STARS), in which items referring to outdated technology were updated. Data came from 100 undergraduate psychology students at Universitas Sumatera Utara. Each of the six subscales was analyzed with the Rasch rating scale model to examine item fit, rating scale functioning, dimensionality, reliability and separation, and differential item functioning (DIF) by high school track and entry cohort. Correlations with statistics course grades (n = 69) provided criterion-related evidence. Forty-five of the 51 items fit the model. Person reliability ranged from .71 to .86, and thresholds were ordered in every subscale, although respondents barely distinguished between the two highest categories of Worth of Statistics. Four items showed DIF by entry cohort, which appears to reflect whether students had already taken a statistics course. Anxiety subscales correlated negatively with course grades (ρ = -.28 to -.40). The Indonesian STARS shows promising measurement properties, but several items need review, and the results remain preliminary until back translation and expert review are completed.

Keywords: statistics anxiety, Rasch model, data literacy, education for sustainable development, Indonesia

articles_hidden.title: Moment-to-Moment Affect During Film-Induced Somatic Anxiety
articles_hidden.authors: Micah G. Allen
articles_hidden.abstract: A viral video of a dangerous stunt can make a viewer's palms sweat and heart race, even though they know they are safe. Such videos let us study emotion as it naturally unfolds, building, persisting and receding. Here we characterise the response to one such film moment by moment and present the open-source browser platform we built to do so. Viewers rate valence and arousal continuously on an affect grid embedded in the video. Each rating is stored with the frame on screen, the film pauses when viewing is interrupted, and participants are trained and their input checked. The film was a 13.5-min silent first-person recording of unsecured climbing. An exploratory sample (n = 21) informed preregistered tests in an independent confirmatory sample (N = 124). Arousal rose as the climb progressed, held a plateau for several minutes and then declined towards baseline, with valence most unpleasant during the plateau. This time course was highly reproducible across samples. Somatic anxiety increased substantially after the film (dz = 1.03), and participants with larger increases had rated it as more arousing and unpleasant. The film thus carries viewers through a reproducible, interoceptively charged emotional episode, and the platform can characterise other stimuli. Researchers can ask how the shift from a calm to an aroused state changes brain connectivity, interoception and emotion, and whether it is heightened in anxious people. Platform, data and reference time courses are openly available.

articles_hidden.title: Quality of Life and the Case for Consent-Based Psilocybin Access – Questions on the Regulatory Framework and Cost
articles_hidden.authors: Janis Ancans
articles_hidden.abstract: Legal access to psilocybin almost always requires a medical diagnosis first, usually treatment-resistant depression (TRD) or severe PTSD, as though informed consent alone was not sufficient. This article makes two connected arguments. Extending the autonomy argument already accepted for terminally ill patients, competent adults who understand the risks of a psilocybin experience should be able to choose it for reasons of psychological wellness or existential anxiety relief, not only because a clinician has certified a qualifying illness, a right the legal literature calls “cognitive liberty”. Just as important, the cost of access is not fixed; it reflects the regulatory framework under which psilocybin is provided. No jurisdiction has yet completed medicines authorisation pathway; the furthest-advanced clinical programme, Compass Pathways' COMP360, met its Phase 3 primary endpoint and reported six-month durability data for TRD by July 2026, and its developer has since signalled an annual cost close to that of esketamine nasal spray, USD 50,000–65,000, or roughly USD 17,000–22,000 per dose. Meanwhile, Australia's narrower authorised-prescriber legal route for TRD, using GMP-manufactured but unregistered psilocybin, already costs AUD $20,000 per course. Three distinct non-medical routes cost far less. Truffles in the Netherlands, sold under food law with no diagnosis and no supervision required, and Colorado and Oregon's state-licensed psilocybin services, which require no diagnosis but do involve a supervising facilitator, cost up to $3,000 per session. Removing the diagnosis requirement while leaving this cost structure untouched risks replacing the regulatory barrier with the wealth-based one, unless expanded access is paired with public subsidy. Article also briefly reviews the safety evidence, the political origins of psilocybin's scheduling, and the double standard in how its risks are treated. A Canadian case illustrates the institutional and regulatory framework dysfunction, a dying man denied psilocybin for existential relief while approved for medical assistance in dying within weeks, before the article closes with policy recommendations addressing both access and funding.

articles_hidden.title: Psilocybin-Assisted Therapy for Existential Distress in Serious and Life-Limiting Illness: Emerging Trial Evidence, Barriers to Access, and the Case for Individualized Eligibility
articles_hidden.authors: Janis Ancans
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Background. Existential distress and treatment-resistant depression are common and difficult to manage in patients with serious and life-limiting illnesses. Psilocybin-assisted therapy has shown early promise for these conditions, but access outside research settings remains narrow, inconsistent, expensive and often shaped by outdated eligibility rules. These include extremely limited lists of diagnosis- or just blanket age-based cut-offs, that are not grounded in evidence specific to palliative populations. Regulators slowly adjust to the state-of-the-art knowledge generated by psilocybin-assisted therapy, and overall, often present poor understanding of palliative populations specific needs.
Objective. To review current and emerging clinical evidence for psilocybin-assisted therapy in serious and life-limiting illness, highlighted with the examples of the EU “Horizon Europe” funded PsyPal project and a Johns Hopkins-led trial in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and to examine the regulatory, informational, and financial barriers that shape access for palliative populations.
Findings. Randomized trials in cancer-related existential distress report sustained reductions in depression and death anxiety. Furthermore, a majority of participants in the founding psilocybin studies rated their session among the most meaningful experiences of their life. Project PsyPal is currently the first randomized trial of psilocybin therapy in non-oncology palliative populations, enrolling patients with COPD, ALS, multiple sclerosis, and atypical parkinsonian disorders across four European sites with no upper age limit; a separate trial at Johns Hopkins is testing psilocybin for mood and hopelessness in ALS specifically. Real-world cohort data from Oregon's regulated program corroborate meaningful symptom improvement and low serious-adverse-event rates. Access, however, remains constrained by diagnostic and research-representation gaps, high out-of-pocket cost, and inconsistent regulatory pathways, illustrated by a Canadian patient refused psilocybin for existential relief who was approved for medical assistance in dying within weeks.
Conclusion. Clinical evidence relevant fort to palliative and serious-illness populations is accumulating rapidly. Eligibility frameworks for psilocybin-assisted therapy in palliative care should be built on individualized clinical assessment rather than systematic exclusions, paired with funding mechanisms that prevent access from becoming a function of wealth alone.

articles_hidden.title: My Personality—Wrapped: Protocol for a Measurement-Burst Design Study to Investigate the Development and Dynamics of Individual Differences Across Time
articles_hidden.authors: Amanda Jo Wright; Peter Haehner; Michael Dominik Krämer; Nicholas Poh-Jie Tan; Christopher James Hopwood; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles_hidden.abstract: People and their environments continuously shape one another across time. Understanding person-environment transactions is essential for describing, predicting, and explaining the dynamics and development of individual differences. Yet, progress on this has been constrained by two common limitations: study designs driven by practical rather than theoretical considerations and neglecting how person-environment processes unfold across multiple timescales. Here, we present the rationale and design of the My Personality––Wrapped (MPW) Study, a measurement-burst study designed to investigate how individual differences in personality, well-being, attitudes, social and interpersonal behaviors, and health develop and dynamically fluctuate alongside environmental influences across multiple timescales. Across 1 year, participants (Nmax = 1,230) completed baseline (T0) and post-study (T6) assessment batteries, five bimonthly surveys (T1–T5), and 15 pseudorandomly scheduled 1-week bursts comprising mobile sensing, experience sampling, daily, and weekly surveys. This intensive, multi-method study provides comprehensive cross-timescale data on psychological constructs and contextual experiences. The MPW Study is designed to advance the field’s understanding of temporal dynamics underlying individual differences by disentangling within-person processes from between-person differences, facilitating theory development and testing of multi-timescale person-environment transactions, and informing future theory-driven research on the dynamics of personality and well-being, social and health processes, and life disruptions.

articles_hidden.title: The Same Memory Retrieved Differently: Competition Enables Flexible Generalization in Hippocampus-like Networks
articles_hidden.authors: Robby Ralston; Brandon Turner; Vladimir Sloutsky
articles_hidden.abstract: Hippocampus supports the retrieval of richly detailed episodic memories from sparse cues. However, an event can be detailed and also lead to generalization. To explain both phenomena, researchers have proposed multiple memory systems or distinct memory traces for specific and general content. In contrast, we argue that a single system can support both specificity and generalization. To do this, we present ATHENA, a formal framework that reinterprets cognitive memory models as recurrent neural networks. We show that many episodic memory models are single-step approximations of dynamic networks with competitive retrieval mechanisms, similar to Modern Hopfield Networks. Notably, under a cognitive interpretation, the intensity of the competitive process is a psychologically-meaningful parameter that shapes generalization in the network. Through simulations, we demonstrate that modulating this parameter during retrieval leads the same traces to produce qualitatively different forms of generalization over the same memory traces. We then extend our analysis to sequential memory, and show how the same competitive retrieval process can be combined with known hippocampal circuits to achieve more sophisticated forms of generalization. These results demonstrate the flexibility of single-system memory retrieval and highlight the interplay of specific and general mnemonic content.

articles_hidden.title: Concordance of Parents’ Anger Responses are Linked with Parents’ and Adolescents’ Psychopathology Symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Ilyaz; Prakash Thambipillai; Amy Byrd; Salome Vanwoerden; J. Richard Jennings; Stephanie Stepp; Vera Vine
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Parents’ emotions shape children’s understanding of emotions and their management. Children of parents with borderline personality disorder (BPD), in which anger dysregulation is a cardinal symptom, are at elevated risk of psychopathology, which tends to onset in adolescence. The nature of anger dysregulation associated with parental BPD symptom severity and how it relates to adolescents’ psychopathology is not well understood. We characterized parents’ anger dysregulation multimodally and examined how concordance across emotion channels (e.g., subjective, and physiological) predicted both parent BPD symptoms and child psychopathology symptoms. Method: Participants were 162 parents (Mage =40.37 years; 93% women; 47% racial/ethnic minority) of young adolescents oversampled for emotion dysregulation (Mage=12.59 years; 47% women; 60% racial/ethnic minority). Parents’ BPD symptom severity was clinician-rated using semi-structured interview, and adolescents’ psychopathology symptoms were assessed by parent- and adolescent-report on a well-known, validated questionnaire. During a dyadic, parent-child conflict interaction, parents’ anger responses were measured in two ways, using respiratory sinus arrythmia (RSA; low values indicating stress-like responding) and self-reported anger. Results: Using polynomial response surface modeling, we found that parental BPD feature severity (Model 1) and child psychopathology severity (Model 2) were each related to greater numerical misalignment between parental anger responses, primarily manifesting in this sample as a combination of low RSA and high subjective anger, or anger concordance. Conclusions: Findings help show which forms of parental anger dysregulation are related to psychopathology in parents and adolescents, which could have implications for understanding the intergenerational transmission of psychopathology.

articles_hidden.title: From the Inside Out: School Stressors Identified by Autistic and ADHD (AuDHD) Students Experiencing School Non-Attendance
articles_hidden.authors: Jia Ying Sarah Lee; Dawn Adams; Chris Paradisis; Raechel Smart; Tiffany Westphal; Leah Heale; Kate Simpson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Research into school non-attendance is expanding, yet the perspectives of young people, particularly neurodivergent students, remain underrepresented. Card-sorting tasks offer a promising, accessible method for capturing these perspectives. The Student Stress Investigation (SSI) uses a structured card-sort approach to facilitate young people’s self-report of school-related stressors.

This study used the SSI to explore school-based stressors among 31 children and adolescents (mean age = 12.16 years) diagnosed with both autism and ADHD (AuDHD). On average, they missed 3.46 days of school per month. Participants first categorised stressors as relevant or irrelevant, then ranked relevant items from smallest to largest stressors.

The most frequently identified major stressors were classroom environments that were too loud or quiet (35.5%), uninteresting tasks (32.2%), unpredictability (29.0%), school days being too long (29.0%), and being rushed (29.0%). Qualitative responses highlighted variability in how stressors were experienced. For example, some students reported that the classroom being too loud or quiet was a sensory-related stressor, while others reported it as having an impact on attention or executive functioning.

These findings provide direct insight into the everyday school experiences contributing to stress and non-attendance among AuDHD students. The results underscore the value of self-report tools and highlight the need for targeted, individualised, and proactive adjustments to reduce stress that may in turn support an increased capacity to consider a return to school.

articles_hidden.title: Interpretability in the Limit: How Can Understanding Machines Help us Understand Human Language?
articles_hidden.authors: Najoung Kim; Ethan Gotlieb Wilcox
articles_hidden.abstract: In the coming years, interpretability research will uncover a vast set of machine constructs: causally efficacious representations and processing mechanisms underlying the use of language and other intelligent behavior in AI systems, including LLMs. Assuming that interpretability will be as successful as can be reasonably hoped for (interpretability in the limit), how can the discovery of machine constructs shape linguistics and cognitive science? First, we provide several axes of analysis that can help scientists conceptualize the internal mechanisms discovered in machines. Even under the assumption that interpretability in the limit guarantees that all constructs are causally implicated in a system's behavior, scientists may want to consider several additional properties, including constructs' theoretical status, domain status, ontological status, and complexity. Second, we argue that scientists should prioritize recurrent constructs, meaning those that surface across a diversity of models converging on behaviors of interest while varying on other axes such as architecture, training data, objective function, language, and modality. Finally, we provide three routes for how machine constructs can inform linguistic and cognitive theories, emphasizing that all of these routes treat machine constructs as hypotheses, where additional theorizing and experimentation by domain experts are required. We conclude with several recommendations that can be implemented now for improving the long-term success of this program.

articles_hidden.title: Consensus Embedding Geometry for Taxonomy Discovery in Psychological Domains
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Steven Stutts; Jeffrey Humpherys; Ting Shen
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychological domains contain many constructs whose meanings are specified through natural-language definitions and examples. Organizing these vocabularies requires methods that connect semantic representations to interpretable categories and expose the effects of analytical choices.
