Similarly, recent studies suggest that the decline of metacognition observed with age might be reduced by cognitive reserve in the memory domain, but the domain-generality of such effect remains unexplored. This study is part of a published study investigating the effect of age on cognition and metacognition in episodic memory, semantic memory, executive functioning, and visual perception (Meunier-Duperray et al., 2025). Here, we focused on cognitive reserve measured by the CRIq on cognition (i.e., task performance) and metacognition in a subsample of 319 participants (aged from 18 to 79). We expected an effect of cognitive reserve only on tasks sensitive to age-related decline: episodic memory, executive functioning, and visual perception for task performance and episodic and semantic tasks for metacognition. Overall, these results suggest evidence for the null hypothesis for the effect of cognitive reserve on the age-related decline in cognition and metacognition. Only anecdotal to small evidence was found for an effect of cognitive reserve on episodic memory performance across the lifespan suggesting that reserve reflects earlier individual differences rather than differences in the rate of decline. However, the low variability of our high-reserve sample may have masked some effects.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring the Role of Physical Effort in the Rewarding Value of Sedentary Behavior
articles_hidden.authors: Silvio Maltagliati; Pam ten Broeke; Philippe Sarrazin; Ryan Rhodes; Erik Bijleveld; Genevieve Fridlund Dunton; Cedrick Bonnet; Benjamin Gardner; David A. Raichlen; Matthew W Miller
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Sedentary behavior is commonly studied based on the value of the higher-order task being performed, such as watching TV, using a phone, or playing video games. However, it is possible that the low physical effort associated with these behaviors also contributes to their appeal. That is, individuals may be drawn not just to the task but to the low effort it is paired with. This study aims to test this possibility by manipulating body position (sitting vs. standing) while participants engage in a familiar sedentary task (i.e., playing Tetris). Methods: To test this hypothesis, we manipulated body position during a smartphone video game task to examine how sitting versus standing affected the rewarding value assigned to the game. Results: Our results (two independent studies, N = 228 and N = 129) show that the rewarding value of this sedentary behavior also stems from the low effort cost associated with sitting. Conclusions: These findings suggest that the perception of effort may contribute to influencing sedentary preferences and provide valuable insights for interventions aimed at reducing excessive sedentary behavior, such as targeted strategies to increase the valuation of physical effort.

articles_hidden.title: Sampling Thoughts During Music Listening: A Systematic Comparison of Probe-caught, Self-caught and Retrospective Thought Reporting Methods
articles_hidden.authors: Nao Toyama; Kelly Jakubowski
articles_hidden.abstract: Music listening experiences dynamically unfold over time. However, as previous research has relied predominantly on short music excerpts and retrospective post-listening self-reports, how qualitative thought content unfolds during extended listening remains underexplored. Crucially, addressing this requires effective real-time sampling, yet direct empirical comparisons of such methods––i.e., experimenter-led versus participant-led approaches––and their impact on data quality and listener experience are remain lacking. To address these gaps, the present study systematically compared three experience-sampling methodologies (probe-caught, self-caught, and a retrospective control) using participants’ own smartphones during an 18-minute video of a classical music performance. While the control group yielded significantly fewer thoughts, both experimental groups (probe- and self-caught) reported a comparable total number of thoughts. The probe-caught method exhibited greater inter-participant stability and generated significantly more detailed qualitative descriptions. Importantly, participants’ subjective perceived interference on their listening experience was low and did not differ across groups, confirming that real-time thought reporting did not disrupt the natural listening experience compared with traditional retrospective reporting. By validating the efficiency, stability, and minimal invasiveness of the probe-caught method, this study provides an empirical foundation for future research investigating real-time subjective experiences across diverse listening environments.

articles_hidden.title: Iconicity and Age Make Distinct Contributions to Symbolic Correspondence in Early Childhood
articles_hidden.authors: Keyi Yang; Ruoxi Chen; Suizi Xue; Jiajia Zhou; anonymous; Juan Wang; Jingmei Wang; Jinliang Qin
articles_hidden.abstract: Iconicity has been proposed to support children’s symbolic understanding, yet it remains unclear when iconicity contributes to symbolic correspondence and how this contribution varies across early childhood. The present study examined semantic judgments in 204 Chinese preschool children (Mage = 5.36 years, SD = 0.78; 102 boys) across three representational formats: line drawings, Oracle Bone script, and simplified Chinese characters. Children judged whether sequentially presented picture–symbol pairs referred to the same objects or actions, allowing broad format differences to be distinguished from graded item-level iconicity within each format. Children were consistently more accurate when rejecting mismatches than when confirming matches. Iconicity was especially informative when children had to confirm that different forms shared a meaning. Diffusion decision modeling further showed that this advantage was expressed in the accumulation of decision-relevant evidence during confirmation. Older age was associated with more efficient evidence accumulation for establishing semantic correspondence across representational formats, but age did not systematically strengthen or weaken the iconicity-drift relation. These findings suggest that iconicity and age make distinct contributions to symbolic correspondence: iconicity functions as a task-dependent source of information, whereas age-related differences are characterized by broader gains in the efficiency of establishing correspondence across symbolic forms.

articles_hidden.title: Sentiment Analysis of Clinical Interviews Identifies Language Markers of Identity Diffusion in Adolescents with Personality Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Katarina Lodrant; Filip Melinscak; Ayse Nur Beris; Valentin Schneider; Klara Czernin; Anselm Bründlmayer; Paul Plener; Frank Scharnowski; David Steyrl; Clarissa Laczkovics
articles_hidden.abstract:
Identity diffusion – a fragmented sense of self and others maintained by splitting-based defenses – is a core feature of impaired personality functioning, theorized to involve heightened negative affectivity and affective instability. Evidence from other psychopathologies suggests that markers of affective disturbances can be automatically extracted from spontaneous speech, yet the linguistic correlates of identity diffusion have rarely been examined – particularly in adolescents, the age group in which personality pathology assessment is most challenging but also most consequential for early intervention.
Transcripts of the Structured Interview of Personality Organization (STIPO) for adolescents were analyzed in a sample of 72 German-speaking participants (50 patients, 22 healthy controls) spanning the full spectrum from consolidated identity to severe identity diffusion. An interpretable lexicon-based sentiment analysis framework combined word frequency measures (LIWC) with continuous word-level valence indices (VADER), capturing both the prevalence and the dynamics of emotional tone.
Greater identity diffusion was associated with higher affective variability (r = .48–.55), a more negative overall affective orientation (strongest effect: r = −.62), more frequent negative affective language, and more extreme negative expression, with weaker evidence for reduced positive language. Measures of positive extremes, affective expressiveness, and verbosity showed no significant associations.
Identity diffusion in adolescents is thus associated with a distinctive affective language profile, detectable from clinical interview transcripts using sentiment analysis. The results are consistent with psychodynamic accounts of splitting and affective dysregulation, and support the potential of automated language analysis as a reproducible, scalable complement to clinical assessment.

articles_hidden.title: NICE’s 2026 Consultation Draft Guideline for OCD and BDD (GID-NG10435): A Critical Appraisal with Secondary Analysis of NICE’s Published Data
articles_hidden.authors: Himanshu Tyagi; Mark Paramlall
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. In September 2026 the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) opened consultation on the first batch of its update to the 2005 guideline for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) (GID-NG10435). The draft replaces stepped care with matched care and reviews first-line treatment.

Methods. We appraised the draft and its supporting documents against six questions informed by selected AGREE II domains, analysing NICE’s published effect estimates, sample sizes, sensitivity analyses and economic results descriptively; every value was checked against its source document. Comparison guidelines were identified by a documented search.

Results. The adult OCD review included 82 randomised controlled trials and the BDD review 13 studies. The committee cited small samples and wide credible intervals when it did not recommend metacognitive therapy (52 participants) or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR; 59 participants). Self-administered cognitive behavioural therapy with therapist support, the second adult option, rests on 61 participants, with a wider credible interval than EMDR’s, and was recommended on other documented grounds. The top-ranked adult option had a probability of 0.17 of being the most cost-effective. The first-listed BDD option ranked fifth of nine in the network meta-analysis. The draft gives no drug-specific dose targets, no consolidated definition of an adequate trial and no primary severity measure for allocation or response. Treatment after non-response to an adequate trial is outside the scope of Batch 1; on the assumptions in NHS England’s 2013 specification, a cascade beginning with 48 million adults in England and Wales yields approximately 48,000 people not responding to a serotonin reuptake inhibitor followed by local graduated exposure. All six selected multimodal OCD comparison guidelines address augmentation; none provides a treatment pathway for BDD.

Conclusions. The draft rests on a substantial evidence synthesis. The published rationale does not fully explain why small samples and imprecision precluded recommendations for some treatments but not others; several operational parameters are not specified; and further-line treatment is outside the first batch.

articles_hidden.title: How and why to read (and write and publish) academic research
articles_hidden.authors: Patrick E. Savage
articles_hidden.abstract: This article is designed to concisely teach undergraduate and new graduate students lessons in reading and writing I have learned in my past two decades as a university student, teacher, and researcher (including through publishing, retracting, correcting, and republishing articles in outlets with varying levels of “impact” and publication fees). Don’t just start at the beginning of an academic article/book and try to read straight to the end! Instead, I recommend starting by reading the title(s)/author(s) and abstract(s), then the figures, reading the Discussion section, and skimming/spot-checking the references, peer reviews, and data (e.g., spreadsheets, audiovisual stimuli, surveys), if available. Only once you have done this and evaluated whether it seems worth your time do I recommend deciding whether to read every word of some/all sections/chapters (and any accompanying supplementary material) or digging deeper into reanalysing/replicating the data. I recommend writing accordingly so that most of your key information will be conveyed even if your reader only gets through your title, abstract, and figures. I discuss various strategies to improve your own academic reading/writing and the broader culture of academia, from practical (e.g., formatting and tracking references and citations using Zotero and Google Scholar, asking constructive questions rather than self-promoting comments, publishing using Peer Community In Registered Reports, using the “sandwich thesis” model for PhD dissertations) to philosophical (e.g., ethical issues in authorship, citation, AI, publishing, and funding). I explain the intended goals of academic research (to create and distribute valuable new knowledge) and perverse incentives that lead us astray from these goals (e.g., chasing prestige and funding). I conclude by contemplating if and how we should dismantle the current extortionary academic-industrial complex and re-design it to align with its intended goals.

articles_hidden.title: Item-dropping to improve in-sample Cronbach's alpha can harm true reliability: A Monte Carlo simulation
articles_hidden.authors: Ze Freeman; Ian Hussey
articles_hidden.abstract: Cronbach’s alpha is the most commonly reported metric of reliability in psychological measurement, and statistical software encourages a common post hoc revision: dropping the item whose removal most improves in-sample alpha. A Monte Carlo simulation examined what this practice does to true reliability, varying items per scale (5 to 40) and sample size (20 to 1,000), with item pools generated from a loading distribution fitted to 3,783 factor loadings from real psychological scales. Two strategies, always dropping the nominated item or dropping only when in-sample alpha improves, were evaluated against the population alpha and true reliability of the retained items. The bias in the reported alpha itself was modest, overstating true reliability only in short scales at small samples and understating it elsewhere. The decision was another matter: at the smallest scale and sample size, dropping reduced true reliability in 46.7% of the replications in which the conditional rule acted, despite requiring an apparent improvement, and almost the entire apparent gain was selection optimism. Stricter decision rules helped only in large samples: with N of 200 or more, acting only on apparent gains above .02 kept the probability of harming the scale at or below 7%, whereas at N = 20 no threshold examined made the decision safe. Because this risk depends on scale length and sample size, given loadings typical of trait scales, it is knowable before data are collected, whereas nothing inside the alpha-if-item-removed table distinguishes a genuinely weak item from a sampling artefact.

articles_hidden.title: Dissociable neural oscillations track subjective value under risk and ambiguity
articles_hidden.authors: Shuting Mei; Leyou Deng; Gökhan Aydogan; Christian Carl Ruff; Ya Zheng
articles_hidden.abstract: How the brain values uncertain prospects and translates them into choices is a central question in decision neuroscience. Current accounts propose that decisions under risk and ambiguity share a valuation process that integrates outcome with probability information, with ambiguity additionally requiring evaluation of the uncertainty about the probabilities themselves. Here we used computational modeling to estimate trial-wise subjective value and tested whether it was tracked by shared or distinct neural dynamics under risk and ambiguity. Participants accepted or rejected risky and ambiguous monetary gambles while we recorded neural activity using electroencephalography (Experiment 1) and magnetoencephalography (Experiment 2). Across both experiments, alpha-band (9–14 Hz) activity localized to the precuneus and superior parietal cortex tracked subjective value under both risk and ambiguity. By contrast, delta-band (1–3 Hz) activity localized to the ventromedial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortices tracked subjective value only under ambiguity. These findings reveal dissociable neural signatures for the two forms of uncertainty and suggest that the brain resolves ambiguity by combining a shared valuation process indexed by alpha activity with an additional process indexed by delta activity that may reflect the motivational salience of options with ambiguous outcome probabilities.

articles_hidden.title: Consistency: A Critical but Often Overlooked Requirement for Causal Inference in Psychological Research
articles_hidden.authors: Lukas Junker; Michael P. Grosz
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychologists are often interested in specific causal quantities (“What is the effect of reducing social-media scrolling by 20 minutes on well-being?”) but tend to focus on vague questions (“Does ‘time spent on social media’ predict well-being?”). There is a mismatch between the causal effects researchers care about and the associations and correlations they compute. In this article, we highlight consistency as a foundational requirement for causal inference that can bridge this mismatch and make statistical estimates causally interpretable. Consistency shows how causal quantities are interpretable only when (a) the causal quantity of interest—the causal estimand—is described precisely enough that it does not bundle different versions of the treatment (e.g., passive scrolling, reading distressing news, or chatting with friends on social media) that have different effects, and (b) the way that the treatment variable changes in the data matches this causal estimand of interest. We clarify these requirements and illustrate how to state and assess them in settings common in psychological research, with a focus on indirect experimental manipulations and multidimensional constructs. Making this step explicit helps researchers articulate their estimands more transparently and is a prerequisite for other concerns such as confounding and model specification.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable mediated effect of police work stress on life satisfaction: A comment on Qiu et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles_hidden.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Qiu et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking police work stress to decreased life satisfaction. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported police work stress, perceived social support, sleep disturbance, and life satisfaction are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles_hidden.title: Health care practitioners’ knowledge, attitudes and perceptions of psychedelic treatments for mental disorders: A scoping review
articles_hidden.authors: Jacqueline Samantha Womersley; Gabriela Iacovou; Yumna Kathrada; Marnus Janse van Vuuren; Hannah Lukic; Soraya Seedat
articles_hidden.abstract: Interest in psychedelic treatments for mental health conditions is growing. Health care professionals will be key in the implementation, recommendation, and administration of psychedelic-assisted therapy (PAT) if and when it is approved for clinical use, making their knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions (KAPs) central to successful translation into practice. We conducted a scoping review of health care professionals’ KAPs toward the psychedelic treatment of mental health conditions. Thirty-nine studies, comprising both quantitative and qualitative investigations, were included. The number of studies, and range of health care professionals surveyed, increased over time, though research remained concentrated in North America, Europe, and Australia. Participants mostly performed well on objective knowledge assessments, but this did not necessarily align with subjective knowledge, which indicated lower self-reported confidence in PAT theory and practice. Attitudes toward psychedelics’ therapeutic potential, safety, and legalisation were generally favourable, although concerns included potential misuse, risk of precipitating subsequent psychiatric disorders, and cognitive impairment. Participants generally perceived psychiatrists and specialised facilities as most suitable for PAT administration, and the need for further research was strongly supported. A lack of trained personnel and resources, and cost, side effect, and misuse concerns, were the most frequently endorsed barriers to implementation. Research into health care professionals' KAPs regarding psychedelic treatment is maturing, but important gaps remain: granular insight into KAPs toward specific compound-disorder combinations is lacking, and geographic coverage does not reflect the global burden of mental illness. Addressing these gaps will be important as PAT moves closer to clinical implementation.

articles_hidden.title: Choosing Stimuli Wisely by Using Individual Differences: A Step-by-Step Tutorial for the One-Stimulus-Per-Factor Principle in Vision Science and Optometric Assessment
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Given that data collection time in vision research and clinical assessment is limited, investigators and clinicians must select stimuli that maximize diagnostic information with minimum redundancy. This article proposes that analyzing individual differences—through factor analysis (FA), principal component analysis (PCA), and multidimensional scaling (MDS)—offers a principled approach. The covariance structure of individual variation reveals the minimum number of independent factors underlying a visual function, and therefore the minimum number of stimuli needed for efficient, non-redundant characterization. I term this the One-Stimulus-Per-Factor Principle: one well-chosen stimulus per factor is both necessary and sufficient. A complementary rule governs discovery: at least two to three stimuli per expected factor are needed to establish the factor structure. Converging evidence from luminance and chromatic contrast sensitivity, stereoscopic disparity, motion, hue scaling, face recognition, perceptual organization, and other domains shows that the dimensionality of individual variation is often lower than dense sampling suggests—and sometimes higher than sparse clinical testing captures. The approach also tests construct validity, revealing whether behavioral measures index the mechanisms investigators assume. These findings carry implications for clinical instruments across contrast sensitivity, color vision, stereopsis, and visual field assessment, many of which either oversample a single factor or undersample the full factor space. The same framework clarifies psychiatric applications—including contrast-sensitivity changes in depression, schizophrenia, and ADHD—by separating retinal-neural deficits from optical contributions such as higher-order aberrations and from attentional lapses, and it extends to oculomotor biomarkers. The article develops the Principle as a step-by-step tutorial, with a worked example.

articles_hidden.title: Musical Groove as Stabilization of Coordinated Movement: A Dynamical and Embodied Approach to Musical Rhythm
articles_hidden.authors: Ji Chul Kim
articles_hidden.abstract: Research has shown that the bodily experience of pleasurable urge to move to music, called groove, is the strongest for rhythms with an intermediate level of syncopation. Current theories explain groove in terms of predictive processes in the brain, as an active inference which resolves prediction errors caused by syncopation. Here we present an alternative explanation of groove from a new dynamical and embodied approach to music perception and action. The new theory, called embodied dynamics of music (EDM), describes musical rhythm as a dynamic pattern of coordinated movement distributed in the brain and the body and governed by the principles and constraints of coordination dynamics. Specifically, beat-based rhythm is described as a coordinative structure in which beat-carrying oscillatory movements provide anchor points for coordinating discrete movements corresponding to individual rhythmic events. In this view, syncopation is a potentially destabilizing force in the coordinative structure, and groove is an active engagement that stabilizes the coordinative structure by reinforcing beat-carrying oscillation with body movement. We support this theory with an analysis of coordination dynamics and a minimal dynamical model of groove which stabilizes syncopated coordination with a metronome by amplifying its self-sustained oscillation.

articles_hidden.title: Identity Centrality and Trauma- and Stressor-related Psychopathology: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Kari Ellen James; Blake M McKimmie; Fiona Maccallum
articles_hidden.abstract: Over the past two decades there has been growing interest in how events, roles, or relationships that are central to an individual’s identity relate to trauma- and stressor-related psychopathology. However, the field lacks a systematic review to synthesize current knowledge across various facets of identity centrality and guide future research in meaningful ways. This systematic review and meta-analysis of the relationship between identity centrality and trauma- and stressor-related psychopathology identified 154 studies (96.1% traumatic stress, 9.7% prolonged grief) representing 66,371 individual participants. Three constructs were identified: event centrality (96% of studies), role centrality (1.9% of studies), and relationship centrality (2.6% of studies). Meta-analysis of 124 studies examining event centrality (k = 249) revealed a medium to large positive association between measures of centrality and severity of traumatic stress and prolonged grief symptoms (mean effect size of r = .446). However, heterogeneity was high. Moderators of outcomes included event type and cultural background. Notably, most studies were cross-sectional (86.4%), precluding causal conclusions. However, emerging evidence indicates that identity centrality and symptom severity may follow independent trajectories over time, raising questions about whether centrality represents a cause or consequence of distress, or a distinct process, and about the role of associated appraisals. Further, the literature is dominated by studies from WEIRD countries. The field would benefit from systematic reporting of key study characteristics such as time since index event, and studies designed to examine causal relationships. Further, most attention has been paid to event centrality, yet this is only one form of identity centrality. Constructs such as role centrality and relationship centrality should be further investigated where theoretically indicated.

articles_hidden.title: Where, Not How Far: Gender-Diverse Pronoun Use and the Ideal Singing Voice
articles_hidden.authors: Logan Barrett
articles_hidden.abstract: Many transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) people want their voices to change, but how pronoun use, a public expression of gender that only partly overlaps with identity labels, relates to the voice people want is unknown. In an online survey (N = 2,536), participants placed their current and ideal singing voices on a 5-point masculine–feminine scale. In exploratory analyses, participants who used they/them pronouns, alone or with she or he (n = 130), wanted larger changes than binary-pronoun users (n = 2,272; d = 0.84, 95% CI [0.66, 1.02]). The difference was robust to age and sex assigned at birth and was attenuated but still present after adjustment for gender identity and recruitment cohort. Among TGD participants, however, the two pronoun groups wanted changes of similar size (d = 0.11 [−0.16, 0.37]), so the full-sample contrast largely reflected comparison with cisgender binary-pronoun users. Pronoun use instead distinguished the destination of change: among TGD participants, 48.1% of gender-diverse pronoun users placed their ideal at the gender-neutral midpoint, compared with 18.3% of binary-pronoun users, whose ideals more often lay at a masculine or feminine pole. A moderation pattern in which singing-related gender incongruence strengthened the link between desired change and the acoustics of a chosen model singer did not replicate in a held-out test set and is not supported. Pronoun use appears to index where, more than how far, people want their singing voices to go; vocal goals and the scales that measure them should accommodate gender-neutral targets.

articles_hidden.title: Willpower or Choice? A Within-Country, Cross-Linguistic Comparison of Free Will Judgments
articles_hidden.authors: Alison Oliver; Paulius Rimkevičius; Renato Cesar Cardoso; Marcel Brass; Uri Maoz
articles_hidden.abstract: Does the language we speak influence how we think about free will? Previous work has often compared free will judgments across linguistic and cultural groups without isolating language from broader cultural differences. More recent work has found cross-cultural variation, but these designs could not determine whether language itself contributed to that variation. Here we report two exploratory studies in which language was varied while culture was held relatively constant. In Study 1, monolingual English- and French-speaking Canadians rated comics depicting choice and willpower on whether they represent free will. The English phrase free will makes will, and so willpower, salient; the French phrase libre arbitre makes choice salient (as in “to arbitrate”). If language shapes the concept, English-speakers should associate free will relatively more with willpower, and French-speakers relatively more with choice. They did not: the two groups showed almost exactly the same preference for choice, and equivalence testing rules out anythingbeyond a small difference. Study 2 asked why choice comics were favored. Participants rated thesame comics on choice, willpower, doing what one wants, and absence of constraints. Across thenine comics, free will judgments closely tracked ratings of doing what one wants and of choice, but tracked absence of constraints less closely. Free will might therefore be associated most closely with choice and doing what one wants.

articles_hidden.title: Wrong Note, Wrong Time: Age and Musicianship-Related Influences on Rhythmic and Melodic Timing
articles_hidden.authors: Logan Barrett; Sarah Anne Sauvé; Andrea Rita Halpern; Benjamin Zendel
articles_hidden.abstract: Musical expectancy theory posits that listeners anticipate both the pitch that will occur and when it will occur; however, the interaction between these dimensions across age and expertise is less understood. In this study, 175 adults (ages 18–82; musicians and non-musicians) rated the final note of short monophonic melodies on its melodic and temporal fit. Endings were systematically manipulated in terms of pitch (tonal, chromatic, or atonal) and timing deviations. Results showed a strong effect of melodic expectancy: pitch deviations substantially reduced goodness-of-fit ratings, whereas timing shifts had comparatively weak effects. Musicians gave lower ratings overall, indicating heightened sensitivity to expectancy violations, whereas non-musicians were more lenient. Although age alone did not predict ratings, an age × musician interaction emerged: older musicians diverged most strongly from older non-musician peers, suggesting that expertise sharpens expectancy sensitivity across the lifespan. These findings demonstrate that pitch dominates expectancy judgments, while also revealing how aging and musicianship jointly influence the perception of musical errors—an area that remains underexplored in music cognition.

articles.title: Unequal Parenting across Childhood: How Class Differences in Parental Control of Screen Use Reverse with the Child's Age
articles.authors: Abel Aussant; Andreas Roaldsnes
articles.abstract: Research usually treats class differences in parenting style as constant throughout childhood. We show instead that they can reverse with the child's age. Our case is parental control of children's screen use, for which expert advice is restrictive when children are young and divided when they are adolescents. We draw on an original survey of 20,670 Norwegian households with children aged 3 to 17 to estimate class differences in time limits, control of content and the negotiation of rules at each age. We find that better-resourced parents are stricter than others with young children, but more permissive with adolescents. The composition of the resources available to the household shapes the pattern: income and education have different, complementary associations with parental control. The observed reversal across childhood suggests that the advantage of well-resourced families in child rearing lies less in a fixed repertoire of practices than in adaptability, a capacity to adjust as the appropriate practice changes with the child's age.

articles.title: Are EU Kidding Me? Notes from a Poorly Drafted Social Media Ban
articles.authors: Michael Veale
articles.abstract: In September 2026, the European Commission published a proposed EU KIDS Act, responding to the demand for restrictions and further design obligations applying to digital services accessible to children, including social media. This Article argues that regardless of what one believes about the merits of this policy direction, the EU KIDS Act is not the legislative text we need. The scope and drafting are little short of chaotic, full of holes, enormous ambiguities, and unintended consequences. Recitals contradict articles. The use of scope borrowed from other pieces of legislation not designed for this purpose brings services into scope that should not be subject to the relevant provisions, like book-recommendation websites, music services, or exercise trackers. The infrastructural requirement for assurance of age and parental responsibility attestation simply omits enormous issues of complex families and childhoods. Complex design obligations are written in ways that can be plausibly interpreted as implicitly prohibiting entire swathes of products, such as voice assistants. This Article outlines these issues, and many more. The Commission should withdraw this proposal and reissue a workable and realistic text.

articles.title: Safe (felt) by design: Understanding cyclists’ needs for traffic guidance at roadworks – A mixed-methods study on behaviour, perception, and infrastructure requirements
articles.authors: Frederik Hilden; Peer-Benedikt Degen; Robin von Elm; Angela Francke
articles.abstract: Introduction: Urban construction sites frequently disrupt cycling infrastructure and create safety risks for vulnerable road users. Despite regulatory frameworks for temporary traffic management, cyclists often encounter unclear or unsafe guidance around roadworks. Empirical evidence on how cyclists actually respond to such conditions remains limited. This study investigates cyclists’ behaviour, routing decisions, and safety perceptions at urban construction sites. Method: A mixed-methods design combined behavioural observations and a nationwide survey. Observational data were collected at four construction sites in Hamburg, Germany using inductive loop sensors and video recordings, capturing 146.168 bicycle passages. Behavioural interactions were coded to identify compliance, routing choices, and conflict-avoidance strategies. In addition, a web-based survey of 1,071 cyclists across Germany examined perceived safety, behavioural adaptation, and infrastructure preferences at roadworks. Results: Observational analysis identified substantial deviations from designated traffic guidance: 42% of 790 coded cyclist interactions involved non-compliant behaviour, such as riding on sidewalks or against the intended direction. Route choice was primarily influenced by motorized traffic volume and pavement quality. Cyclists frequently selected routes that maximized perceived safety and riding comfort rather than following formal guidance. Despite frequent non-compliance, cyclists often adopted cooperative strategies, including speed reduction and conflict avoidance with pedestrians. Conclusions: The findings highlight a gap between formally regulated traffic guidance and cyclists’ safety perceptions and behaviour. Temporary infrastructure that lacks clarity, comfort, or protection can lead to widespread deviations from prescribed routes. Practical applications: Temporary traffic management at construction sites should prioritize intuitive guidance, surface quality, and physical separation from motorized traffic. Incorporating cyclist needs into roadwork design can reduce conflicts and improve safety for vulnerable road users.

articles.title: Where Silicon Samples Go Wrong: Item-Level Coefficient Distortion in LLM-Simulated Chinese Public Opinion
articles.authors: Mingkun Cui; Shenghao Xiong
articles.abstract: Do regressions fitted to survey responses simulated by large language models return the coefficients human data would? We used four 2026 models to generate responses to the full attitude-item bank of two Chinese General Social Survey waves, conditioning on 1,000 respondents’ demographic profiles per wave and requesting each person’s most likely answer. For 10 items analyzed in both waves, we compared human and simulated coefficients on the human-anchored scale, with Holm adjustment across 240 tests. The 28 supported differences concentrate in three patterns: an inflated income gradient in perceived fairness, an urban–rural gradient in premarital-sex morality where the human coefficient is near zero, and an overstated sex difference in gender-ability beliefs. Marginal fit does not locate these distortions. Standardizing each source by its own standard deviation changes 33 test decisions, showing why regression validation requires a declared outcome scale.

articles.title: Passive Behavioral Tracing: A Non-Interventional Fairness Protocol for Cooperative AI
articles.authors: kazutaka hayashi
articles.abstract: Emerging AI governance regimes, including the EU AI Act's post-market monitoring obligation and the NIST AI RMF's measure function, require ongoing fairness monitoring but leave open which statistics should satisfy it. Interventional audits (A/B tests, counterfactual procedures, adversarial probing) manipulate the system, and often the people, under audit, and are episodic where monitoring is continuous. This article argues that a useful part of that monitoring can be done passively, and proposes Passive Behavioral Tracing (PBT), a protocol that audits fairness in AI-mediated cooperative systems using only behavioral traces the system already records. PBT formalizes four constructs computable from ordinary logs (consistency of treatment, parity across naturally occurring groups, proportionality to contribution, and drift over time) and combines them into two indicators, PBT-Ethics and PBT-Coop. A Monte Carlo study with released code shows that the constructs form two families: reciprocity and parity register unfair treatment whether it has always existed or began recently, while consistency and drift respond to change, and only drift locates when the change happened. This distinction carries regulatory weight: unfairness present since deployment implicates a system's design, while unfairness with an onset points to a dateable change, and the two call for remedies that a single score cannot separate. The study also shows the protocol's limits: mild, sustained unfairness against a small group is often missed. All results come from a stylized synthetic model; PBT is a specification validated in principle and complementary to interventional audits, not a finding about any operating system.

articles.title: Urban Human-Canine Conflict Mitigation: A 2023 Pilot Study on Stray Dog Population Management in Chembur, Mumbai
articles.authors: Ojus Wankhede
articles.abstract: This study investigates the urban stray dog population in Mumbai, Maharashtra, and proposes actionable policy recommendations to mitigate human-canine conflicts. A mixed-methods retrospective pilot study was utilised, incorporating a March 2023 community survey (n=91) in the Chembur area, alongside site visits to local Non-Governmental Organisations and semi-structured interviews with Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) officials. The survey revealed that 61.53% of respondents supported the relocation of stray dogs, whereas only 21.97% supported neutering. The findings indicate a pressing need for enhanced infrastructural capacity within the Animal Birth Control (ABC) programme. Core policy recommendations include the systematic expansion of sterilisation drives, the integration of private veterinary practitioners into mass vaccination campaigns, and the strict enforcement of the Animal Birth Control Rules, 2023.

articles.title: The Grumpy Meme and Irritability Ecology: How Low-Intensity Negative Affect Spreads, Survives, Sediments, and Becomes a Workplace Climate
articles.authors: Koichi Hiraoka
articles.abstract:
Research on negative affect in organizations has largely focused on relatively visible phenomena such as anger, aggression, abusive supervision, workplace bullying, and incivility. Yet much of everyday organizational life unfolds between overt anger episodes, when no one is shouting but employees still monitor facial expressions, short replies, sighs, silence, or reduced responsiveness and conclude that someone appears grumpy. Such low-intensity signals may alter whether people approach, speak, seek advice, or share information. To theorize this domain, this paper distinguishes Irritability, Grumpiness, and the Grumpy Meme, and introduces Irritability Ecology as an integrative framework.
Irritability refers to a relatively low-intensity internal affective state that need not be externally expressed. Grumpiness refers to socially perceivable expressions through which others infer that a person appears to be in a bad mood. The Grumpy Meme refers to a socio-affective transmission process in which perceived grumpiness alters another person’s affect or behavior and is subsequently re-expressed in another interaction. Thus, irritability may exist without observable grumpiness, while perceived grumpiness does not necessarily demonstrate underlying irritability.
The paper argues that low-intensity negative affect may survive in workplaces because it is inexpensive to express, highly repeatable, difficult to sanction, and often protected by ambiguity regarding both the event and the actor’s intention. Repeated expressions may accumulate through Affective Sedimentation, creating background vigilance, mood-reading, and eventually a workplace climate. A two-axis model of anger and irritability is proposed, yielding four affective climate types: Calm–Stable, Quiet Tension, Eruption–Recovery, and Pervasive Anger–Irritability. The paper further introduces Affective Non-Transmission as the capacity to experience negative affect without automatically transferring it to others, and connects this capacity to post-conflict relational repair.
Irritability Ecology is therefore not a weaker version of Anger Ecology. Whereas Anger Ecology examines the visible fire of workplace affect, Irritability Ecology examines the ambient climate that persists between fires. The framework shifts attention from identifying “grumpy people” to examining how low-intensity negative affect is expressed, transmitted, sustained, sedimented, interrupted, and repaired within organizational environments.

articles.title: The sociolinguistic labor of incarcerated people
articles.authors: Gabriella Licata; Robert Tyler; Mesro Coles; Anthony Habib Watkins; Brian Asey Gonsoulin
articles.abstract: Through participatory action research, we draw on interviews with 40 incarcerated students to examine how linguistic practices are shaped by institutional power in carceral environments. We argue that the magnitude of surveillance under incarceration produces sociolinguistic labor: the effortful management of one’s communicative repertoire. Our analysis identifies a distinctive form of dual-direction sociolinguistic labor, whereby incarcerated individuals are required to extend their repertoires both toward stigmatized vernaculars to gain social capital and toward hyperstandardized registers for institutional capital. We examine this dynamic across educational, social, and procedural domains, with particular attention to boardspeak—an emotionally-constrained, bureaucratic register through which rehabilitation is performed and assessed at a Board of Parole hearing. By situating these practices within broader critical linguistic theories and perspectives, we show incarcerated people self-surveil and create, prompting varying levels of sociolinguistic labor and innovation that are mediated by race, ethnicity, ability, socioeconomic class, and in-group membership. These findings demonstrate how high-stakes, surveilled environments intensify the stakes of language use and reshape the boundaries of communicative agency.

articles.title: The Intersection of Fascia, Fascism, and Language: Reframing Neurodivergence as an Adaptive Response to Environmental Stress
articles.authors: Isha Sarah Snow
articles.abstract: This theoretical paper argues that global autism prevalence data are better read as a map of social ecology than as a map of biology. Diagnostic prevalence reflects the interaction of neurodevelopmental variation, distress, recognition and diagnostic access, and I argue that identified rates rise where relational buffering weakens, institutional demands intensify, and diagnostic systems are primed to read difference as dysfunction. The argument integrates three domains that are rarely analyzed together. First, fascia is treated as a body-wide communication network that densifies under chronic stress, and I propose, as a hypothesis, that the cell danger response (Naviaux, 2014, 2025) may link sustained social threat to physiological rigidity. Second, language is treated as regulatory infrastructure: drawing on Jackson et al. (2019) and Fricker’s (2007) concept of hermeneutical injustice, a dominant diagnostic language shapes how bodily states are interpreted, governed, and pathologized. Third, fascism, which shares its etymological root with fascia in the Roman fasces, is used as a conceptual analogy for systems in which control replaces communication and feedback is suppressed. Apparent anomalies in prevalence across India, Spain, Japan, Australia, and the Nordic countries are examined, and a testable prediction is stated for each. The paper distinguishes established findings from its own hypotheses throughout. The paper concludes that the aim is less distress, not less autism, which shifts intervention upstream toward environments that restore co-regulation and tolerate difference.

articles.title: The ALPS Index: A Global Estimate of the Average Number of Languages a Person Speaks
articles.authors: Areg Hovhannisyan
articles.abstract:
How many languages does the average person speak? The question has an established qualitative answer, that "probably more than half of the world's population is bilingual" (Grosjean, 2012), but no quantitative one at global scale.

We audited individual language repertoire in 237 jurisdictions with 8.16 billion residents. Survey, census and reference sources were mapped onto a common conversational threshold (CEFR level A2) and a common individuation standard (ISO 639-3), graded on a seven-band evidentiary scale, and treated for twelve documented biases of census and survey instruments. The resulting index, ALPS (Average Language a Person Speaks), is the population mean of individual repertoire size.

The global population-weighted value is 1.568 languages per person. Its grade band, 1.42 to 1.70, reflects the evidentiary grade of the sources, not sampling error. The alternative specifications we could compute place the figure between 1.53 and 1.60; an adjustment for the ages of survey respondents lowers it by at least 0.041; the value documented by official and survey instruments alone is 1.48. As a mean, the figure limits the share of people who speak two or more languages to no more than 57% (42%–70% across the band).

The unweighted mean across jurisdictions (1.87) is well above the weighted mean: individual multilingualism is concentrated in smaller populations. Group-level linguistic diversity and individual repertoire are only moderately associated (r = 0.43). A direct arithmetic test locates incomplete domestic bridging: in ten jurisdictions holding 38.9% of the audited population, mean repertoire is below the level that complete bridging through the largest first language would require; in three of them (India, Ethiopia and Côte d'Ivoire, 19.8%) the shortfall exceeds the jurisdiction's band.

The audit synthesises existing sources and involves no new fieldwork. Its central limitation is that source quality is distributed inversely to linguistic diversity. For each specification choice whose effect can be computed, we report the value the alternative would produce; the choices whose effect cannot be computed are named.

articles.title: Unmade Ground: Displacement, Dispossession, and the Erosion of Spatial Memory Among Kurdish Forced Migrants
articles.authors: Ramazan BOZTEPE
articles.abstract: Forced displacement does not merely relocate people; it dismantles the material infrastructure through which place becomes memory. Drawing on 80 semi-structured interviews with Kurdish participants in their region of origin (n=25), Central Anatolia (n=25) and Western Europe (n=30), this article examines how the destruction, abandonment and transformation of inhabited space unmakes collective and intergenerational memory. Using Cernea's (1997) Impoverishment Risks and Reconstruction model alongside Malkki's (1992) critique of sedentarist assumptions about place, the analysis identifies four interlinked processes: urban redevelopment, rural demographic hollowing, diaspora gentrification, and the institutional foreclosure of access to common and sacred land. Participants describe memory as materially anchored, carried in streets, soil and threshold spaces, so that narrative transmission alone cannot repair its loss. The article argues that spatial memory loss is a distinct impoverishment risk inadequately addressed by existing frameworks, extends Cernea's model by specifying the memorial stakes of lost access to common property, and proposes the concept of inherited spatial memory: attachment to places the second generation has never physically inhabited.

articles.title: The geopolitics of academic publishing: the case of Kazakhstan
articles.authors: Eva Hartmann; Aikerim Bektemirova
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Publications in Scopus- and Web of Science-indexed journals have become the global benchmark of academic excellence. This article examines how Kazakhstan has placed this new ‘gold standard’ at the centre of its academic publishing policy, which has become a key part of its university reform agenda since 2010. Using a Gramscian lens on power and knowledge, we show how the government employs this policy to position itself between the West and Russia in a shifting geopolitical context. The adoption of this benchmark not only changes how Kazakhstan's academic community relates to the broader academic world. It also significantly reshapes the hierarchy within Kazakhstan’s academic community. We argue that this has profound implications for the societal role of universities and academic research and their ability to address local challenges. Our study makes both empirical and theoretical contributions to the growing literature on the geopolitics of knowledge, highlighting the interplay among local, national, and global dynamics.

articles.title: Who Manufactured Pseudo-History Theories? The Emergent Collective Creation of Historical Narratives on the Chinese Internet
articles.authors: ZY Liu; Di Yuan
articles.abstract: This paper examines the formation, expansion, and functions of pseudo-history theories (伪史论) on the Chinese internet from the perspective of cultural economics, and proposes the analytical concept of “Emergent Collective Creation.” This concept refers to the process whereby a large number of relatively independent content producers, acting on the basis of their respective local motivations and in the absence of any unified overall plan, generate a collective narrative system that exceeds the original planning and control of any single participant through imitation, competition, the recombination of arguments, and the migration of topics. The paper first investigates relevant figures who possess formal academic credentials or publishing experience and analyzes the pathways through which early pseudo-history resources entered public circulation. It then takes as examples the extension of pseudo-history theories from ancient Greece and Rome to other civilizations, historical figures, and issues concerning Chinese dynastic history, exploring how competition for traffic, content imitation, and the selective recombination of historical materials drive narrative expansion. Finally, using online controversies surrounding the film The Penghu Naval Battle as a case study, it analyzes how pseudo-history theories have been deployed by different participants in conflicts over historical identity and in online opinion confrontation, and discusses possible links between controversial historical discourses and public trust in academic authority. The paper argues that even dispersed individual actions lacking unified coordination may, through indirect interaction, produce collective narrative outcomes and enable pseudo-history theories to move from a form of content competition for traffic into ideological contention. Because this study relies primarily on publicly available online materials, publications, and media reports, and lacks internal platform data as well as continuous records at the creator level, the mechanisms identified remain exploratory explanations whose chains of transmission, causal relations, and actual effects await further verification.

articles.title: Agreement under abstention: an agreement–abstention–conflict triple and sharp bounds for Fleiss' kappa
articles.authors: Maikel Yelandi Leyva Vázquez; Alexis Matheu Pérez; Bastián Gutiérrez Vargas
articles.abstract: Raters in agreement studies are often allowed to abstain, for example by answering "can't tell" or "unsure". Abstentions are usually deleted or recoded, and each treatment carries an untested assumption about why raters abstained. We show how to report Fleiss' kappa without such an assumption. Assigning the abstentions to categories changes both the observed agreement and the category totals that determine chance agreement, so the extremes of kappa require optimising the two jointly. A dynamic programme gives the exact extremes over all such completions for two or three categories, with completions that attain and thereby certify them; closed-form bounds enclose them for more categories. A budget interval and tipping points grade conclusions by how far the missing ratings must depart from a reference predictive model. The shares of agreeing, abstaining and conflicting rater pairs, (pA, pU, pC), serve as an intuitive summary. Under independent sampling of units the sample extremes converge to the population identified set, and an exploratory unit bootstrap supports a three-outcome decision: adequate, inadequate or undetermined. In simulations at 2–10% abstention, estimator errors depended on the mechanism; the budget interval contained the complete-data kappa in 97–100% of replicates under random abstention but 44–51% under value-dependent abstention, and population decisions were undetermined in 43–76% of replicates. In crowdsourced weather-sentiment labels, listwise deletion declared agreement adequate where the three-outcome decision was undetermined; in safety ratings of chatbot conversations, listwise estimates fell on both sides of the interval.

articles.title: Are Women Comedians Less Funny?: Empirical Analysis of Gender Differences in 1-on-1 Competitive Comedy
articles.authors: Yuhei Yamaguchi
articles.abstract:
"Is there a difference in funniness between men and women?'" This study addresses this question. The perception that "women are less funny than men" is widespread, and some studies have indeed shown that men have a better sense of humor. In addition, in industries dominated by men, the presence of women tends to be relatively low. In the comedy industry, where men make up the overwhelming majority, women comedians are thus exposed to a double stereotype of this kind. We examined whether, under such a double stereotype, women comedians are able to be as funny as men comedians. We collected and analyzed data on a total of 3,925 matchups from a television program in which comedians compete directly over funniness in one-on-one contests. The results showed that, although a simple statistical model makes men comedians appear funnier, an analysis using a model that accounts for individual funniness revealed no significant difference in funniness between men and women.
Although concerns remain about the generalizability of the findings, the results call into question existing research on gender differences in sense of humor, as well as the associated stereotypes.

articles.title: A Sociolinguistic Inquiry into Vietnamese Swearing: Regional Variation and Cross-Cultural Parallels
articles.authors: Hàng Hỷ Vinh
articles.abstract: This exploratory, pilot-scale study investigates the Vietnamese swearing construction built from an obscene verb, a kinship term and a second-person pronoun (địt mẹ mày, đụ má mày 'fuck your mother', mả cha mi 'your father's grave') through two questions: how kin-directed swearing differs across regions and which part of the construction reveals the speaker's region (RQ1); and why Vietnamese swearing targets kin and women, viewed against the full repertoire of swearing themes in Vietnamese and neighbouring languages (RQ2). It combines eight Vietnamese dictionaries (1651–2021) and comparative dictionaries of Mường, Cham, Teochew and Cantonese with an online convenience-sample survey of 50 young speakers across four regions, a small Quốc ngữ prose corpus, and a thematic comparison with ten other language communities. For RQ1, the dictionaries show no regional boundary in the verb before 1931, whereas the survey finds a clear North/South split in both the verb and the word for "mother"; regional information is asymmetric, with Southern and Central forms acting as strong markers while standard-compatible forms (địt, mẹ) and online abbreviations (đm, vkl) spread across all regions. For RQ2, sex and kin dominate the free lists; the mother-directed sexual formula occurs in Vietnamese, Chinese, Thai, Hindi and English but is absent from Japanese, so it cannot be attributed to Confucian heritage alone. Kin-directed swearing is rated more offensive than self-directed swearing and triggers more active responses; swears that deny the hearer's descent (đồ con hoang, cả họ nhà mày) are the heaviest and the least mitigated among friends. Young respondents name affection for kin, not family face, as the main reason; we read this as a contemporary synchronic reinterpretation of templates whose diachronic origin lies in honour-based lineage norms. Taken together, the target of kin-directed swearing is the hearer's legitimate standing within the lineage. Results describe young, internet-using speakers and should be read as hypothesis-generating.

articles.title: Impact of Social Media Platforms on Youth: An Anthropological Study
articles.authors: Sivakumar A
articles.abstract:
Social media has become a ubiquitous sociocultural phenomenon, transforming how young people communicate, socialize, and construct identities. This anthropological study examines social media use among young people aged 18–25 in urban and semi-urban areas of Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, South India. It explores usage patterns, self-identity expression, maintenance of social relationships, digital literacy, and the influence of gender, education, and socioeconomic background on digital participation. It also considers how young people perceive social media’s everyday effects on their social and cultural lives.

A mixed-methods design was adopted. Quantitative data were collected through a questionnaire administered to 60 youth respondents, while semi-structured interviews were conducted with 10 participants. The questionnaire demonstrated high overall reliability (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.91), and its individual scales showed acceptable to high reliability. Content validity was reviewed by experts, while exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses were used to assess construct validity. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests of independence; qualitative data were analyzed thematically using NVivo.

Findings indicate that social media is embedded in young people’s everyday lives: 73.3% reported using platforms more than once daily. WhatsApp (93.3%), Instagram (88.3%), and YouTube (81.7%) were the most widely used platforms. Entertainment (90.0%) and maintaining contact with friends (85.0%) were the leading purposes, followed by information seeking (63.3%) and identity expression (35.0%). Digital literacy levels were low for 23.3% of respondents, medium for 48.3%, and high for 28.3%. Differences were particularly evident in advanced skills, including evaluating information and managing privacy.

Hypothesis testing found significant associations between digital literacy and frequency of use (p = 0.048; Cramér’s V = 0.324), digital literacy and platform diversity (p = 0.047; Cramér’s V = 0.283), gender and identity expression (p = 0.037; Cramér’s V = 0.331), and gender and platform choice (p = 0.041; Cramér’s V = 0.326). Other hypothesized relationships were not statistically significant. The qualitative analysis identified five themes: curated identity performance, digital kinship and connectivity, stratified digital competencies, gendered digital surveillance, and ambivalent impression perceptions.

The study contributes to digital anthropology by illustrating how global platforms are locally adopted in South Indian contexts, how social relationships are sustained in digital spaces, and how digital literacy may function as cultural capital. It offers recommendations for educators, parents, policymakers, platform designers, and young people to promote more equitable and beneficial digital participation.

articles.title: Remembering without institutions: legal-political memory, oral transmission, and diaspora identity among Kurds in Turkey and Europe
articles.authors: Ramazan BOZTEPE
articles.abstract: Drawing on 80 interviews across three sub-samples — the Kurdish-majority region of Turkey (n=25), Central Anatolia (n=25), and the European diaspora (n=30) — this article examines how legal-political memory of forced displacement is transmitted across generations. Using an inductively developed 11-category thematic coding framework, we find a sharp geographic gradient in informal oral transmission (64% Region, 40% Central Anatolia, 16.7% diaspora), with an inverse rise in institutional/archival memory in the diaspora (50%, versus 16–20% in Turkey; suggestive rather than conclusive once corrected for multiple comparisons). Spatial displacement is narrated concretely in the region of origin but gives way, in the diaspora, to an abstract negotiation of layered belonging. We suggest that memory transmission without institutional archives relies on embodied domestic channels vulnerable to migration's ruptures — a vulnerability diaspora communities compensate for through new institutional infrastructures rather than reconstruction. The article offers a comparative, exploratory account of how a stateless-nation diaspora reconstructs continuity across ruptured contexts.

articles.title: Visual Resistance Assemblages: Recurring Multimodal Configurations in Kenya’s Gen Z Finance Bill Protests
articles.authors: Castro Chebukosi
articles.abstract: Social-media protest communication is increasingly multimodal, combining language, imagery, typography, sound, performance and platform-specific features. While existing research has demonstrated how such resources produce meaning within individual artefacts and genres, comparatively less attention has been given to how functionally related multimodal configurations recur across heterogeneous artefacts within the same protest corpus. This study addresses this corpus-level problem through a qualitative multimodal analysis of 72 protest artefacts published or circulated on X during Kenya’s June–July 2024 Finance Bill protests, analysed through multimodal social semiotics and cross-artefact comparison. The analysis identifies five recurring configurations: Constitutional Legitimation, Distributed Agency, Comparative Fiscal Information Design, Visual Witnessing and Collective Identity, and Satirical Recontextualization. These configurations are not treated as mutually exclusive artefact categories; rather, they represent recurring relationships among heterogeneous semiotic resources that retain comparable communicative functions despite variation in genre and surface realisation. The study proposes the concept of Visual Resistance Assemblages (VRA) as a descriptive analytical unit for identifying such corpus-level recurrence. The findings demonstrate how constitutional discourse, distributed participation, comparative fiscal reasoning, collective representation and satirical recontextualisation were organised through heterogeneous multimodal resources. VRA complements existing multimodal, assemblage-oriented and digital activism approaches by shifting attention from multimodality within individual artefacts to recurring multimodal organisation across protest corpora.

articles.title: The Emotional Meaning and Sociocultural Implications of 'Eojunggan-hada' in Korean Society: An Exploratory Study
articles.authors: Heeju Lee
articles.abstract: This study explores how the Korean expression 'eojunggan-hada' (being in-between) extends beyond simple linguistic ambiguity to reflect issues of personal identity and social belonging. Unlike previous Korean linguistics research that focused on linguistic ambiguity and mitigation expressions, this study defines 'eojunggan-hada' as a way of being positioned at the boundaries of identity and belonging, analyzing its sociocultural implications. A survey of 111 respondents revealed that participants frequently experience being in-between in daily life (mean 3.44), perceiving it more as a product of social structural conditions (mean 3.46) rather than personal character traits (mean 3.22). Notably, daily experience of in-betweenness showed a strong positive correlation with attributing it to one's personality (r = .64, p < .001), suggesting that the more frequently people feel in-between, the more they blame their own character for it. Qualitative analysis of open-ended responses confirmed that being in-between functions simultaneously as discomfort and survival strategy. This study conceptualizes 'eojunggan-hada' as a boundary emotion formed within Korea's unique collectivist culture and relational pressures, proposing that it represents not individual indecisiveness but rather a way of existence created by social structures.

articles.title: Manufactured Desire： How Social Media and Influencer Agencies Sexualise and Monetise Pregnant Influencers
articles.authors: Yuting Qin
articles.abstract: This article examines how pregnant influencers on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, are sexualised and monetised through the interlocking practices of the platform, influencer agencies and influencers themselves. Taking the 2024 controversy around the appearance influencer YīLìXiǎoShāZi and the # 孕妇摇 (Pregnancy Swing Dance) challenge as its point of departure, the study combines visual analysis of top-ranked Douyin posts, in-depth interviews with an influencer, an influencer agency employee and a platform employee, and sentiment analysis of 4,874 user comments. This article interprets platform monetisation structures and influencer agency production routines as organising influencers’ embodied labour into standardised production roles and measurable commercial attributes. It proposes the “factory of desire” as a framework for understanding how platforms, influencer agencies and influencers mutually enable and constrain the commodification of pregnant bodies. Interviewees described unwritten rules through which sexualised content can remain visible under mainland China's restrictions on pornography: perceived emphasis on skin exposure in automated moderation, a grey zone known as 擦边 (cābiān, "skirting the boundary"), and appeals framed around "pregnancy beauty". The analysis suggests that these commercial and regulatory conditions can encourage pregnant influencers to reproduce porn chic conventions, while constraining their subsequent commercial options. Within the sampled comments on videos criticising the sexualisation of pregnancy, disgust had the highest average model score; these findings describe this selected discussion rather than public opinion as a whole.

articles.title: Decolonising Water Diplomacy: Concepts, Debates, and Practice
articles.authors: Mohsen Nagheeby
articles.abstract: Water diplomacy is commonly presented as a practical response to tensions over shared waters. It brings together negotiation, technical expertise, international water law, basin institutions, and practices of cooperation and peacebuilding. Yet the terms through which water diplomacy is often organised — security, cooperation, neutrality, development, expertise, and peace — are not politically innocent. They are shaped by histories of empire, unequal treaties, colonial borders, geopolitical asymmetries, donor agendas, and knowledge hierarchies. This article introduces decolonising water diplomacy as an emerging orientation that does not reject diplomacy, law, science, or cooperation, but asks how their assumptions, procedures, and outcomes are historically produced. It defines water diplomacy, situates it in relation to water security, water peace, critical hydropolitics, water justice, and decolonial thought, and explains what a decolonial perspective adds in practice. The article argues that decolonising water diplomacy does not simply add justice to existing approaches; it asks how peace, security, and cooperation are defined, whose histories and knowledges they privilege, and how they might be reworked toward historical responsibility, epistemic justice, recognition, dignity, and more accountable forms of peace.

articles.title: Generalised Conversational Implicature in Kenyan Generation Z Digital Protest Discourse: Q-, I-, and M-Heuristics in the 2024 Finance Bill Protests on X
articles.authors: Castro Chebukosi; Bernard Kodak; Jane Ombati
articles.abstract: The June–July 2024 Finance Bill protests in Kenya produced a distinctive corpus of digitally mediated political communication in which Gen Z-associated protesters on X (formerly Twitter) relied on omission, shared background knowledge and stylistic markedness to construct political meaning beyond the literal content of their posts. This study examines how such strategies generated Generalised Conversational Implicature (GCI), applying Levinson’s (2000) Q-, I-, and M-heuristic framework to a purposively sampled corpus of 72 protest artefacts retrieved from X in June 2026. Using thematic and pragmatic coding, the analysis shows that condensed slogans, mobilisation language and constitutional citation generated Q-heuristic implicatures through informational economy; shared political, cultural and generational knowledge generated I-heuristic implicatures; and marked linguistic, visual and performative choices generated M-heuristic implicatures, extending Levinson’s lexical account of markedness into a multimodal register. The three heuristics frequently layered within single artefacts, and thematic coding further revealed six protest-specific inferential patterns beyond Levinson’s original typology: anti-co-optation, constitutional-sovereignty, trauma-memory, care-based, data-activism and digital-network patterns. The study demonstrates how GCI analysis can be extended to fast-paced, multimodal, digitally networked political communication when its categories are made explicit and their limits are clearly bounded.

articles.title: Modeling Cooperation as Information Flow: Ripple Structures and Behavioral Digital Twins
articles.authors: kazutaka hayashi
articles.abstract:
Recent advances in articial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models, have
signicantly improved performance in language understanding, vision, and reasoning. How-
ever, a fundamental limitation remains: current AI systems still lack an explicit under-
standing of the logical structure by which humans make decisions within specic situations
and relationships. This limitation is not merely a shortage of intelligence, but a missing
layer of context-dependent decision logic. This study proposes a theoretical framework and
methodological protocol that redenes human cooperation as an observable information ow
rather than a psychological or moral phenomenon. We model cooperative propagation as
Ripple structures, which are directional causal chains of actions in which A helps B and B in
turn helps C, and we introduce the concept of a Behavioral Digital Twin, dened as a map-
ping of decision logic derived from situation, relationships, and action history. We further
present a non-interventional observational protocol for capturing naturally occurring coop-
erative behaviors through naturalistic observation environments, and outline a validation
framework for future empirical work. All behavioral events remain voluntary; the proto-
col introduces observation infrastructure without prescribing or incentivizing actions. All
gures and examples in this manuscript are conceptual illustrations intended to clarify the-
oretical constructs. This work aims to provide a foundational layer connecting AI research,
social systems research, and Web3 governance.

articles.title: Flourishing and Health in Kenya. Philosophical Perspectives and Empirical Insights.
articles.authors: Maike Ritzer; Steffen Flessa
articles.abstract: Numerous studies have demonstrated positive associations between broader dimensions of wellbeing and health. However, evidence from Kenya on this association is scarce and mostly focused on broad evaluative measures of wellbeing, such as life satisfaction. This study draws on conceptualizations of wellbeing from Sub-Saharan African philosophical literature as motivation for examining various specific dimensions of wellbeing in the Global Flourishing Study and analyzing their association with subsequent health in Kenya as a case study, using a longitudinal panel design. Data were drawn from waves 1 (2023; n=11389 individuals) and 2 (2024; n= 7698 individuals) of the Global Flourishing Study. The data are representative of the general population in Kenya. Linear regression models with a lagged dependent variable are used to test the association of wave 1 wellbeing indicators with subsequent physical and mental health at wave 2. The findings indicate that several dimensions of wellbeing - including livelihood security, satisfaction with personal relationships, meaning and purpose, agency and freedom to pursue what is most important in life - are positively associated with subsequent self-rated physical and mental health in Kenya.

articles.title: Watchdog Capture and the Social Licensing of Child Harm: A Case Study of Common Sense Media and OpenAI
articles.authors: Travis Gilly
articles.abstract:
This paper examines a structural failure mode in the validation chain that legitimizes consumer artificial
intelligence products marketed to or used by minors: a child safety advocacy organization that arrives at
each crisis after journalists and litigants have already exposed it, or plays the harm down when it arrives
first, and that enters endorsement, development, and funding relationships with the firm whose product
produced the harm. It documents a twenty-three year response pattern at Common Sense Media (CSM),
a United States based organization that reports reaching more than 150 million users and 1.4 million
educators worldwide each year, across three crisis cycles: YouTube Kids during the Elsagate incidents
of 2017, video game loot boxes between 2017 and 2019, and generative artificial intelligence chatbots
between 2023 and 2026. The paper situates the pattern within Carpenter and Moss’s (2014) account of
corrosive capture, regulatory intermediary theory, and the social license literature. It argues that CSM’s
September 2025 endorsement of OpenAI’s parental controls as “a good starting point,” controls that
contemporaneous reporting described as developed by OpenAI with CSM, and CSM’s January 2026
ballot measure merger with OpenAI, which dropped provisions from CSM’s original ballot initiative that
had tracked its vetoed bill, together constitute a transfer of social license rather than a substantive safety
remedy. It then examines the October 2026 risk assessment in which CSM’s Youth AI Safety Institute,
funded in part by the OpenAI Foundation, rated ChatGPT for Teens an Unacceptable Risk on the strength
of a parental notification mechanism that CSM had helped develop and had endorsed at launch. CSM’s
own October 2025 review had already tested that mechanism, recorded parental alerts arriving more than
twenty-four hours after a tester discussed suicide, and recorded the account bypass, yet described the
product as meaningful progress and kept it rated for teens thirteen and up for a further 349 days. Archived
copies of CSM’s ChatGPT rating page show that the product carried a thirteen and up label from October
2023 and a Moderate risk rating from August 2024 through at least September 2025, so that the rating
available to parents on the day a sixteen year old user died after extended use of ChatGPT was Moderate.
The October 2026 findings were authored for the public by the former newspaper columnist who had
documented the bypass three days after launch, without reference to that earlier reporting. The paper
proposes public record indicators for detecting watchdog capture in other consumer safety intermediaries.
