articles.title: Silicon Ethics: Comparing the Dynamics of Human and LLM Responses to Ethical Dilemmas
articles.authors: W. Russell Neuman
articles.abstract: A key element in alignment research is commonly captured by the phrase “alignment with human values.” Human ethical judgment, however, is plural, unstable, affectively charged, socially embedded, and often justified after the fact. This article proposes a systematic comparative methodology emphasizing the potential complementarity of how human and silicon ethics may differ.   Drawing on literature of moral psychology, it identifies five dynamics of human ethical judgment systematically comparing them with their functional analogues in generative models. The goal is not to anthropomorphize LLMs or treat human judgment as a gold standard, but to compare the latent structures of the dynamics in vivo and in silico. The article argues that such comparison can extend alignment research beyond mimetic reproduction of human preferences toward compensatory intelligence: AI systems that help humans notice neglected consequences, test consistency, consider alternative moral frames, and deliberate more responsibly about their own commitments.

articles.title: Apuestas en Chile: regulación y peso económico de un mercado en expansión
articles.authors: Andrés Araya; Fabian Belmar; Xiomara Kuwae; Sebastián Aliaga
articles.abstract: El mercado de apuestas ya no puede entenderse solo como una actividad presencial. La expansión de internet, los teléfonos inteligentes, los medios de pago digitales y la publicidad deportiva trasladó parte relevante del juego de azar hacia plataformas online. Chile reguló históricamente el juego mediante autorizaciones parciales: hípica, loterías, casinos municipales y casinos bajo la Ley N.º 19.995. Ese diseño permitió ordenar segmentos específicos, pero quedó tensionado frente a un mercado digital transnacional. El juego de azar es un problema de política pública, no solo una actividad recreativa. Involucra recaudación fiscal, competencia entre operadores, protección al consumidor, prevención de lavado de activos, integridad deportiva y riesgos asociados al juego problemático. El mercado online no autorizado se ubica en una zona compleja: no forma parte del mercado autorizado, pero tampoco ha sido desplazado de manera efectiva. La Corte Suprema ha declarado ilegales las apuestas online no autorizadas, mientras persisten dificultades prácticas de fiscalización, persecución penal y control de dominios. En 2025, el mercado regulado registró ingresos brutos del juego por $787.281 millones (0,23% del PIB) y generó $148.712 millones en recaudación específica asociada al juego de azar, sin considerar IVA ni impuesto a la renta. Cerca del 70% del mercado regulado corresponde a casinos físicos. Este informe estima el mercado online no autorizado como la brecha entre la tendencia contrafactual del mercado regulado y sus ingresos efectivamente observados. En 2025, esa brecha alcanzó $431.489 millones (0,13% del PIB), es decir, poco más de un tercio de la industria. Bajo una tasa específica de 20% sobre ingresos brutos del juego, la pérdida potencial de recaudación sectorial asociada al mercado online no autorizado se aproxima a $86.298 millones en 2025.

articles.title: Similar disruptions, different reactions? Refugee crises and the politicization of immigration in Sweden and Switzerland
articles.authors: Marco Bitschnau; Didier Ruedin; Anders Hellström; Marie Sundström
articles.abstract: We investigate how major refugee crises affected the immigration debate in Sweden and Switzerland, two countries that have long been among the most popular European destinations for immigrants in general and refugees in particular. Analysing claims from newspapers during two crises, the Balkans refugee crisis of the 1990s and the European refugee crisis of 2015–16 (N=3,593), we find (1) fairly diverse patterns of politicization, with slightly greater polarization in Switzerland but higher salience peaks in Sweden; (2) no significant differences in how actors position themselves in relation to the status quo; and (3) substantial differences in how they use certain frames. We conclude that despite their proximity to immigration matters, refugee crises do not always lead to more politicized debates. There may be some crisis impact—but certainly no reason for crisis determinism. Instead, factors such as the domestic context and the relative shock value of each crisis appear to be relevant and should be given more consideration.

articles.title: A Step, Not a Slope: The Global Rise of Anti-Government Protest, 1990–2025
articles.authors: Sanmit Tanmay Ratnaparkhi
articles.abstract: Analysts have described the 2010s as an era of mass protest and expect protests to continue to increase. How did the frequency of antigovernmental protests change globally from 1990 to 2019? And what does the pattern imply for the years ahead? This is the question of the study. We used linear regression with annual counts of protests from the Mass Mobilization dataset (15,143 protests in 168 countries, 147–160 in any one year). The data was well fit by a simple linear trend (adding around 12 protests a year), but the fit was much better with a model that included a one-time shift in 2011: protests jumped by around 244 events per year after 2011, with little or no year-on-year trend. The break in 2011 was detected independently by a structural break test. After controlling for world population growth, the step remained significant. ACLED data for the period 2021-2025 did not show a significant further increase in the global total, although protests rose sharply in some countries and fell in others. Armed rebellion was not counted, so falling protest numbers may partly reflect a change in the form of dissent rather than a decline in dissent itself, as in Myanmar after 2021, where dissent became armed resistance. So global protest seems to have reached a new, higher plateau rather than to be on a steady upward climb, warning against linear projections of ever-increasing dissent.

articles.title: Following the Feedback: Audience Engagement and Politicians’ Issue Attention on Social Media
articles.authors: August Lohse; Tobias Priesholm Gårdhus; Snorre Ralund; Hjalmar Bang Carlsen
articles.abstract: Political representatives increasingly communicate in social media environments where every message generates immediate and quantified audience feedback. Although likes are not a representative measure of public opinion, they provide information about which issues attract attention from politicians' online audiences. We examine whether politicians devote more attention to issues that generate high engagement. Our analysis draws on 128,204 Facebook posts published by 123 Facebook-active Danish Members of Parliament between 2011 and 2018. We find that issues receiving relatively more audience feedback are consistently more likely to appear in politicians' subsequent posts. This pattern is present across political topics and different forms of engagement, but weakens during election campaigns, when heightened electoral incentives and institutional constraints coincide. The findings show that quantified platform feedback is systematically linked to the allocation of political attention, but that this alignment varies with the context in which politicians communicate.

articles.title: My (22m) Girlfriend (23f) Comes Home and Does Nothing”– Gendered Perceptions of Paid and Unpaid Work in Reddit Relationship Discussions over Time
articles.authors: Birgit Zeyer-Gliozzo; Johanna Hölzl; Gundula Zoch; Philipp Doebler
articles.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic reignited longstanding debates around gender inequalities in paid and unpaid work. While survey research has advanced our understanding of these disparities, it typically relies on predefined categories and is susceptible to social desirability and recall bias. Online postings, by contrast, capture intimate experiences in real time but rarely include demographic attributes. We leverage a unique dataset of discussions in Reddit relationship communities that combines rich descriptions of conflicts around (un)paid work with demographic information to examine: Which topics do men and women discuss in relationship conflicts around paid and unpaid work? We use Large Language Models (LLMs) and systematically vary GPT-family models and prompting strategies to classify manifest (demographic information) and latent variables (whether posts discuss romantic relationships, paid, and unpaid work) in Reddit posts. Using classifications from the best-performing approach, we apply Structural Topic Models to explore which topics partners discuss and how discussions evolve over time. We find temporary pandemic shifts in topics, and women more often discuss mental health in paid work-related conflicts, while men more frequently emphasize career objectives. In conflicts related to unpaid work, men more frequently express concerns about sexual intimacy. Our analysis offers new insights into topics driving relationship conflicts around (un)paid work. We also contribute to the growing literature on LLMs’ capabilities and limitations in classifying social-science constructs. By combining demographic information with sensitive narratives, our dataset captures forms of relational conflict rarely accessible in survey or social-media research, opening promising avenues for future research.

articles.title: In Silico Advertising Tests
articles.authors: Marta Trales; Guillaume Hochard; Christophe Benavent
articles.abstract:
This research examines whether large language model agents can produce analytically useful evidence for advertising testing when treated as synthetic respondents rather than as substitutes for human consumers. We report an in-silico comparative post-test of two television advertisements in the French telecommunications market, conducted on a panel of 800 profile-conditioned consumer agents. The study evaluates the synthetic corpus through internal validity criteria: whether the questionnaire covers the main dimensions of advertising response, whether evaluative dimensions form coherent relations, whether the two stimuli are discriminated across preference labels, scores, lexical patterns and semantic embeddings, and whether responses vary intelligibly across social profiles.
The results indicate that the synthetic panel produces structured and interpretable evidence. The contribution is not that the analysis discovers a contrast invisible in the advertisements themselves: Bouygues and Orange are clearly built around different persuasive registers. Rather, the contribution is methodological. The synthetic-interview pipeline consistently recovers and differentiates these registers across preference labels, scores, lexical patterns and semantic comparisons. Bouygues is associated mainly with creative, humorous and memorable qualities,
while Orange is associated with reliability, informativeness, purchase orientation and overall preference. This structure is visible quantitatively in the main six dimensional coding scheme. Among all 800 synthetic agents, Bouygues leads on creativity (83.6% versus 14.8% for Orange), whereas Orange leads on informationseeking or consideration (76.8% versus 14.8% for Bouygues) and overall preference (54.8% versus 20.6% for Bouygues), with the remaining responses classified as mixed or neutral. The analysis remains deliberately limited to synthetic respondents.
Claims about similarity to human preferences or market behaviour would require external comparison with representative human data or market-level indicators.

articles.title: Organicity And Structural Coincidence. Intellectual Activity Across Fields
articles.authors: Matteo Puoti; Antoine Roger
articles.abstract:
Intellectual activity is examined as a crucial component in the formation of dominant principles of perception, classification, and action. Drawing on Bourdieu’s field theory, the analysis focuses on the structural coincidence of struggles across relatively autonomous fields, showing how concordant principles may emerge without central coordination and contribute to naturalising the established order. Gramsci’s concepts of organicity, intellectual function, civil society, and common sense broaden this perspective by extending the range of agents, practices, and institutions implicated in hegemonic processes. This also foregrounds their relational and pedagogical dimensions and the need for an empirical inventory of the sites and symbolic forms through which common sense takes shape. Hegemony is thus treated as the contingent outcome of differentiated struggles whose effects become aligned across fields. A case study of agricultural capitalism in Romania illustrates the empirical operationalisation of this framework.

For a fuller discussion and further developments of these themes:
https://www.routledge.com/On-Gramsci-and-Bourdieu-Hegemony-Fields-and-Tools-for-Social-Research/Puoti-Roger/p/book/9781041299523

articles.title: Why We Cling to Flawed Influencers: Psychological Mechanisms Behind Loyalty to Deceptive Social Media Figures
articles.authors: Asma Alolyan
articles.abstract:
Abstract  
Existing studies on loyalty to social media influencers have mainly focused on cognitive  dissonance, parasocial bonding, halo effect, social identity, and just world belief, each in  isolation. This paper advances another argument: that these five mechanisms occur not  independently but in a predictable sequence, each reducing psychological resistance to the next,  producing loyalties more resistant than any single mechanism alone. We call this the  compounding loyalty model. Cognitive dissonance is the initial motivation causing a follower to  realise something is wrong; parasocial bonding makes rationalisation a requirement, not an  option; the halo effect provides a surface level base for maintaining trust despite misbehaviours;  social identity makes loyalty costly to lose; and just world belief provides a final, motivated  argument that deception did not happen at all. We draw this model from cases including James  Charles (2021) and Ramon Abbas, convicted of fraud in 2022. Media literacy, ethical marketing  and platform policy are discussed. 

Keywords: Influencers, social media, Cognitive dissonance, Para-social relationships, Halo  effect, social identity theory, just world hypothesis, Compounding loyalty model.

articles.title: Research and Impact of Prompt Engineering Nexus on Programming and Routine Tasks: Exploring Future Possible Directions
articles.authors: Felix Reichel
articles.abstract:
Prompt engineering has developed as a transformative subfield in artificial intelligence
(AI), enabling humans to enhance AI systems through structured (PROLOG-like) instructions
to perform specific tasks. This paper shines a light on its multi-dimensional impact on
programming, routine tasks and broader AI applications, drawing on insights from recent
studies. By using techniques such as parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), zero-shot
learning, multi-shot learning and linguistic feature analysis, prompt engineering often is used
to tackle remaining issues in software engineering (SE), language processing (NLP) and AI
safety. The body of literature highlights its role in optimizing AI performance, reducing
computational overhead and reducing biases. Additionally, it highlights critical gaps in 
current methodologies, such as the comparative energy intensity of state-of-art large language
models (LLMs) and the requirements for adaptive and scalable prompt crafting strategies.
Finally, the paper suggests future directions for research, highlighting the importance of
human-centered design and collaboration to advance the field.

articles.title: Unexpected heat suppresses emigration from the world's poorest countries
articles.authors: Ashley Vicary
articles.abstract: Whether climate stress displaces people or traps them in place is unresolved. The common intuition is displacement: crops fail, heat becomes unliveable and people leave. Other work predicts the opposite for poor countries, where migration abroad is expensive and the shock that sharpens the wish to leave can destroy the means to go. Estimates disagree, partly because realized temperature mixes warming that households anticipated with warming they did not. I isolate the unanticipated part with temperature forecast errors, the warmth or cold a forecast missed, and estimate their effect on monthly international migration from countries holding most of the world’s population. Here I show that unexpected warmth does not detectably move migration on average, but that in low-income countries an unexpectedly hot month lowers departures over the following year. No richer income group shows a detectable response. The migration suppression is strongest where incomes depend on agriculture, also appears outside the growing season and leaves in-migration flat, consistent with heat removing the means to move. For the poorest countries, unexpected heat may hold people back rather than push them abroad. Projections and policies built around displacement may overstate departures from these countries and overlook those who cannot afford to leave.

articles.title: Defaulting to Decarbonization?  Financial Insolvency and the Energy Transition in India’s States
articles.authors: Johnathan Guy
articles.abstract:
How do financial constraints shape the energy transition in developing countries? I study this question in India, where electricity procurement is governed at the subnational level. Electoral politics motivates state governments to subsidize electricity consumption, resulting in financial stress for electricity distribution utilities (DISCOMs). Using multiple sources of original data on utility and plant operations, I investigate the relationship between financial distress and decarbonization. I theorize that the effect of utility insolvency depends on the margin considered—dispatch vs. capacity investment—and on institutions. Counterintuitively, but consistent with my theory, I find that financial stress is associated in the short run with greater relative procurement of renewable energy and less procurement of fossil fuels. Mechanism tests suggest that coal dispatch is more sensitive to liquidity constraints, as distressed DISCOMs cut back on coal deliveries while renewable energy remains protected by “must-run” dispatch regulations. In contrast, I find at most weak evidence that insolvency raises challenges for decarbonizing electricity in the long run: insolvency shows no relationship with renewable-energy tendering, only suggestive evidence that it slows renewable capacity investment, and similarly weak evidence that it curtails expansion of transmission lines that renewables need to scale. The results qualify the conventional wisdom that electricity utility
insolvency is a binding constraint on the energy transition.

articles.title: Larger, younger, faster, harder: expansion, transformation, and inequality in YouTube’s creator economy (2019–2026)
articles.authors: Bernhard Rieder; Adrian Padilla; Ariadna Matamoros-Fernández; Òscar Coromina
articles.abstract: The growth of YouTube's creator economy raises a question that accounts of individual success and precarity cannot settle: how are the conditions of participation changing across the platform? Comparing two population-scale crawls from 2019 and 2026, we examine expansion, changes in production, and the distribution of attention across millions of channels. The population above the 1,000-subscriber threshold for advertising monetization grew from 4.4 million to 24.5 million, while its video catalogues grew ninefold. Expansion was strongest in South, Southeast, and East Asia, with India's share of channels declaring a country rising from 10 to 27 percent. This growth accompanied substantial turnover: most channels recorded in 2019 had no recent upload in 2026, and continued participation differed sharply by prior standing. Production also changed fundamentally. Median video duration fell from 247 to 60 seconds, with shortening across every content category and channel size. Among channels above 100,000 subscribers, new entrants accounted for most of the shift toward short form, while most continuing incumbents also shortened their output. Attention became more concentrated even among the same channels observed at both dates, and advertising revenue grew more slowly than the population meeting the subscriber threshold. These findings show how the output imperative extends from producing more to adapting what is produced, while sustained participation remains sharply unequal. They also place the increasingly Asian geography of the creator economy at the center of questions about platform labor, opportunity, and precarity.

articles.title: Perceived Manipulation, Fairness, and Trust in Competitive Mobile Gaming: A Cross-Cultural Analysis of Player Discourse
articles.authors: Hanieh Hatefi Yousefi
articles.abstract:
Perceptions of fairness play a central role in player experience within competitive mobile games, yet the processes through which players develop and sustain beliefs about manipulation remain insufficiently understood. This study investigates fairness-related discourse across two cultural and platform contexts through a five-year longitudinal qualitative analysis (2022–2026) of player-generated content from competitive mobile backgammon games.
The primary corpus consists of more than 52,000 Persian-language player reviews collected from Iranian app distribution platforms, supplemented by anonymised customer support transcripts. The comparative corpus comprises a stratified random sample of 750 negative reviews drawn from 4,116 reviews posted on an anglophone app-store listing over the same period. Using Inductive Thematic Analysis (ITA), the study identified seven recurring themes: dice manipulation, pay-to-win mechanics, bot opponents, connectivity sabotage, predetermined outcomes, statistical anomaly reporting, and support dismissal. These themes were subsequently organised into three higher-order meta-themes: Perceived Agency Erosion, Trust Erosion, and Statistical Misinterpretation.
The findings reveal both convergent and culturally distinct patterns. Beliefs that game outcomes are manipulated through unfair dice behaviour emerged as the dominant theme in both datasets, suggesting common cognitive mechanisms underlying fairness perceptions in stochastic competitive environments. At the same time, the two contexts differed in their developmental trajectories, complaint framing, and institutional response structures. Fairness-related complaints increased substantially across the Persian-language corpus over the study period, whereas comparable concerns remained relatively stable within the anglophone sample. Players in both contexts employed statistical reasoning to support manipulation claims, although the rhetorical and cultural framing of these arguments differed. Institutional responses to complaints also varied structurally, yet both contexts exhibited patterns that players frequently interpreted as dismissive or insufficiently responsive.
These findings contribute to research on player psychology, digital trust, and cross-cultural user experience by demonstrating how perceptions of unfairness emerge through the interaction of cognitive biases, community discourse, and platform communication practices. The study further highlights the importance of transparency design and context-sensitive trust-building mechanisms in competitive free-to-play games.

articles.title: Beyond the Joke: A Thematic Content Analysis of Russian-Linked Meme Pages Targeting Azerbaijan
articles.authors: Gudrat Guluyev
articles.abstract: As internet memes evolved from mere entertainment into a tool of digital propaganda, their role in modern warfare has become increasingly significant. This study examines their role in the case of Russian-linked information operations targeting the Azerbaijani audience on Facebook.  While the existing literature on meme-based Russian propaganda focuses heavily on the United States and Ukraine, the South Caucasus, one of the important regions of Russia’s “near abroad” policy, remains overlooked. The research addresses this critical gap by analyzing how these strategies are adapted to Azerbaijan's specific cultural and political context. The study relies on qualitative, multimodal analysis and emergent coding of 78 memes from nine Russian-linked Facebook pages targeting Azerbaijan between January 2023 and December 2024. The analysis identifies four consistent themes (the negative othering of the West, the discrediting of Western leaders, the reframing of the Nagorno-Karabakh Conflict, and the promotion of Azerbaijani sovereignty) and various propaganda techniques that have already been revealed in existing studies. The research paper concludes that these pages conduct a systematic influence campaign that sophisticatedly blends pro-Russian narratives with culturally conservative and patriotic domestic sentiments to resonate with the local audience.

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (VIII): Five Ideological Tendencies within Han Nationalism and Their Real-World Demands
articles.authors: ZY Liu
articles.abstract: This article is an exploratory study in the series “Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s.” It examines different ideological tendencies within Han nationalist discourse on the Chinese Internet. Unlike approaches that treat Han nationalism as a single political position, this article argues that contemporary Han nationalism on the Chinese Internet is not a unified movement with a common political program, but a collection of ideological tendencies formed around different real-world problems. Based on long-term observation of relevant online discourse, historical narratives, cultural phenomena, and public discussions, the article identifies five ideal types: establishment Han nationalism, renunciation-oriented Han nationalism, left-wing Han nationalism, cultural Han nationalism, and right-wing Han nationalism. These five tendencies primarily focus, respectively, on policy correction; central–local relations and fiscal responsibility; ethnic and class inequality; Han cultural identity; and population decline and the long-term demographic continuity of the Han. Although they share dissatisfaction with some differentiated ethnic policies and particular historical narratives, they differ substantially in their explanations of the causes of these problems and in their proposed solutions. Some of their demands also overlap with left-wing politics, liberalism, or regional autonomy. Han nationalism therefore cannot simply be equated with nationalism in the conventional right-wing sense. Its internal political demands in fact reflect real tensions in Chinese society concerning employment, working conditions, fiscal pressure, regional governance, population decline, marriage and fertility, and cultural identity. This article does not attempt to estimate the actual social size of these tendencies. Instead, it treats the five categories as analytical ideal types for understanding internal differences within Chinese Internet Han nationalism in the 2020s.

articles.title: Did local authorities lose revenue following banning unhealthy food advertising?
articles.authors: Mark Alan Green; Emma Boyland
articles.abstract: UK local authorities are increasingly exploring restrictions for the advertising of unhealthy foods on their estates to promote healthier food environments. Concerns about effects on revenue can be a barrier to progress. In this study, we provide preliminary evidence that these policies did not negatively affect total advertising revenue across four local authorities in North West England. In some cases, we found that revenue increased post-implementation.

articles.title: Conceptualizing Political Consumerism in the Attention Economy
articles.authors: Christopher Starke; Claes de Vreese; Natali Helberger
articles.abstract: Social media platforms increasingly become targets of politically and ethically motivated user protest, yet existing approaches do not sufficiently explain how deliberate platform use can operate as political participation. This conceptual paper extends the established concept of political consumerism to the attention economy, defining it as individuals’ market-oriented behaviors to punish or reward social media platforms on political or ethical grounds. It argues that three main factors constrain political consumerism on social media platforms: opaque value extraction, limited ethical alternatives, and high switching costs. Because political consumerism can take many forms, the paper suggests distinguishing user actions by their economic impact and whether they signal user preferences to the platform company. It further explains how social media literacy and regulation can improve the legibility and actionability of these practices. Finally, it outlines methodological implications for studying political consumerism through mixed-method designs that combine user motivations with behavioral data.

articles.title: Resilience in a Discordant Security Culture: Georgia between Institutional Continuity and Political Realignment
articles.authors: Mariam Bibilashvili
articles.abstract: Challenging the common understanding in the relevant literature, this study reconceptualizes resilience to hybrid threats as a politically mediated process rather than purely a matter of institutional capacity-building. To examine how policy frameworks and political rhetoric interact to shape resilience, it traces Georgia’s security culture in the aftermath of the Russo-Georgian war. Through intertextual discourse analysis, the article cross-examines the institutional architecture of digital resilience, encompassing cybersecurity (systemic), media regulation (protective) and media literacy (empowerment) measures, with the government’s shifting rhetoric (2023–2025), while interview data provide contextual insights. The analysis reveals a discordant security culture manifested in fragmented governance and discursive struggle over resilience. Although formal policy frameworks normatively align with the West and consistently identify Russia as the principal security threat, governmental rhetoric portrays the same Western actors as sources of foreign interference and prioritizes political autonomy over cooperation while still invoking commitments to the constitutionally enshrined Euro-Atlantic trajectory. This dichotomy between institutional design and political discourse results in strategic ambiguity. It suggests that in hybrid regimes formal frameworks may function symbolically to signal external alignment, while practice is determined by short-term political calculations and discretionary authority, leaving institutions and societies vulnerable to evolving forms of foreign interference.

articles_hidden.title: The Impact of Maternal Preconception Health on Long-Term Child Health and Developmental Outcomes: A Scoping Review
articles_hidden.authors: Catherine Stewart; Katie Harron; Jennifer Hall
articles_hidden.abstract:
The preconception period is a critical window during which maternal health and behaviours can influence pregnancy and offspring outcomes. However, preconception care remains limited, and existing research has largely focused on short-term pregnancy or neonatal outcomes. This scoping review aimed to synthesise evidence on the associations between maternal preconception health and long-term health, developmental, and educational outcomes in children.

Primary studies were eligible if they examined the independent effect of maternal preconception health on child health and developmental outcomes assessed after age 1 year and up to 18 years. Five databases (MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science) were searched. Data were extracted using a standardised form and summarised descriptively. Studies were mapped by type of preconception exposure and child outcome.

From 9,539 records identified, 186 studies met the inclusion criteria. Preconception BMI was the most frequently studied exposure (n=130) while neuro/cognitive development (n=83) was the most common outcome. Higher preconception BMI was consistently associated with adverse long-term outcomes, including higher offspring BMI and poorer cognitive, behavioural, and developmental outcomes. Pre-existing maternal physical and mental health conditions were also linked to poorer child health and developmental outcomes. Evidence for preconception smoking, alcohol, and substance use was limited but suggested potential harms, while diet quality and supplementation were generally associated with beneficial outcomes.

These findings highlight the preconception period as a key opportunity for intervention to support positive outcomes for children and underscore the need for higher-quality, long-term research to inform policy and practice.

articles_hidden.title: Gender and long-term trends in educational attainment, income and returns to education in Norway
articles_hidden.authors: Liza Reisel; Adrian F. Rogne; Sara Seehuus
articles_hidden.abstract: This study addresses the economic returns to education among men and women in Norway, during five decades of changing and widening gender disparities in educational attainment. We ask how gender differences in educational attainment and returns have contributed to change and persistence in the gender income gap, and whether young men have started trailing behind due to women’s relative gains in higher education. Analyses based on Norwegian register data show that while rising real incomes have contributed to a narrowing relative income gap, the absolute gap has decreased more slowly. In the past decade, both real incomes and the gender income gap have stagnated. While both men and women in Norway have increased their education levels, women’s gains have been mainly in higher education, while men’s gains have disproportionately been in vocational upper secondary education. Contrary to the situation in the US and other liberal market economies, income growth among younger cohorts of men with vocational education in Norway has recently outpaced every other group, resulting in a decreasing college premium. Women’s relative gains in higher education are partly offset by their lower incomes at all education levels, and the relatively strong income growth among men with vocational degrees.

articles_hidden.title: Who stops answering? Breakoff, smartphone use and educational bias in a web survey
articles_hidden.authors: Alžbeta Ľudmová; Martin Kreidl; Barbora Hubatková; Martin Lakomý
articles_hidden.abstract:
Survey data collection has been moving towards the online self-administered mode (CAWI), which is usually seen as an effective answer to falling response rates and rising fieldwork costs. This mode, however, comes with drawbacks of its own, especially when respondents use a smartphone to fill out the survey. Related major challenge is a higher tendency of these respondents to break off, i.e. to end the interview before completion. Breakoff matters most when it occurs non-randomly and compounds existing biases, such as those based on age or education. To find out whether it does, we used questionnaire data and paradata from the CAWI component of the first wave of the second cycle of the Czech Generations and Gender Survey (2020–2022; N = 5,468, 244 breakoffs). Treating each of 118 unfiltered questionnaire items as one unit of analytical time, we analysed progression through the questionnaire using Cox regression supplemented by Kaplan–Meier survival curves. Younger respondents broke off somewhat more often than older ones, though the difference was not statistically robust. The education gradient was both steeper and more persistent: 7% of the least educated broke off as compared with 3% of the most educated, and device only partly explained this gap, leaving education and device to operate as largely independent processes. The gap was, however, concentrated on small screens - among smartphone users, breakoff rose from 4% among the most educated to over 11% among the least educated, while on larger devices it stayed flat at 3–4%. Breakoff thus adds to, rather than merely reflects, the educational bias of self-completion samples. 

Keywords: breakoff; web surveys; smartphone; device effects; survival analysis; paradata; representativity; Generations and Gender Survey

articles_hidden.title: Under what conditions does complexity become unmanageable? A capacity threshold for megaprojects
articles_hidden.authors: Matthias Huemmer
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose. Project complexity research describes complexity in rich dimensional detail but rarely states the condition under which it stops being manageable. This paper states one and derives what remains possible past it.
Design/methodology/approach. Conceptual theory elaboration from the delivering organization’s standpoint, building on requisite variety, organizational information processing and bounded rationality, illustrated with a worked calculation and a documented revision series from a public inquiry.
Findings. Complexity becomes unmanageable from within at a point of no return: when the capacity demanded of a governance level exceeds the information-processing capacity available to it, set by its binding constraint, to the degree that the level can no longer remove its overload with its own means. Past it the feasible response set collapses to three moves, deceleration, external capacity and requirement reduction, because every other method consumes the missing capacity. In megaprojects the threshold falls early, because both sides of the balance are fixed before work begins. The Elbphilharmonie's public record shows the predicted signature: revisions moved both ways before contract award and one way after it.
Research limitations/implications. The threshold is stated as a testable claim, not a measured constant. Five propositions with falsification conditions follow.
Originality/value. Not a new inventory of complexity but a threshold within the inherited mechanism, and the identification of the translation of requirements into demanded capacity as the operation where complexity becomes subjective and manageable.

articles_hidden.title: Overcoming inertia: Addressing barriers to managing coastal legacy waste in a changing climate
articles_hidden.authors: Isabel Cotton; James J. Porter; James S. Robinson; Rhys H.S. Kelly; Ute Kelly; Megan Clinch; Rhys E. M. Jones; Deborah P. Dixon; Patrick Diamond; Suzy O’Hara
articles_hidden.abstract: Climate change will increase the number of legacy waste sites (older waste sites without pollution control mechanisms) that are at risk of coastal flooding and erosion in the UK and worldwide. Whilst the need to adapt to coastal change is well documented, the combined risks of coastal change and legacy waste has received less attention. Through interviews and workshops with policy stakeholders, this paper explores current perspectives on the barriers to managing coastal legacy waste in England and Scotland. Both the interviews and workshops reveal a high awareness of the potential risks from coastal legacy waste. However, limited sources of funding, alongside knowledge gaps on the nature of pollutant risk, many competing priorities at a local authority level, and a lack of clarity on roles and responsibilities, is creating an inertia that frustrates the proactive management of the issue. Using Moser and Ekstrom’s (2010) adaptation planning cycle as an analytical framework, findings reveal that managing legacy waste is unable to progress beyond the first stage of adaptation planning due to these systemic barriers. Overall, findings indicate the urgent need for a long-term strategy designed at a national level that provides sufficient resources and capacity-building for proactive local governance.

articles_hidden.title: Heterogeneous Effects of Local Government Financing Channels on Industrial Structure: Evidence from Provincial-Level Panel Data in China
articles_hidden.authors: Liangkun Shi; Huanqi Wu; Hanfei Yang
articles_hidden.abstract: Local government financing channels provide an essential perspective for understanding the investment decisions of local governments and their economic effects. In China, broadly defined local government debt includes two categories: statutory debt and the debt incurred by local government financial vehicles (LGFVs). This paper uses provincial-level panel data from 2016 to 2025, constructs a data-driven industrial structure index, and estimates a two-way fixed-effects model controlling for the overall debt scale. The empirical evidence suggests that the different financial channels on industrial structure are associated with different and opposing changes in industrial structure. When the debt composition shifts toward LGFV debts, the share of relatively high-productivity efficiency industries increases, particularly that of the tertiary sector. In contrast, when the debt composition shifts toward statutory debt, the share of relatively low-production efficiency industries increases, particularly that of the secondary sector. Therefore, the composition of local government debt, rather than its scale alone, is relevant to changes in regional industrial structure.

articles_hidden.title: Archaeologies of Indigenous Foodways and Collective Capacities
articles_hidden.authors: Molly Carney
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent archaeological scholarship has embraced food security and food sovereignty frameworks to connect past foodways to present-day crises. However, these studies require critical examination of the colonial origins and ideological foundations of these frameworks, which emerged from industrialized western economic paradigms that do not align with Indigenous worldviews. Drawing on food studies scholarship, I argue that archaeologists must move beyond the uncritical adoption of food security and sovereignty frameworks to embrace culturally grounded paradigms developed by and for descendant communities. This paper advocates for reframing North American archaeological investigations of foodways through Indigenous philosopher Kyle Powys Whyte’s concept of collective capacities: webs of relationships among humans, non-human beings, and landscapes organized together to support responses to change and continuance. As a linking tool, collective capacities help archaeologists carry out the material and analytical work that Indigenous Food Sovereignty movements call for. An archaeology of collective capacities shifts our focus to understanding how food systems functioned as relational infrastructures of care, responsibility, and reciprocity that sustained communities across millennia. In this contribution I outline an archaeological framework identifying key material signatures of collective capacities. Applying this framework to the Pend Oreille Valley in northeastern Washington State, I demonstrate how paleoethnobotanical and archaeological data from the last 1,500 years reveal Indigenous food systems were sustained through active management, coordinated labor, and intergenerational knowledge transmission across climatic and sociopolitical changes. I also consider how contemporary practices of reciprocity and relationality mirror the archaeological record of stability and stewardship. By centering culture-specific terminology and philosophies, an archaeology of collective capacities offers a methodological and theoretical approach that supports, rather than imposes frameworks upon, past societies while documenting the enduring systems that enabled communities to thrive across deep time.

articles_hidden.title: Extractive conditionality: Participation and datafication in the Netherlands
articles_hidden.authors: Marijke Roosen
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on welfare conditionality has shown how access to social assistance is tied to behavioural and informational obligations. It has paid less attention to what recipients’ compliance produces for welfare institutions. This article develops the concept of extractive conditionality to describe arrangements in which activities and information provided under conditions of material dependency are transformed into institutionally usable resources. Drawing on an interpretive case study of Dutch social assistance, the analysis combines autobiographical testimony with policy documents, official evaluations and investigative journalism. It identifies two dimensions of extraction. First, activation requirements mobilise recipients’ time and activity even when they do not facilitate durable labour-market exit. Second, disclosure requirements generate information that can be standardised and reused for purposes such as organisational oversight and risk classification. These processes are extractive when recipients have little control over how their compelled contributions are subsequently used. The article further develops the hypothesis that this institutional productivity may help reproduce conditional arrangements despite their limited success in reducing welfare dependency. It shows how policies may fail to achieve their stated objectives while continuing to generate organisational capacities. The concept redirects analysis from what conditionality demands towards what compliance produces, who can use these outputs and how they may contribute to the persistence of conditional welfare.

articles_hidden.title: The Digital Undertow of Penal Supervision: An Ethnography of Electronic Monitoring in Belgium
articles_hidden.authors: Marijke Roosen
articles_hidden.abstract: Electronic monitoring (EM) relies on digital systems to supervise people in the community, but these systems also organise the work of monitoring officers. This article examines how digital monitoring systems shape officers’ everyday work and decisions, and how these practices give meaning to penal supervision. It draws on 74 days of observation and 22 interviews with control-room officers in Belgium, conducted between 2014 and 2017. Using a strong sociomaterial perspective and the concept of the digital undertow, the analysis connects three aspects of supervision: the recording and potential scrutiny of officers’ activities, their assessments of monitored individuals, and their emphasis on rule-following. The findings show how telephone exchanges, software records and organisational expectations together shape what requires attention, and which responses count as responsible work. Officers interpret compliance as preparation for reintegration, while accurate and traceable actions become ways of demonstrating professional responsibility. These practices involve judgement and negotiation, even when officers describe their decisions as required by rules. The article contributes to research on digital penal work by showing how the practical organisation of information connects assessments of monitored individuals to standards of professional competence. It identifies processes through which institutional values acquire meaning in everyday supervision.

articles_hidden.title: Spiritual Healing Methods in Los Angeles: the Cultural Heritage and Western Representation of Alternative Medicines
articles_hidden.authors: Scott Altsuler; Eric Heller
articles_hidden.abstract: Throughout the United States of America, complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) has become increasingly popular over the past fifty years. These include any practices that stem from tradition and spirituality rather than practices that are derived from empirical evidence. With many popular spiritual healing practices originating from specific traditions across the world and across a wide range of time, there is much to explore about the mechanisms through which culturally specific spiritual healing practices adapt to Western consumerist culture. In the current study, we examine the cultural origins and development of CAM, mostly the use and popularization of Reiki, Yoga, and ayahuasca. We interviewed six spiritual health practitioners in the greater Los Angeles area to understand the modern CAM practitioner’s perspective on how spiritual healing methods have taken hold in Western culture, how they align with the original practice’s tradition, and how they have adapted to modern consumer culture. This study explores how Los Angeles’ cultural emphasis on individuality and marketability has cultivated an environment for its population to disseminate and recontextualize traditional spiritual healing methods to fit contemporary mental health demands.

articles_hidden.title: Issue Accountability Among Public Meeting Commenters
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander Sahn; Tyler Simko
articles_hidden.abstract: Standard theories of accountability suggest politicians respond to voter preferences for fear of electoral sanction, yet many voters are ill-informed about policy actions. One solution to this tension is that a small group of highly engaged citizens, an issue public, may generate the conditions for accountability. We test this claim by tracking over 7,000 members of the public who submit comments on land use policies in San Francisco, CA. We measure commenters’ expressed preferences on proposed agenda items, survey them following the decision, and observe subsequent political activity with administrative data. We show that over three-quarters of commenters accurately recall their past positions, but most do not learn the subsequent policy action and rarely update their political attitudes. However, we find that a subset of anti-development voters are more likely to contribute to ideologically aligned candidates when they do not see their preferred policies enacted; yet pro-development commenters do not.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) for Coding Open-Ended Survey Responses: A Total Survey Error Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Laone Maphane; Gabriele Durrant
articles_hidden.abstract:
Open-ended questions are commonly used in survey research to supplement closed-ended questions by capturing respondents’ views, reasons, and priorities in their own words. However, coding these responses for analysis remains time-consuming and difficult to standardise. Recent advances in automated coding, especially through large language models (LLMs), have renewed interest in using open-ended responses at scale, but their evaluation is often difficult and framed mainly in terms of classification accuracy and agreement with human coding. This paper develops a Total Survey Error framework for evaluating automated coding of open-ended survey responses as part of survey measurement and data production. Model outputs are assessed using existing human-coded data as a high-quality operational benchmark, with the evaluation examining six complementary dimensions, such as processing agreement, measurement validity, prevalence distortion, coding density, response-form sensitivity, and operational reliability. The framework is applied to data using open-ended survey responses from the National Centre for Social Research (NatCen). The paper aims to inform how automated coding systems, including LLMs, can be assessed in practice, and what issues survey researchers should consider when evaluating their suitability for open-ended survey coding, and how improved coding may enable wider use of open-ended questions in large-scale quantitative surveys.
Keywords: automated coding; large language models; measurement validity; open-ended survey responses; survey data quality; Total Survey Error

articles_hidden.title: The Subnational Fertility Transition in Italy (1871-1971): A Century of Fundamental Change
articles_hidden.authors: Riccardo Omenti; Nicola Barban; Michail Raftakis
articles_hidden.abstract: The Italian fertility transition has drawn sustained interest from historical demographers, thanks to rich archival sources, especially parish records, and a well-established scholarly tradition. Yet no study has offered a comprehensive account of how the transition unfolded subnationally across the second half of the nineteenth and first half of the twentieth centuries. Drawing on extensive yet underutilised data from the Italian National Institute of Statistics (ISTAT), we present annual total fertility rate (TFR) estimates for all Italian provinces covering the historical period 1871–1971, using an established Bayesian modelling framework. Combining convergence analysis with measures of relative dispersion and variability, we examine whether provincial fertility differences widened or narrowed over the transition. We further investigate urban-rural fertility trajectories within Italy’s nine most populous provinces. The results reveal a geographically uneven transition: northern and central provinces led the fertility decline, while southern provinces lagged behind, resulting in divergence across provinces. Nonetheless, urban–rural differences narrowed substantially in northern and central provinces and remained negligible in southern provinces. These findings underscore the spatial heterogeneity of Italy’s fertility transition, displaying the co-existence of increasing provincial disparities with diminishing urban-rural differences in the areas leading the fertility decline.

articles_hidden.title: An Empirical Study on How Private College Counseling Perpetuates Structural Disadvantage A Mixed-Methods Study Combining Survey, Interview, and Social Media Content Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Alayna ellahi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Equitable access to higher education is widely regarded as a cornerstone of social mobility, yet the rapid growth of an independent educational consulting (IEC) industry has introduced a market-driven layer of college admissions guidance available only to families who can pay for it. This study investigates whether private college counseling functions as a neutral support service or as a mechanism of structural disadvantage that converts economic capital into institutional advantage, drawing on Pierre Bourdieu's theory of cultural and social capital. Using a triangulated, mixed-methods design, the study combines a 20-respondent Likert-scale survey of students and parents, semi-structured interviews with six purposively sampled respondent groups (student and parent users and non-users, school-based counselors, and private consultants), and an original content analysis of eight social media acceptance posts from a private counseling agency, coded against a seven-theme promotional codebook. Findings converge across all three methods: 82% of survey respondents reported that private counselors reveal "unspoken" admissions criteria unavailable to public-school peers; 65% identified fee-based, unadvertised opportunity-brokering as a distinguishing service; and interviews revealed overwhelming cross-group consensus — among both users and non-users of private counseling — that the practice constitutes an unfair structural advantage rather than a neutral commercial service. The content analysis found that aspirational imagery and institutional-legitimacy signaling appeared in 100% of coded posts, empirically confirming the marketing mechanisms respondents described. The study concludes that, absent structural reform — expanded public counseling capacity

articles_hidden.title: Enhancing Dementia Awareness and Specialized Nurse Training in the Gulf: A Policy Roadmap for Oman, Qatar, UAE, and Saudi Arabia
articles_hidden.authors: Sukant Khurana; Sanampreet Kaur; Mohammad Saddam Khan; Gaurav Deepak Patel; Prajwal Anand; K. Vijaya Lakshmi; Ahmad; Brooks Robinson
articles_hidden.abstract: The countries of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) are projected to see more than a threefold increase in dementia by 2050, due to a rapidly aging population. However, health care systems across Oman, Qatar, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia are still skewed towards acute rather than chronic care.  Nurses are the primary dementia caregivers, but  they often are not specialists. This situation is exacerbated by non-standardized curricula, heavy reliance on expatriate workforce, linguistic and cultural barriers, high workforce turnover, limited career incentives, and low public and institutional awareness, which delays diagnoses.This study synthesizes available regional and international evidence on dementia related nurse training and workforce preparedness in the GCC and develops evidence-informed policy recommendations for strengthening dementia education and workforce capacity. We propose several regional recommendations including accredited certification, compulsory continuing professional development, multidisciplinary care teams, and awareness-raising initiatives. Coordinated investment in specialized nurse training and workforce policy is important to prepare GCC healthcare systems for the region’s growing dementia burden.

articles_hidden.title: When Execution Is Cheap: Specification, Evaluation, and Rent Capture in AI-Enabled Work
articles_hidden.authors: Babu George
articles_hidden.abstract: As artificial intelligence lowers the cost of executing well-specified tasks, economic value may shift toward defining desired outcomes and evaluating machine-generated outputs. This paper examines the conditions under which that shift creates economic rents and identifies who may capture them. It separates defining success into four activities: eliciting intent, selecting among admissible specifications, ratifying a choice, and validating outputs. Two models clarify the underlying mechanisms. The first shows that gains from cheaper execution approach a ceiling determined by evaluation cost, which makes evaluator attention more consequential as generation becomes inexpensive. The second shows that generating more candidates increases the marginal value of proxy fidelity, linking abundant output to specification overfitting and Goodhart-type failures. These mechanisms indicate where value may concentrate without determining who receives the returns. Rent requires inelastic supply, exclusion from the created surplus, and the absence of cheaper substitutes. These conditions are most likely when specifications scale across many executions, ratification carries liability, trust institutions certify judgment, organizational systems control codified knowledge, or concentrated model providers set influential defaults. The analysis further distinguishes machine-checkable evaluation against a stated specification from a principal’s assessment of fit to purpose. The former is increasingly commoditized; the latter remains tied to authority, attention, and accountability. The paper develops six testable predictions and a factorial experiment examining evaluation costs, specification fidelity, authority drift, and psychological ownership. Cheap execution relocates bottlenecks, while institutions and market structure determine whether specification, evaluation, default setting, or scarce execution inputs generate rents and who captures them.

articles_hidden.title: The prestige precedes the prize: Top-journal papers and new federal grants
articles_hidden.authors: Haining Wang
articles_hidden.abstract: Evaluators and scientists treat a top-journal paper as a step toward the next grant. We asked whether it is one. We linked 2.19 million last-authored papers by 1.07 million US scientists, 2014–2021, to new lead-investigator awards from the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation, defining top journals as the 5% most cited in their topic and year. The design rests on timing and on holding the scientist fixed: if a top-journal paper brings grants, the advantage should open after the paper. Top-journal papers were followed by a new award twice as often as other papers (55.3 against 26.3 per 1,000), yet the difference was as large two years before publication. For the same scientist, award rates after a top-journal paper and another paper differed by −0.3 per 1,000 (95% confidence interval −8.0 to 7.4), an upper limit at 25% of the difference between scientists. Researchers' small lead over matched researchers was similar before and after their first top-journal paper (3.1 and 3.3 per 1,000). Within three years, journal prestige worked mainly as a record of accumulated advantage, and the funding gap should not be read as the return on one more top-journal paper.

articles_hidden.title: GLCI (Global Linguistic Connectivity Index): How Connected Is the World?
articles_hidden.authors: Areg Hovhannisyan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Eight billion people speak more than seven thousand languages. If two of them meet by chance, how 
likely is it that the one listening understands the one speaking, without a translator? We estimate 
about one chance in nine. Greenberg (1956) defined this probability for a single population as an 
index of communication; we compute it for the world. The data come from an audit of individual 
language repertoire compiled from hundreds of census, survey and reference sources, mapped onto 
a common conversational threshold (level A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference for 
Languages, CEFR) and a common individuation standard (ISO 639-3, the language codes of the 
International Organization for Standardization). That audit, reported with ALPS (Average Language a 
Person Speaks) in Hovhannisyan (2026a), covers 237 jurisdictions and 8.16 billion residents; 
connectivity is computed for the 216 with language-level data, which hold 8.09 billion, while the 
other 21, with 69 million residents, have a national ALPS value but no language rows. The audit is 
extended with a directional table of intelligibility between related languages, which covers 591 
language pairs, most of them assessed and few measured. The resulting index, the Global Linguistic 
Connectivity Index (GLCI), is the probability that a randomly drawn listener comprehends a randomly 
drawn speaker. 
GLCI is 0.1129 (95% interval 0.1083–0.1176); the interval covers only row-level, sampling-type 
uncertainty in the input shares, and single modelling choices move GLCI between 0.096 and 0.134 
(§6.1). Within a single jurisdiction the probability is 0.6284 (0.5907–0.6660), a pair-weighted figure 
dominated by India and China; across two jurisdictions it is 0.0747 (0.0711–0.0788), and because 
91% of pairs span two jurisdictions, the lower value governs. Connectivity is concentrated: nearly a 
third of cross-jurisdiction pair mass lies below 0.01, and the median pair sits at 0.022. It also rests on 
one language. English carries 39.2% of global connectivity and 61.9% of the connectivity between 
countries. 
In a simple model relating repertoire to connectivity, which languages are learned matters far more 
than how many. At a mean repertoire of four languages per person, GLCI is 98%, 58% or 15% 
depending on the allocation rule, that is, chiefly on which languages are learned and also on where. 
Compared with a dataset that other researchers built from Ethnologue, the LINGACON estimates 
agree closely on first languages (r = 0.951). On the full layer, leaving out the intelligibility term that 
the other dataset lacks, they are 1.45 times higher, and the difference lies mainly in the coverage of 
acquired languages.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring Nonlinear Associations Between AI Comment Volume and Retail Investor Sentiment
articles_hidden.authors: Yuze Tang
articles_hidden.abstract: Artificial intelligence comment generators have proliferated in online stock forums. However, how AI comment volume associates with retail investor sentiment, and whether this association is conditional on market volatility and annual AI comment density, remain under-explored. Using weekly data from the East Money Stock Forum and the Shanghai Composite Index spanning May 2019–October 2024 in China, this paper proposed a two-detector ensemble for AI comment detection, then investigated nonlinear associations between AI comment volume and retail investor sentiment under three tiers of market volatility and six annual AI comment densities. Our generalized additive model (GAM) results show that AI comment volume exhibits a weak, net-positive nonlinear association with mean retail investor sentiment, and a very weak net-negative nonlinear association with sentiment divergence. We find no statistically significant pairwise differences in these associations across low-, medium- and high-volatility levels. For annual AI comment density, statistically significant cross-density differences are observed for sentiment standard deviation in multiple year pairwise comparisons, whereas only one comparison yields significant differences for mean sentiment. Collectively, our findings indicate that merely considering the number of AI comments provides limited information regarding the sentiment of retail investors.

articles_hidden.title: Une approche dynamique de la réception des pré-annonces pharmaceutiques dans les réseaux sociaux - Le cas des vaccins contre la Covid-19 sur twitter
articles_hidden.authors: Olivier Caron; Christophe Benavent
articles_hidden.abstract:

dans la conversation publique ? Les travaux sur la transmission sociale établissent qu’un message se transforme à mesure qu’il circule et s’assimile aux préoccupations du milieu qui le reçoit.
À partir de ce cadre, de l’amplification sociale du risque et du Persuasion Knowledge Model, nous étudions les préannonces d’efficacité de Pfizer/BioNTech, Moderna et AstraZeneca sur
le Twitter francophone, comparées à des événements où les mêmes entreprises font l’actualité sans être à l’origine de la nouvelle. Deux temporalités apparaissent. Le contenu du débat se
transforme presque immédiatement, puis se réinscrit dans des préoccupations préexistantes, comme l’obligation vaccinale ou l’actualité politique. Le jugement de l’entreprise apparaît plus
tard : les utilisateurs passent surtout du relais du message à l’évaluation de son émetteur, sans hausse nette de la négativité des jugements déjà exprimés. Cette bascule est absente lorsque
l’entreprise est seulement l’objet de l’information. Une préannonce met en circulation deux objets : un message et celui qui le porte.

articles_hidden.title: Who protects Science Diplomacy from being weaponised?  The role of domestic policies
articles_hidden.authors: Eva Hartmann
articles_hidden.abstract:
Many researchers have voiced concerns about the weaponisation of policy-relevant international research collaborations. But why does this pose a problem? This contribution develops a Neo-Gramscian notion of science diplomacy to explain how processes of weaponisation risk undermining the mediation role of scientific research, its capacity to integrate diverse perspectives and values, and, consequently, its ability to mediate between conflicting norms, values and interests.
Drawing on Nicos Poulantzas’s state theory, the article further elaborates the concept of mediation and illuminates the role of national parliaments as an important mediator between academia and civil society, more generally, and the government. The empirical study explores parliamentary deliberations of the UK National Security Bill in the House of Commons and the House of Lords. It shows how the parliamentary scrutiny failed to curb the significant expansion of governmental authority justified in the name of security, with important consequences for how academics engage with other governments as part of science diplomacy. 
The findings shed light on the significance of public policy and domestic political struggles for international politics. In the context of an ongoing crisis of multilateralism, domestic political dynamics have become even more important.

articles_hidden.title: Climate Change and the Socio-Political Foundations of Welfare
articles_hidden.authors: katharina.zimmermann@uni-hamburg.de
articles_hidden.abstract:
As climate change and decarbonization become central sources of political conflict in Europe, welfare states are increasingly invoked as institutions capable of cushioning transition costs, managing distributional conflict, and stabilizing democratic legitimacy. The article identifies three perspectives in which this expectation appears: green-growth approaches expect welfare institutions to secure the social conditions of low-carbon accumulation; social-democratic and labour-oriented approaches seek to renew class compromise through just transition policies; and post-growth or sustainable-welfare approaches ask whether welfare can be reorganized around needs, sufficiency, and planetary boundaries. Despite their differences, all three perspectives rely on a shared assumption: that the welfare state can provide socio-political stability under ecological constraint. This article problematizes this assumption by reconstructing the historical foundations of welfare-state stabilization. It argues that twentieth-century welfare capitalism functioned as a form of socio-political glue: it mediated the tension between capitalist market inequalities and democratic claims to equality by making market dependence bearable, class compromise plausible, and bounded solidarity legitimate. Yet this glue was fossil in character. It depended on sustained growth, fossil-energy regimes with underpriced social and ecological costs, institutionalized labour relations, nationally bounded solidarity, and the externalization of social and ecological costs.
Climate change unsettles each of these stabilizing mechanisms. It strains the growth-dependent balance between commodification and decommodification; reconfigures class compromise by politicizing fossil-dependent forms of production, consumption, status, and deservingness; and destabilizes closure and containment by making externalized costs return materially, politically, and morally. The article therefore argues that climate change should not be understood only as a new generation of social risks to be absorbed by existing welfare institutions. More fundamentally, it challenges the welfare state’s historically established capacity to process risks, conflicts, and legitimacy claims in familiar ways. Rather than presuming which form of “green glue” should replace the fossil compromise, it calls for a more systematic analysis of the democratic conflicts through which competing projects of welfare-state stabilization are negotiated: who should be protected, who should pay, which losses count as legitimate, which ways of life remain publicly recognized, and through which democratic procedures new forms of socio-political glue can be built under ecological constraint.

articles_hidden.title: Why the Left Leans Socialist and the   Right Leans Capitalist: Class, Coalitions and Where the Link Breaks
articles_hidden.authors: Kaushik E
articles_hidden.abstract:
Political labels are often assumed to map neatly onto economic systems: the left is 
expected to favor socialism and the right capitalism. This paper asks why that pattern exists 
and why it breaks down in some countries. It first examines four explanations for the pattern: 
historical origins, class interest, core values, and coalition bundling. It then compares 
cases, including Sweden, China, the United States and India, where party labels and 
economic policy diverge. The paper argues that the link between political stance and 
economic policy is contingent rather than necessary, and that it varies with a party's voter 
base, a country's history, and its state capacity. The findings suggest that left-right labels 
are an unreliable guide to actual economic policy.

articles_hidden.title: KONTINUITAS DAN REKONTEXTUALISASI UJUNGAN GUMELEM: RITUAL, REPERTOAR TUBUH, DAN LEGITIMASI WARISAN BUDAYA PADA 2026
articles_hidden.authors: Dwi Scativana Isnaeni
articles_hidden.abstract: Ujungan merupakan praktik budaya yang berkembang dalam masyarakat agraris di wilayah Gumelem, Kecamatan Susukan, Kabupaten Banjarnegara. Dokumentasi akademik mengenai Ujungan telah berlangsung sekurang-kurangnya sejak 1999 dan berkembang melalui kajian mengenai ritual meminta hujan, pertunjukan, perubahan fungsi, makna filosofis, terminologi budaya, serta iringan gamelan. Artikel ini bertujuan membaca kembali dokumentasi tersebut untuk menjelaskan bagaimana Ujungan mempertahankan unsur-unsur identitas praktik sekaligus mengalami perubahan konteks sosial, performatif, dan kelembagaan. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif interpretif melalui analisis dokumen historis dan budaya. Sumber dipilih berdasarkan keterverifikasian identitas bibliografis, keterkaitan langsung dengan Ujungan, lokasi, periode dokumentasi, dan fokus kajian. Gumelem Wetan dan Gumelem Kulon diperlakukan sebagai lokasi yang berbeda, sedangkan Ujungan di Pelana, Banyumas, dan Kasepuhan Cibadak digunakan sebagai pembanding regional. Hasil kajian menunjukkan bahwa kontinuitas Ujungan tidak terutama terletak pada ketidakberubahan bentuk, melainkan pada keberulangan sejumlah relasi antara ritual, air dan hujan, penggunaan tubuh, aturan pertarungan, otoritas pengendali, musik, dan tindakan sosial setelah konfrontasi. Dokumentasi 1999, 2010, 2012, 2014, 2018, 2020, 2021, 2022, dan 2026 memperlihatkan bahwa unsur-unsur tersebut bertahan dengan konfigurasi yang tidak selalu sama. Penetapan Ujungan sebagai Warisan Budaya Takbenda Indonesia pada 2026 menambahkan konteks legitimasi kelembagaan, tetapi tidak dapat diperlakukan sebagai bukti otomatis keberlanjutan. Artikel ini mengusulkan konsep kontinuitas berlapis melalui rekontextualisasi untuk memahami Ujungan sebagai praktik ritual-performatif yang dapat berubah tanpa kehilangan seluruh hubungan dengan sejarah, komunitas, dan pengetahuan tubuh yang menopangnya.

articles_hidden.title: Does Crop Diversification Improve Rural Household Income in Bangladesh?
articles_hidden.authors: Imran Hossain
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper examines whether crop diversification improves household income among rural farming households in Bangladesh, using data from the Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES) 2022. Using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression with division fixed effects and robust standard errors, the study finds that diversification has a strong and stable positive effect on crop sales income, but not on total household income once household characteristics are controlled. This suggests that diversification operates primarily through the agricultural income channel. The findings carry practical implications for agricultural extension policy in Bangladesh.

articles_hidden.title: Urban Typology is Not Destiny: The High-Modernist Tower and Slab as a Global Outlier in Singapore
articles_hidden.authors: Reuben Xianwei Wang
articles_hidden.abstract:
In global architectural literature, the mid-century high-modernist tower-and-slab block is widely pathologized as a failure of top-down social engineering. Anti-modernist critics routinely embrace architectural determinism, blaming concrete geometry for social decay. This paper challenges that consensus by examining Singapore, where high-modernist public housing constructed by the Housing & Development Board (HDB) shelters over 80 percent of citizens in safe, equity-building estates. Building on Katherine Bristol’s critique of the "Pruitt-Igoe myth," I demonstrate that building typology possesses marginal agency; the global demise of the high-rise slab resulted from welfare state retrenchment, fiscal starvation, and municipal abandonment. In Singapore, the typology succeeded due to a unique political-economic triad: radical land nationalization, captive domestic capital, and sovereign geographical enclosure.

I adopt an object-oriented ontology and James Scott's notion of metis to argue the built form not as an empty vessel but being instrumental constructs that whose users will always develop new Métis and practical knowledges on how to maximise the utility of an urban form. I exemplify the Singaporean architects adapted the slab through vernacular inventions like the open-air "void deck." Ultimately, typology is not destiny but should be understood instrumentally.

articles_hidden.title: The EU’s Biotech Industrial Policy: Between Competitiveness and Geoeconomics
articles_hidden.authors: Jaša Veselinovič
articles_hidden.abstract: This contribution examines the European Union’s emerging biotechnology industrial policy in the context of intensifying US–China technological rivalry, focusing on the relationship between competitiveness, strategic autonomy, and corporate power. The proposed EU Biotech Act seeks to strengthen the sector through regulatory simplification, public financing, strategic projects, and enhanced intellectual property protection. However, its competitiveness-oriented approach obscures the geopolitical and distributional implications of biotechnology policy. The EU’s reluctance to localise production or restrict global interdependencies is driven by the integration of European pharmaceutical multinationals into global value chains and their dependence on US markets and Chinese biotechnology ecosystem. Consequently, strategic autonomy tends to be framed as synonymous with the global profitability of pharmaceutical corporations rather than broader societal resilience. By situating the Biotech Act within debates on intellectual monopoly capitalism, this short reflection questions whether extending intellectual property rights and reducing regulatory barriers will reinforce an increasingly extractive pharmaceutical business model. It ultimately calls for reconsidering the social purpose of EU industrial policy and whether biotechnology sovereignty should prioritise corporate competitiveness or pharmaceuticals as a public good.

articles_hidden.title: Standpoint Theory and the Enactment of the Social Relation of Comradeship through Social Research
articles_hidden.authors: Ioana Cerasella Chis
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper discusses the ethico-political impetus for seeking to establish the social relation of comradeship with socially marginalised research participants of projects concerned with social justice and countering structural oppression. To this end, the paper explores Olufemi O. Táíwò’s (2020) distinction between liberal and constructive approaches to Standpoint Theory, before considering the social relations of allyship and comradeship through the context of a project that examined structural disablement and precarious work in the UK. In light of this analysis, I call on other social researchers to consider the necessity of enacting the social relation of comradeship with socially marginalised participants as a way of affirming mutual recognition, strengthening emancipatory research, and producing socially useful dialogic knowledge.

articles_hidden.title: Developing and Evaluating UTAUT-Informed YouTube-Based Lessons for Grade 11 Oral Communication During Emergency Remote Teaching
articles_hidden.authors: Jo Michael Llamelo
articles_hidden.abstract: This study reports the development and evaluation of YouTube-based lessons for Grade 11 Oral Communication at a private senior high school in the Philippines during emergency remote teaching in Academic Year 2020–2021.
